topics.t: What is accounting? Identify, measure, record, communicate
topics.h: Every single UPI payment at a college canteen leaves a trail. Accounting is the art of turning thousands of such trails into one clear story: did the canteen make money this year?
p: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information about an organisation to the people who need it for decisions.
Identifying: deciding which events are financial transactions worth recording. Buying stock is recorded; the owner's friendly chat with a customer is not.
Measuring: expressing every recorded event in money (₹). Only what can be measured in money enters the books.
Recording: writing transactions in date (chronological) order in books of original entry, then classifying them into accounts and summarising them into statements.
Communicating: presenting the summarised information (profit and loss account, balance sheet, reports) to users in a form they can understand and act on.

ex.q: Arjun runs a mobile-repair shop. Today (i) he bought spare parts for ₹8,000, (ii) a new competitor opened next door, (iii) he paid shop rent ₹5,000. Which events enter his books, and at what value?
st: Ask: does the event change the business's financial position and can it be measured in money?
(i) Purchase of spare parts: yes, measured at ₹8,000.
(ii) A competitor opening: important, but no money value changes hands, so it is not recorded.
ex.a: Events (i) and (iii) are recorded, ₹13,000 in all; event (ii) is not recorded.

topics.rl: Indian Railways handles crores of rupees of ticket sales every day. Its accountants identify each sale, measure it in rupees, record it, and finally communicate the yearly results to Parliament and the public.

rv.summary: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information about a business to users for decisions. Only events that can be measured in money are recorded.
focus: Name the four activities and what each one does
Decide whether an event is a transaction that should be recorded
Find the total amount recorded from a list of events
remember: Identifying → Measuring (in ₹) → Recording (chronological order) → Communicating
After recording: classifying into accounts and summarising into statements
An event is recorded only if it changes the financial position and can be measured in money
traps: Don't record events with no money value, like a competitor opening or a staff member resigning
Recording is not the whole of accounting; it is only one stage

topics.t: Book-keeping, accounting and the information system
topics.h: Book-keeping is like scoring every ball in a cricket match. Accounting is the analyst who studies the scorecard and tells the captain why the team lost.
p: Book-keeping is the recording stage: identifying, measuring, recording and classifying transactions. It is routine and largely clerical.
Accounting begins where book-keeping ends: it summarises, analyses and interprets the recorded data and communicates the results.
Book-keeping is the base of accounting; accounting has a wider scope and needs judgement.
Accounting works as an information system: inputs are transactions; processing is recording, classifying and summarising; outputs are financial statements and reports for decision makers.
Because it communicates the financial results of every kind of enterprise in a common form, accounting is called the language of business.

ex.q: A shop's clerk writes all sales and purchases into books daily. At year-end, a chartered accountant reads the books and tells the owner that profit fell because of rising transport costs. Which part is book-keeping and which is accounting?
st: The clerk's daily recording of transactions = book-keeping.
Analysing the books and explaining why profit fell = analysis and interpretation, which belongs to accounting.
Passing the conclusion to the owner = communicating, also accounting.
ex.a: The clerk does book-keeping; the accountant's analysis, interpretation and communication is accounting.

topics.rl: At a start-up such as a Bengaluru food-delivery firm, software records thousands of orders (book-keeping), while the finance team analyses margins per city to decide where to expand (accounting as an information system).

rv.summary: Book-keeping is the routine recording stage; accounting goes further and summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates. Accounting works as an information system and is called the language of business.
focus: Tell book-keeping tasks apart from accounting tasks
Input, processing and output of the accounting information system
Why accounting is called the language of business
remember: Book-keeping: identify, measure, record, classify
Accounting adds: summarise, analyse, interpret, communicate
Input = transactions; processing = record, classify, summarise; output = statements and reports
traps: Don't call interpretation of results a book-keeping task
Book-keeping is the base of accounting, not the other way round

topics.t: Users of accounting information
topics.h: When a bank like SBI decides whether to lend ₹2 crore to a textile mill in Surat, its credit officer reads one thing first: the mill's financial statements.
p: Internal users work inside the business: owners (is my investment earning?), management (planning, control, decisions) and employees (job security, wages, bonus).
External users are outside the business: investors and potential investors, lenders and banks, suppliers and creditors, government and tax authorities, customers, researchers and the public.
Each user needs different information: lenders need repaying capacity and security; creditors need short-term liquidity; investors need profitability and growth.
Government and tax authorities use accounts to assess tax (income tax, GST) and to frame policy; researchers use them for studies.
Customers want to know that the business will keep supplying goods and honouring warranties.

ex.q: Match the user to the information: (i) Punjab National Bank considering a loan, (ii) workers' union negotiating bonus, (iii) a supplier selling on 30-day credit.
st: (i) A lender wants to know whether the firm can repay principal and pay interest: solvency and repaying capacity.
(ii) Employees want profitability, because bonus and job security depend on profits.
(iii) A trade creditor wants to know whether the firm can pay within a short period: liquidity.
ex.a: Bank: repaying capacity; union: profits for bonus; supplier: short-term liquidity.

topics.rl: Before a company lists on the NSE or BSE, its audited accounts go into the offer document so that lakhs of retail investors can judge its profitability.

rv.summary: Internal users (owners, management, employees) and external users (investors, lenders, suppliers, government, customers, researchers) each use accounts for different needs.
focus: Classify a user as internal or external
Match each user to the information it mainly needs
remember: Internal: owners, management, employees
Lenders → repaying capacity; creditors → short-term liquidity; investors → profitability and growth
Government and tax authorities → tax assessment (income tax, GST) and policy
traps: Don't treat potential investors as internal users; they are external
Suppliers look at short-term liquidity, not long-term growth plans

topics.t: Qualitative characteristics of accounting information
topics.h: A weather forecast is useless if it arrives after the monsoon storm, or if it is wrong. Accounting information has the same test: is it reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable?
p: Reliability: information must be verifiable, faithfully represent what happened, and be free from error and bias. Independent persons using the same method should reach the same figures.
Relevance: information must reach users in time and help them make decisions; it should have predictive value (helps forecast) or feedback value (confirms or corrects earlier expectations).
Understandability: information must be presented clearly so that users with reasonable business knowledge can understand it.
Comparability: users should be able to compare a firm's results over different periods (inter-period) and with other firms (inter-firm). This needs consistent methods and a common format.
These four characteristics decide how useful accounting information is; missing even one reduces its value.

ex.q: A firm changes its method of valuing stock every year without disclosure, so this year's profit cannot be compared with last year's. Which qualitative characteristic is hurt?
st: Ask: can users compare results across periods?
Changing methods each year breaks inter-period comparison.
So comparability is lost (consistency of methods supports comparability).
ex.a: Comparability

topics.rl: RBI asks all banks to publish results in a common format each quarter, so analysts can compare HDFC Bank with Bank of Baroda: comparability in action.

rv.summary: Accounting information is useful when it is reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable. Missing any one of these reduces its value.
focus: Identify which characteristic is hurt in a given situation
Separate features of relevance from those of reliability
Inter-period vs inter-firm comparison
remember: Four characteristics: reliability, relevance, understandability, comparability
Reliability: verifiable, faithful, free from error and bias
Relevance: timely, with predictive or feedback value
traps: Late but accurate information is not unreliable; it loses relevance
Don't mix up inter-period (same firm, different years) with inter-firm (different firms)

topics.t: Objectives, role and limitations of accounting
topics.h: No shopkeeper can remember 10,000 transactions. Accounting is the business's memory, its profit meter and its health report, all rolled into one.
p: Objectives: (1) maintain systematic and complete records of transactions; (2) calculate profit or loss for a period by matching revenues and expenses; (3) show the financial position (assets and liabilities) through a balance sheet; (4) provide information to users for decisions.
Role: accounting is the language of business and a historical record of transactions in date order.
It also reflects current economic reality (how wealthy the business is now), works as an information system and is a service activity that serves decision makers.

Limitations: it ignores non-monetary facts (staff skill, reputation); it records items at historical cost and is affected by changes in price level; it relies on estimates (useful life, bad debts) and on personal judgement in choosing methods.

ex.q: Rohan bought a building in 2005 for ₹40 lakh. Today it could sell for ₹2 crore, yet his balance sheet shows it at cost less depreciation. Which limitation of accounting does this show?
st: The asset is recorded at historical cost, the price paid when acquired.
Its market value has risen because of price-level changes, but books do not show that.
So the balance sheet does not reflect current value.
ex.a: Historical cost and price-level changes make the balance sheet differ from current market values.

topics.rl: An ISRO vendor in Bengaluru may have world-class engineers, but their talent never appears in the balance sheet, because accounting ignores non-monetary facts.

rv.summary: Accounting keeps systematic records, finds profit or loss, shows financial position and informs users. It is limited because it ignores non-money facts, uses historical cost and depends on estimates.
focus: List the four objectives of accounting
Roles: language of business, historical record, current economic reality, information system, service activity
Recognise each limitation from an example
remember: Profit = Revenues − Expenses of the same period
Balance sheet shows financial position on a date
Limitations: non-monetary facts ignored, historical cost, price-level changes, estimates and judgement
traps: Don't confuse the balance sheet (a date) with the profit and loss account (a period)
A balance sheet does not show the current market value of assets

topics.t: Basic terms I: entity, transaction, assets, liabilities, capital
topics.h: Every business, from a pani-puri stall to Reliance, sits on one simple balance: what it owns equals what it owes to outsiders plus what it owes to its owner.
p: Entity: an organisation with a separate identity, like a shop, firm or company. A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth between the business and another party.

Assets: economic resources owned or controlled by the business that will bring future benefit. Non-current assets are held for long-term use (land, building, machinery); current assets are converted to cash within one year or the operating cycle (cash, debtors, stock).

Liabilities: amounts the business owes to outsiders. Non-current liabilities are payable after more than a year (long-term loan); current liabilities are payable within a year (creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft).
Capital: amount invested by the owner. It is the owner's claim on the assets, so Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

ex.q: Neha's boutique has cash ₹30,000, stock ₹70,000, furniture ₹50,000, creditors ₹40,000 and a 3-year bank loan ₹60,000. Find her capital.

topics.rl: A Kochi spice exporter's warehouse (non-current asset), its stock of cardamom (current asset) and its loan from SIDBI (non-current liability) all appear in its balance sheet.

rv.summary: Assets are resources the business owns, liabilities are amounts owed to outsiders, and capital is the owner's claim. Capital = Assets − Liabilities.
focus: Find capital or assets from the given figures
Classify items as current or non-current assets and liabilities
Decide whether an event is a business transaction
remember: Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Current = within one year (cash, debtors, stock; creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft)
Non-current = long-term (land, building, machinery; long-term loan)
traps: Don't add liabilities to assets when finding capital; subtract them
An order placed or a manager appointed is not a transaction yet

topics.t: Basic terms II: revenue, expense, expenditure, profit, gain, discount
topics.h: A sweet shop sells ₹1,00,000 of laddoos in Diwali week, gets a 10% trade discount from its supplier and also sells an old fridge at a profit. Are all these 'profit'? Accounting says no.
p: Sales: amount from selling the goods or services the business deals in. Revenue: amounts from regular operations, including sales, commission, interest, rent and dividends received.

Expense: cost used up in earning revenue during the period (rent, wages, depreciation). Expenditure: spending of money or creating a liability; if benefit lasts beyond the year it is capital expenditure (machinery), if within the year it is revenue expenditure.

Profit: excess of revenues over expenses of a period. Gain: profit from incidental or irregular events, such as selling a fixed asset above book value. Loss: excess of expenses over revenue, or money lost without benefit (fire, theft).

Trade discount: reduction in the list price at the time of sale; it is not recorded in the books. Cash discount: allowed for prompt payment; it is recorded (discount allowed is a loss, discount received is a gain).
Net amount after trade discount = List price × (1 − rate). Cash discount is then calculated on this net amount.

ex.q: Goods with list price ₹50,000 are sold at 10% trade discount and 2% cash discount for immediate payment. How much cash is received?

topics.rl: During the Big Billion Days sale, an online seller offers lower prices on MRP (trade discount) and an extra 'instant bank discount' for paying immediately with a card (similar to a cash discount for prompt payment).

rv.summary: Revenue comes from regular operations, gains from incidental events. Expense is cost used up this period; capital expenditure benefits later years. Trade discount is not recorded but cash discount is.
focus: Calculate net sales after trade discount and cash discount
Tell revenue from gain, and expense from expenditure
Find profit or loss from revenue and expenses
remember: Net amount = List price × (1 − trade discount rate)
Cash discount is calculated on the amount after trade discount
Profit = Revenues − Expenses; loss when expenses are higher
traps: Don't calculate cash discount on the list price
Don't record trade discount in the books
Profit on sale of a fixed asset is a gain, not revenue

topics.t: Basic terms III: voucher, goods, purchases, stock, drawings, debtors, creditors
topics.h: When a kirana owner takes a packet of tea home for the family, that tiny act has a name in accounting, and it reduces his capital.
p: Voucher: documentary evidence supporting a transaction, such as a cash memo, invoice, receipt or salary slip.
Goods: items the business buys and sells as its regular activity. Furniture is goods for a furniture dealer but an asset for a lawyer.

Purchases: goods bought for resale or for production, either for cash or on credit. Stock (inventory): goods unsold on a date. Opening stock is at the start of the period; closing stock is at the end.
Drawings: cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use. Drawings reduce capital.
Debtors: persons or entities who owe money to the business, usually from credit sales. Creditors: persons or entities to whom the business owes money, usually for credit purchases.

ex.q: A cycle dealer starts the year with stock ₹40,000, buys cycles worth ₹1,60,000, and at year-end has stock worth ₹30,000. What is the cost of cycles sold?
st: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock.

topics.rl: A Ludhiana hosiery wholesaler sells to hundreds of retailers on credit. Those retailers are its debtors, and the yarn mills it buys from on credit are its creditors.

rv.summary: Vouchers are evidence of transactions. Goods are bought for resale; purchases may be cash or credit. Drawings reduce capital. Debtors owe the business; creditors are owed by it.
focus: Find cost of goods sold from stock and purchases
Find closing capital after profit and drawings
Tell debtors from creditors and goods from fixed assets
remember: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock
Closing capital = Opening capital + Profit − Drawings
Debtors = Credit sales − Cash received from them
traps: Don't call goods taken by the owner 'sales'; it is drawings
Buying fixed assets is not 'purchases'
Furniture is goods for a furniture dealer but a fixed asset for others

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Why accounting needs a theory base: GAAP
topics.h: Imagine every cricket umpire using his own rules for LBW. Scores would be meaningless. Accounts without common rules would be just as useless.
p: If each accountant used personal rules, statements of different firms, or of the same firm in different years, could not be compared or trusted. A common theory base makes accounts uniform, comparable and reliable.
Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are the rules and guidelines followed in recording and reporting business transactions.
GAAP are known by several names: concepts, conventions, postulates, assumptions and modifying principles.

GAAP are man-made. They evolve over time from experience, usage and reasoning, are accepted by professional bodies (like ICAI) and are shaped by law and regulation. They change when business needs change.

ex.q: Two shoe companies value their closing stock differently and do not say so. An investor compares their profits. What problem arises, and what solves it?
st: Different, undisclosed methods make profits non-comparable: a higher profit may come from the method, not from better performance.
Uniform rules, GAAP, applied consistently and disclosed, solve this.
Then inter-firm and inter-period comparisons become meaningful.
ex.a: Profits cannot be compared fairly; following GAAP brings uniformity and comparability.

topics.rl: When SEBI requires every listed company on the NSE to prepare accounts on common principles, a retail investor in Patna can compare Infosys and Wipro on the same footing.

rv.summary: GAAP are the common rules for recording and reporting transactions. They make accounts uniform, comparable and reliable, and being man-made they change with business needs.
focus: Why a common theory base is needed
Other names for accounting principles
How GAAP evolve and who develops them in India
remember: GAAP = Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
Also called concepts, conventions, postulates, assumptions, modifying principles
GAAP are man-made: experience, usage, ICAI acceptance, law and regulation
traps: GAAP are not fixed natural laws; they change over time
Vouchers are evidence of transactions, not accounting principles

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Concepts I: business entity, money measurement, going concern, accounting period
topics.h: When a café owner in Pune pays her child's school fees from the café's cash, the café's books must not call it a business expense. Why? Because, in accounting, the café is a separate person.
p: Business entity concept: the business is separate from its owner. Only business transactions are recorded; the owner's capital is treated as a liability of the business towards the owner.
Money measurement concept: only transactions that can be expressed in money are recorded. Limitation: the value of the rupee changes over time, yet ₹1 of 2005 and ₹1 of today are added as equal.

Going concern concept: the business is assumed to continue for a long time, with no intention to close down. That is why fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation, not at their sale value, and assets are classified as current and non-current.

Accounting period concept: life of a business is divided into fixed periods, usually one year, to measure results. In India the financial year runs from 1 April to 31 March; listed companies also report quarterly (interim) results.

ex.q: Mr Iyer brings ₹5,00,000 into his business and later pays his home electricity bill of ₹4,000 from business cash. How are these treated in the business books?
st: Business entity concept: the business and Mr Iyer are separate.
₹5,00,000 brought in is capital, a liability of the business towards Mr Iyer.
Home electricity bill is a personal expense, so it is drawings, not a business expense.
ex.a: ₹5,00,000 is capital (owed to the owner); ₹4,000 is drawings.

topics.rl: Every listed Indian company, from Maruti Suzuki to Asian Paints, announces quarterly results: the accounting period concept lets investors track performance without waiting for the company's life to end.

rv.summary: Business entity separates owner and business; money measurement records only money items; going concern assumes the business continues; accounting period splits its life into fixed periods, usually a year.
focus: Identify which of the four concepts applies in a case
Treatment of capital and drawings under business entity
Why fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation
remember: Capital is a liability of the business towards the owner (business entity)
Indian financial year: 1 April to 31 March
Going concern → assets at cost less depreciation, current and non-current split
traps: Don't record the owner's personal expenses as business expenses; they are drawings
Money measurement ignores changes in the value of the rupee

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Concepts II: cost, dual aspect and revenue recognition
topics.h: A Jaipur jeweller buys a machine for ₹2,00,000, pays ₹10,000 freight and ₹15,000 for installation. Is the machine recorded at ₹2,00,000? The cost concept says no.
p: Cost concept: an asset is recorded at its acquisition cost, that is the price paid plus all costs to bring it to working condition (freight, cartage, installation). Later it is shown at cost less depreciation. Limitation: historical cost ignores price changes.
Dual aspect concept: every transaction has two equal effects. This gives the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital, which always holds.
Revenue recognition (realisation) concept: revenue is recognised when the right to receive it arises, i.e. when goods are sold or services rendered, not when cash is received.
Credit sales are therefore revenue on the date of sale; an advance received for goods to be delivered next year is not this year's revenue.

ex.q: A machine is bought for ₹3,00,000, freight paid ₹12,000, installation ₹18,000. Five years later its market value is ₹4,50,000. At what cost is it recorded on purchase?
st: Cost concept: include all costs to bring the asset into use.
The later market value of ₹4,50,000 is ignored.

topics.rl: An airline like IndiGo sells tickets weeks in advance. Under revenue recognition it records the fare as revenue only when the flight actually flies; until then it is a liability.

rv.summary: Assets are recorded at acquisition cost (cost concept), every transaction has two equal effects (dual aspect), and revenue is recognised when earned, not when cash is received.
focus: Find the cost of an asset including freight and installation
Show the two effects of a transaction on the accounting equation
Decide when revenue is recognised (credit sales, advances)
remember: Cost = purchase price + freight/cartage + installation
Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Revenue is recognised when goods are sold or services rendered
traps: Don't include running costs like fuel in an asset's cost
An advance received for future goods is a liability, not revenue
Don't revalue assets to market price under the cost concept

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Concepts III: matching, full disclosure and consistency
topics.h: If you count Diwali-season sales in October but the salesmen's commission for those sales in December, October looks super-profitable and December looks terrible. The matching concept stops that illusion.
p: Matching concept: expenses of a period are matched with the revenues of the same period. Expenses incurred but not paid (outstanding) are added; expenses paid in advance (prepaid) are deducted.

Full disclosure concept: all material facts must be disclosed in the financial statements, including notes and footnotes, e.g. contingent liabilities, market value of investments, method of depreciation. Schedule III of the Companies Act lays down the format.
Consistency concept: the same accounting methods (stock valuation, depreciation) are followed year after year, so results are comparable.
Consistency does not forbid change. A method may change when the law or a standard requires it or it gives a better picture, but the change and its effect must be disclosed.

ex.q: Salaries for March 2026, ₹40,000, were paid on 5 April 2026. In which year's profit and loss account is the expense shown?
st: The salary was earned by staff in March 2026, which helped generate March's revenue.
Matching concept: show it in 2025-26, the year of the revenue.
On 31 March it is shown as outstanding salary, a current liability.
ex.a: In 2025-26, as outstanding salary of ₹40,000.

topics.rl: Annual reports of companies like Larsen & Toubro carry pages of notes that explain contingent liabilities and accounting policies: the full disclosure concept at work.

rv.summary: Matching charges a period's expenses against that period's revenue; full disclosure requires all material facts to be shown; consistency keeps the same methods each year, with any justified change disclosed.
focus: Find the expense for a period with outstanding and prepaid items
Identify matching, full disclosure or consistency in a case
When a change of method is allowed
remember: Expense for the period = amount paid + outstanding − prepaid
Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 gives the format of company statements
A change in method must be disclosed with its effect
traps: Don't charge only the cash paid; include outstanding expenses
Consistency does not mean a method can never change

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Concepts IV: conservatism, materiality, objectivity and case spotting
topics.h: A smart accountant is like a careful trekker in the Himalayas: count no summit before reaching it, but pack for every storm. That is conservatism.
p: Conservatism (prudence): anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses. Examples: closing stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower; provision for doubtful debts.
Conservatism should not be overdone; deliberately understating profit creates secret reserves, which is not allowed.
Materiality: items significant enough to influence users' decisions must be disclosed separately; trivial items (a ₹50 stapler) may be treated as expenses even if they last for years.
Objectivity: transactions must be recorded on the basis of verifiable evidence (invoices, receipts), free from personal bias.

To identify a concept in a case, ask what rule the action follows: separation of owner, money value, continuity, period, cost, two effects, earning, matching, disclosure, sameness, caution, significance or evidence.

ex.q: Closing stock cost ₹1,20,000; its market (realisable) value is ₹1,05,000. At what value is it shown, and why?
st: Compare cost ₹1,20,000 and net realisable value ₹1,05,000.
Conservatism: take the lower, to provide for the expected loss.
ex.a: ₹1,05,000, under the conservatism concept.

topics.rl: Banks regulated by RBI must set aside provisions for loans that may go bad, even before the borrower actually defaults: prudence written into rules.

rv.summary: Conservatism means anticipate no profit but provide for all losses; materiality decides what is significant enough to show separately; objectivity requires verifiable evidence.
focus: Value closing stock at lower of cost and net realisable value
Find the effect on profit of valuing stock correctly
Identify conservatism, materiality or objectivity in a case
remember: Closing stock = cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower
Prudence: anticipate no profit, provide for all possible losses
Excessive conservatism creates secret reserves, which is not allowed
traps: Don't value stock at selling price when it is above cost
Small items like a ₹40 calculator need not be treated as assets

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Systems of accounting: double entry and single entry
topics.h: A big hospital like AIIMS records every rupee twice, once as a debit and once as a credit. A tiny tea stall may just keep a cash diary. Both are 'systems', but only one is complete.
p: Double entry system: both aspects (debit and credit) of every transaction are recorded. It is complete and scientific, its arithmetical accuracy can be checked by a trial balance, and it helps detect fraud.
It is used by companies and most organisations; it needs trained staff and is costlier.
Single entry system: an incomplete system in which mostly personal accounts (debtors, creditors) and the cash book are kept. Nominal and real accounts are usually not maintained.
Single entry is simple and cheap, so small traders use it, but no trial balance can be prepared, true profit is hard to find, and it is not reliable for tax or loans.

ex.q: A small cloth trader keeps only a cash book and a list of customers who owe him. Can he prepare a trial balance? Which system is this?
st: He records only cash and personal accounts.
Nominal and real accounts are missing, so debit and credit totals cannot be matched.
This is single entry (incomplete records); a trial balance cannot be prepared.
ex.a: No trial balance is possible; it is the single entry system.

topics.rl: GST law and lenders such as MUDRA-scheme banks rely on proper books; many small traders in Indian bazaars move from a simple bahi-khata diary to double-entry accounting apps as they grow.

rv.summary: Double entry records both aspects of every transaction and allows a trial balance; single entry is incomplete, keeping mainly cash and personal accounts, so it is cheap but unreliable.
focus: Merits and limits of double entry vs single entry
Which accounts single entry keeps
Why a trial balance needs double entry
remember: Double entry: complete, scientific, trial balance possible, helps detect fraud
Single entry: cash book + personal accounts only; no trial balance
Single entry merit: simple and economical
traps: Don't think single entry shows true profit; it does not
A trial balance cannot be prepared from single entry records

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Basis of accounting: cash basis vs accrual basis
topics.h: A tuition centre in Kota collects fees for April in March. Under one basis, March looks rich. Under the other, the money is not yet earned. Which basis is right?
p: Cash basis: entries are made only when cash is received or paid. Income = cash received; expense = cash paid. Outstanding and prepaid items are ignored.
Accrual basis: revenues are recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, whether or not cash has moved. It follows the matching concept.
Companies must follow the accrual basis under the Companies Act, 2013. Cash basis suits small professionals and non-profit bodies with simple needs.
Profit under cash basis = Cash received from income − Cash paid for expenses. Profit under accrual basis = Income earned − Expenses incurred.

ex.q: In 2025-26 a consultant earned fees of ₹6,00,000 but received only ₹5,20,000. Expenses incurred were ₹2,80,000, of which ₹2,50,000 was paid. Find profit under both bases.
st: The difference arises from unreceived fees ₹80,000 and unpaid expenses ₹30,000.
ex.a: Cash basis ₹2,70,000; accrual basis ₹3,20,000.

topics.rl: Government departments in India have traditionally used cash-based accounts, while companies listed on the BSE must use accrual accounting for a true picture of profit.

rv.summary: Cash basis records income and expenses only when cash is received or paid; accrual basis records them when earned or incurred. Companies must use the accrual basis.
focus: Calculate profit under both bases from the same data
Convert accrual profit to cash profit using outstanding items
Treat advances and outstanding items under each basis
remember: Cash profit = Cash received − Cash paid
Accrual profit = Income earned − Expenses incurred
Companies Act, 2013 requires the accrual basis
traps: Don't include outstanding or prepaid items under cash basis
Income received in advance is not income of the current year under accrual basis

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Accounting standards, Ind AS and IFRS
topics.h: Whether a company's accounts are read in Mumbai, London or Tokyo, investors want them written in the same 'grammar'. Accounting standards are that grammar.
p: Accounting standards are written policy documents issued by an expert body that cover the recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of accounting transactions in financial statements.
In India, the Accounting Standards Board (ASB) of the ICAI, set up in 1977, formulates standards; they become mandatory for companies when notified by the Central Government.
Benefits: uniformity in accounting, better inter-firm comparability, fewer alternative treatments, more disclosure and greater reliability.
Limitations: choosing between alternatives is hard, standards may be rigid, and they cannot override the law.

IFRS are global standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). India chose convergence, not direct adoption: Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) are converged with IFRS and apply in phases to listed and large companies (first phase from 1 April 2016).

ex.q: An Indian software company with branches in 40 countries prepares accounts under Ind AS. Why does this help a foreign investor?
st: Ind AS are converged with IFRS, the global standards.
So the company's statements are broadly comparable with those of foreign companies using IFRS.
The investor can compare without re-working the numbers.
ex.a: Global comparability, because Ind AS are converged with IFRS.

topics.rl: When large Indian companies moved to Ind AS from 2016 onwards, foreign institutional investors found it easier to compare them with global peers.

rv.summary: Accounting standards are expert rules on recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure. In India the ASB of ICAI (1977) formulates them, and Ind AS are converged with the global IFRS issued by IASB.
focus: Benefits and limitations of accounting standards
Who issues Indian standards and who issues IFRS
India's convergence approach (Ind AS)
remember: ASB of ICAI, set up in 1977; standards mandatory when notified by the Central Government
IFRS are issued by IASB
Ind AS converged with IFRS; first phase from 1 April 2016
traps: India did not adopt IFRS word for word; it converged
Accounting standards cannot override the law

topics.ch: Part I: Theory Base of Accounting
topics.t: Goods and Services Tax (GST): basics and calculation
topics.h: Before 1 July 2017, a truck carrying biscuits from Delhi to Chennai could face several different state taxes. GST replaced that tangle with 'one nation, one tax'.
p: GST is a comprehensive, destination-based indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services. It came into force on 1 July 2017 and replaced many indirect taxes such as central excise duty (on most goods), VAT and service tax.
Intra-state supply (seller and buyer in the same state): CGST (to the Centre) + SGST (to the State), each at half the total rate. In union territories without a legislature, UTGST replaces SGST.
Inter-state supply (different states): IGST at the full rate, collected by the Centre.
Input tax credit (ITC): GST paid on purchases is set off against GST collected on sales, so tax is paid only on value added. This removes the cascading (tax-on-tax) effect.
Features and advantages: uniform rates and procedures, online compliance through the GST Network (GSTN), wider tax base, transparency and ease of doing business.

ex.q: A Lucknow trader sells goods worth ₹50,000 (a) to a buyer in Kanpur, (b) to a buyer in Patna. GST rate is 18%. Compute the tax.
st: Lucknow and Kanpur are both in Uttar Pradesh: intra-state. CGST 9% = ₹4,500 and SGST 9% = ₹4,500.
Total tax is ₹9,000 in both cases; only the components differ.

topics.rl: GST invoices generated across India flow through the GST Network portal, so a dealer in Guwahati can claim input tax credit for tax his supplier in Surat has paid.

rv.summary: GST is a destination-based indirect tax on supply, in force from 1 July 2017. Intra-state supply bears CGST + SGST (half each); inter-state supply bears IGST; input tax credit removes tax on tax.
focus: Decide intra-state or inter-state and pick CGST/SGST or IGST
Calculate GST, invoice value and net GST payable after ITC
Features and advantages of GST
remember: Intra-state: CGST + SGST, each half the rate; inter-state: IGST at full rate
GST payable = Output GST − Input tax credit
UTGST replaces SGST in UTs without a legislature
traps: Don't charge CGST + SGST on a sale to another state
Don't charge the full rate as CGST; CGST is only half

topics.t: Business transactions and source documents
topics.h: Every entry in the books of a company like Amul begins with a piece of paper or a digital slip: a bill, a receipt, a cheque. No paper, no entry.
p: A business transaction is an exchange of economic value (money or money's worth) between the business and another party. Every transaction has a two-fold effect.
A source document is the written evidence of a transaction, prepared at the time it happens. It is the basis for recording.
Common source documents: cash memo (cash sale), invoice or bill (credit sale), receipt (cash received), pay-in-slip (cash or cheque deposited in bank), cheque (order to a bank to pay), salary slip.

Debit note: sent by the buyer to the seller when goods are returned, informing that the seller's account has been debited. Credit note: sent by the seller to the buyer for goods returned, informing that the buyer's account has been credited.

ex.q: Riya returns damaged goods worth ₹4,000 to her supplier Mehta Traders. Which document does she send, and which does Mehta Traders send her?
st: Riya, the buyer, returns goods and debits the supplier's account: she sends a debit note.
Mehta Traders, the seller, accepts the return and credits Riya's account: it sends a credit note.
ex.a: Riya sends a debit note; Mehta Traders sends a credit note.

topics.rl: When you deposit cash at a bank branch, you fill a pay-in-slip; its counterfoil, stamped by the cashier, is the source document for your entry.

rv.summary: A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth with a two-fold effect. Source documents such as cash memos, invoices, receipts, pay-in-slips, cheques and debit/credit notes are the evidence for recording it.
focus: Match each source document to its transaction
Who sends a debit note and who sends a credit note
What makes an event a business transaction
remember: Cash memo → cash sale; invoice → credit sale; pay-in-slip → bank deposit
Debit note: buyer → seller for goods returned
Credit note: seller → buyer for goods returned
traps: Don't mix up debit note and credit note: the buyer sends the debit note
A cash memo is not used for credit sales

topics.t: Accounting vouchers: types and preparation
topics.h: In a large firm, no accountant writes an entry from memory. A voucher, signed and numbered, travels with every transaction like a boarding pass.
p: An accounting voucher is prepared from source documents. It records the accounts to be debited and credited, and is authorised by a responsible person.
Contents: name of firm, voucher number, date, accounts debited and credited with amounts, narration (brief explanation), and signatures of the preparer and the authoriser.

Cash vouchers: debit voucher (for cash payment) and credit voucher (for cash receipt). Non-cash or transfer (journal) vouchers are used for transactions without cash, e.g. credit purchases or depreciation.
Transaction voucher: one debit and one credit. Compound voucher: one debit with several credits, or one credit with several debits. Complex voucher: several debits and several credits.

ex.q: Rent ₹15,000 is paid in cash. Which voucher is prepared, and what does it show?
st: Cash goes out, so a cash payment voucher, i.e. a debit voucher, is prepared.
Account debited: Rent A/c ₹15,000; account credited: Cash A/c ₹15,000.
Narration: 'Being rent paid for the month'; signed by the preparer and authorised by the manager.
ex.a: A debit voucher: Dr Rent ₹15,000 / Cr Cash ₹15,000.

topics.rl: Government offices in India pass every payment through a numbered voucher signed by the drawing and disbursing officer, so auditors from the CAG can trace each rupee.

rv.summary: Accounting vouchers are prepared from source documents and show the accounts debited and credited, with narration and authorisation. They are cash (debit/credit) or transfer vouchers, and transaction, compound or complex in form.
focus: Choose debit, credit or transfer voucher for a transaction
Classify a voucher as transaction, compound or complex
Contents of a voucher
remember: Debit voucher = cash payment; credit voucher = cash receipt; transfer voucher = no cash
Transaction: 1 Dr + 1 Cr; compound: 1 on one side, many on the other
Complex: several debits and several credits
traps: Don't call a cash receipt voucher a debit voucher; it is a credit voucher
One debit with two credits is compound, not complex

topics.t: The accounting equation: A = L + C
topics.h: No matter what happens in a business, this equation never breaks: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Every transaction is like a see-saw that stays level.
p: Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Variants: Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Liabilities = Assets − Capital.
Every transaction changes at least two items so that the equation still balances.

Possible effects: both sides increase (goods bought on credit); both sides decrease (creditor paid); one asset up and another down (furniture bought for cash); one liability up and another down (creditor paid by a bill payable).
A tabular analysis lists each transaction with its effect on each asset, liability and capital; totals of both sides match after every line.

ex.q: Start: cash ₹1,00,000 = capital ₹1,00,000. (1) Goods bought on credit ₹30,000. (2) Furniture bought for cash ₹20,000. Show the equation after both.
st: (2) Furniture +20,000, cash −20,000: assets change between themselves.

topics.rl: Even a startup in Bengaluru raising ₹10 crore from investors records it as cash up and capital up by the same ₹10 crore, keeping the equation balanced.

rv.summary: The accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Capital always balances because every transaction has two equal effects on its items.
focus: Find the missing item (assets, liabilities or capital)
Show the effect of a transaction on both sides
Build a tabular analysis of a series of transactions
remember: Assets = Liabilities + Capital
Capital = Assets − Liabilities; Liabilities = Assets − Capital
Effects: both sides up, both down, asset-asset swap, liability-liability swap
traps: Buying an asset for cash does not change the totals
A bank loan raises assets and liabilities, not capital

topics.t: Accounting equation: revenue, expenses, drawings and full numericals
topics.h: Sell goods costing ₹10,000 for ₹14,000 and something magical happens in the equation: capital grows by exactly ₹4,000.
p: Revenue and profit increase capital; expenses, losses and drawings reduce capital.
Sale of goods at a profit: cash or debtors rise by the sale price, stock falls by the cost, and capital rises by the profit.
Expenses paid in cash (rent, salary): cash falls and capital falls. Outstanding expenses: liabilities rise and capital falls.
Drawings in cash or goods: assets fall and capital falls.
After a series of transactions, the final balances of the equation give the balance sheet.

ex.q: Capital ₹1,00,000 in cash. (1) Bought goods ₹40,000 cash. (2) Sold goods costing ₹30,000 for ₹45,000 on credit. (3) Paid rent ₹5,000. (4) Withdrew ₹3,000 cash. Find the final capital.
st: Check: cash 52,000 + stock 10,000 + debtors 45,000 = ₹1,07,000 = capital (no liabilities).

topics.rl: A food-truck owner at Juhu beach sees capital rise with every profitable evening and fall every time she takes cash home: the equation tracks her real stake.

rv.summary: Revenues and profits increase capital; expenses, losses and drawings reduce it. A sale at profit changes stock by cost and cash or debtors by sale price, with the profit added to capital.
focus: Effect of sale at profit, expenses, outstanding expenses and drawings
Find closing capital after profit, drawings and additional capital
Find total assets after a series of transactions
remember: Closing capital = Opening capital + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings
Sale at profit: capital rises by (Sale price − Cost)
Outstanding expense: liabilities up, capital down
traps: An outstanding expense still affects the equation even though no cash is paid
Don't add the whole sale price to capital; only the profit

topics.t: Debit, credit and the rules for each type of account
topics.h: Debit is not 'bad' and credit is not 'good'. In accounting, they simply mean left and right, like the two sides of a cricket pitch.
p: An account is a summarised record of all transactions about one item (Cash A/c, Rent A/c). A T-account has the debit side on the left and the credit side on the right.
Assets and expenses/losses: increase is debited, decrease is credited.
Liabilities, capital and revenues/gains: increase is credited, decrease is debited.
Drawings reduce capital, so drawings are debited.
To find the entry: identify the two accounts, decide each one's type, decide increase or decrease, and apply the rule.

ex.q: Paid salary ₹20,000 by cheque. Which account is debited and which credited?
st: Accounts affected: Salary A/c and Bank A/c.
Salary is an expense and it increases: debit Salary.
Bank is an asset and it decreases: credit Bank.
ex.a: Dr Salary ₹20,000 / Cr Bank ₹20,000

topics.rl: When Indian Railways buys a new locomotive on credit, its accountants debit the Locomotive (asset increases) and credit the supplier (liability increases).

rv.summary: Assets and expenses increase on the debit side; liabilities, capital and revenues increase on the credit side. Find the two accounts, their type and direction, then apply the rule.
focus: Pass debit and credit for common transactions
Know which accounts normally have debit or credit balances
Drawings and sale of fixed assets
remember: Assets, expenses, losses, drawings: increase = debit
Liabilities, capital, revenues, gains: increase = credit
Sale of a fixed asset: Dr Cash / Cr Asset A/c, not Sales
traps: Don't credit Sales when a fixed asset is sold
Repaying a loan debits the loan, it does not credit it

topics.t: Traditional classification and the golden rules
topics.h: Long before computers, Indian munims kept the bahi-khata with three golden rules. They still give the same answers as the modern equation approach.
p: Traditional classification: personal accounts (persons, firms, companies, banks, capital, drawings); real accounts (assets such as cash, furniture, goodwill); nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains).
Personal account: debit the receiver, credit the giver.
Real account: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.
Nominal account: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains.
Capital and drawings are personal accounts of the owner. Outstanding and prepaid expense accounts are representative personal accounts.

ex.q: Cash sales ₹15,000. Apply the golden rules.
st: Sales is an income: credit Sales.
ex.a: Dr Cash ₹15,000 / Cr Sales ₹15,000

topics.rl: An old Marwari firm's munim and a modern ERP system at Infosys will both debit Rent and credit Cash when rent is paid: two methods, one answer.

rv.summary: Accounts are personal, real or nominal. Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver. Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out. Nominal: debit expenses and losses, credit incomes and gains.
focus: Classify an account as personal, real or nominal
Apply the golden rules to pass an entry
Representative personal accounts
remember: Personal: debit the receiver, credit the giver
Real: debit what comes in, credit what goes out
Nominal: debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains
traps: Bank and capital accounts are personal, not real
Outstanding salary is representative personal, not nominal
Credit purchase of furniture is not 'Purchases'

topics.t: The journal: format, simple and compound entries
topics.h: The journal is the diary of a business: every transaction enters it first, date by date, before going anywhere else. That's why it's called the book of original entry.
p: Journal: the book of original (prime) entry where transactions are first recorded in chronological order. Recording in it is called journalising.
Format: Date | Particulars (debit account with 'Dr', credit account prefixed with 'To', then narration in brackets) | L.F. (ledger folio) | Debit amount (₹) | Credit amount (₹).
Simple entry: one debit and one credit. Compound entry: more than one debit or more than one credit, e.g. payment with discount.

Typical entries: Capital: Dr Cash / Cr Capital. Cash purchases: Dr Purchases / Cr Cash. Credit sales: Dr Debtor / Cr Sales. Purchases returned: Dr Creditor / Cr Purchases Return. Sales returned: Dr Sales Return / Cr Debtor.
Payment with discount: Dr Creditor (full amount) / Cr Cash (amount paid) / Cr Discount Received (discount).

ex.q: Paid ₹19,600 to Sohan in full settlement of ₹20,000 owed to him. Journalise.
st: Sohan's liability of ₹20,000 is fully cleared: debit Sohan ₹20,000.
Discount received = 20,000 − 19,600 = ₹400: credit Discount Received (a gain).
ex.a: Dr Sohan ₹20,000 / Cr Cash ₹19,600 / Cr Discount Received ₹400

topics.rl: Every UPI transfer you make generates a dated record on the bank's server, the digital cousin of a journal entry.

rv.summary: The journal is the book of original entry where transactions are recorded date-wise with Dr, To and a narration. Entries are simple (one debit, one credit) or compound (more than one on a side).
focus: Journal format and its columns
Pass entries for capital, purchases, sales, returns and settlement with discount
remember: Columns: Date | Particulars | L.F. | Debit ₹ | Credit ₹
Payment with discount: Dr Creditor (full) / Cr Cash / Cr Discount Received
Receipt with discount: Dr Cash, Dr Discount Allowed / Cr Debtor (full)
traps: Don't credit the debtor with only the cash received; credit the full amount
Discount allowed is debited; discount received is credited

topics.t: Special journal entries: drawings of goods, charity, samples, losses
topics.h: A sweet shop gives free laddoos to customers as samples, donates boxes to an orphanage on Independence Day, and the owner takes some home for family. Each one is a different entry.
p: Goods taken by the owner for personal use: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases (at cost).
Goods given as charity: Dr Charity / Cr Purchases (at cost).
Goods distributed as free samples: Dr Advertisement / Cr Purchases (at cost).

Goods lost by fire or theft: Dr Loss by Fire (or Loss by Theft) / Cr Purchases. If insured and a claim is admitted: Dr Insurance Claim (amount admitted), Dr Loss by Fire (balance) / Cr Purchases (cost).
Purchases is credited because these goods were bought for sale but will never be sold; the purchases figure is reduced.

ex.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 were destroyed by fire. The insurance company admitted a claim of ₹35,000. Journalise.
st: Total cost of goods lost = ₹50,000: credit Purchases.
Claim admitted ₹35,000: debit Insurance Claim (an asset, receivable).
Loss not covered = 50,000 − 35,000 = ₹15,000: debit Loss by Fire.
ex.a: Dr Insurance Claim ₹35,000, Dr Loss by Fire ₹15,000 / Cr Purchases ₹50,000

topics.rl: During monsoon floods in Assam, many shops lose stock. Those insured record an insurance claim; the rest record the full loss by flood.

rv.summary: Goods taken for personal use, given as charity, distributed as samples or lost by fire or theft are recorded at cost and Purchases is credited, because they will never be sold.
focus: Pass entries for drawings of goods, charity, samples and losses
Split a fire loss between insurance claim and loss
remember: Drawings: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases (at cost)
Samples: Dr Advertisement / Cr Purchases; charity: Dr Charity / Cr Purchases
Fire with claim: Dr Insurance Claim, Dr Loss by Fire / Cr Purchases
traps: Don't record these goods at selling price
Don't credit Sales or Cash; credit Purchases
Loss by fire = cost of goods − claim admitted

topics.t: Journal entries with GST and set-off of input tax credit
topics.h: A Delhi gadget dealer pays GST on every purchase and collects GST on every sale. At month-end, she pays the government only the difference. Here is how that shows in the journal.
p: Purchase within the state: Dr Purchases, Dr Input CGST, Dr Input SGST / Cr Supplier (or Cash). Inter-state purchase: Dr Purchases, Dr Input IGST / Cr Supplier.
Sale within the state: Dr Customer (or Cash) / Cr Sales, Cr Output CGST, Cr Output SGST. Inter-state sale: Cr Output IGST.
GST paid on expenses (e.g. rent, telephone) is also input tax: Dr Expense, Dr Input CGST, Dr Input SGST / Cr Bank.

Set-off: input IGST is used first against output IGST, then against CGST and SGST. Input CGST is used against output CGST, then IGST. Input SGST is used against output SGST, then IGST. CGST cannot be set off against SGST or vice versa.
Set-off entry: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST (and similarly for SGST). Balance paid: Dr Output CGST, Dr Output SGST / Cr Bank.

ex.q: Within Maharashtra, Asha buys goods ₹1,00,000 and sells them for ₹1,50,000; GST 18%. Find CGST payable after set-off and give the set-off entry.
st: Set-off: Dr Output CGST ₹9,000 / Cr Input CGST ₹9,000 (same for SGST).
ex.a: CGST payable ₹4,500 (and SGST ₹4,500); set-off: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST ₹9,000.

topics.rl: A furniture maker in Jodhpur claims input tax credit on the wood and polish he buys, so his customers in Mumbai do not pay tax on tax.

rv.summary: GST on purchases is debited as input tax (an asset); GST on sales is credited as output tax (a liability). Input credit is set off against output tax by the set-off rules, and the balance is paid.
focus: Pass entries for intra-state and inter-state purchases and sales with GST
Apply set-off rules and find tax payable
Set-off entry and payment entry
remember: Set-off entry: Dr Output CGST / Cr Input CGST (same for SGST)
Input IGST is used first against output IGST, then against CGST and SGST
CGST and SGST cannot be set off against each other
traps: Don't debit 'Output' tax on purchases; use Input
Don't use CGST credit to pay SGST

topics.t: The ledger: format, utility and classification of accounts
topics.h: The journal tells you what happened on 12 June. The ledger tells you how much the business owes Gupta Traders today. Different questions, different books.
p: The ledger is the principal book of accounts. It contains all accounts (cash, debtors, sales, rent and so on), each on a separate page or folio.
Format of a ledger account: debit side (left): Date, Particulars, J.F., Amount; credit side (right): Date, Particulars, J.F., Amount.
Utility: it shows the net position of each account, such as total sales, total expenses, amount owed by each debtor and to each creditor, and its balances are used to prepare the trial balance.

Journal vs ledger: the journal is the book of original entry, records chronologically, and is the basis of posting; the ledger is the principal book, records analytically by accounts, and is the basis of the trial balance.
Permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) are balanced and carried forward; temporary accounts (revenues, expenses) are closed by transfer to the trading and profit and loss account.

ex.q: Classify as permanent or temporary: Machinery, Wages, Creditors, Commission received, Capital.
st: Permanent accounts appear in the balance sheet and continue to the next year: Machinery, Creditors, Capital.
Temporary accounts are closed at year-end to the P&L or trading account: Wages, Commission received.
ex.a: Permanent: Machinery, Creditors, Capital; temporary: Wages, Commission received.

topics.rl: Your bank passbook is a copy of your account in the bank's ledger: every deposit and withdrawal, with a running balance.

rv.summary: The ledger is the principal book holding every account on a separate folio. Permanent accounts are carried forward; temporary (revenue and expense) accounts are closed to the trading and P&L account.
focus: Ledger account format
Journal vs ledger
Classify accounts as permanent or temporary
remember: Ledger columns each side: Date | Particulars | J.F. | Amount
Journal: chronological, original entry; ledger: analytical, principal book
Permanent: assets, liabilities, capital; temporary: revenues, expenses
traps: The trial balance is prepared from the ledger, not the journal
Don't carry forward revenue or expense accounts

topics.t: Posting from the journal and balancing ledger accounts
topics.h: Posting is like delivering letters: each journal entry has two addresses, the account debited and the account credited, and each must receive its copy.
p: Posting is transferring journal entries to ledger accounts. In the account debited, write the entry on the debit side as 'To [name of the account credited]'. In the account credited, write it on the credit side as 'By [name of the account debited]'.
Compound entries: each debit and each credit is posted separately. In each account, the other side's accounts are named (for one-to-many entries, each counter account is named with its own amount).
Cross references: L.F. in the journal shows the ledger page; J.F. in the ledger shows the journal page. They prove the posting is done and allow tracing.
Balancing: total both sides, put the difference on the smaller side as 'By/To Balance c/d', and bring it down on the opposite side as 'To/By Balance b/d'.

ex.q: Entry: Dr Furniture ₹30,000 / Cr Cash ₹30,000. How is it posted?
st: Write the ledger page in the journal's L.F. column and the journal page in each account's J.F. column.
ex.a: Furniture A/c Dr side: To Cash ₹30,000; Cash A/c Cr side: By Furniture ₹30,000.

topics.rl: When a Flipkart customer pays by UPI, the system 'posts' the receipt to the customer's account and to the bank account at once: automated posting.

rv.summary: Posting moves journal entries to ledger accounts: 'To' the credited account on the debit side, 'By' the debited account on the credit side. Balancing puts the difference on the smaller side as Balance c/d.
focus: Post simple and compound entries to the right side
Balance an account and state the nature of the balance
Use of L.F. and J.F.
remember: Debit side: 'To [account credited]'; credit side: 'By [account debited]'
Balance c/d goes on the smaller side; Balance b/d on the opposite side
L.F. in journal = ledger page; J.F. in ledger = journal page
traps: Don't write the account's own name in its own account
Debit side bigger means a debit balance, but c/d is written on the credit side

topics.t: The cash book and the simple (single column) cash book
topics.h: A busy dhaba in Murthal handles hundreds of cash bills a day. Writing a journal entry for each would take forever. The cash book does the job in one line each.
p: The cash book records all cash receipts and cash payments. It is a book of original entry and, at the same time, it is the cash account of the ledger, so no separate cash account is kept.
Simple (single column) cash book: debit side (left) for receipts, credit side (right) for payments. Columns on each side: Date, Particulars, L.F. (or R.No./V.No.), Amount.
Receipts are entered as 'To [account from which cash came]'; payments as 'By [account for which cash was paid]'.
It begins with the opening cash balance on the debit side ('To Balance b/d').
Credit transactions are never entered in the cash book; only cash ones are.

ex.q: Cash in hand 1 April ₹20,000. Received from Ravi ₹15,000; paid wages ₹6,000; cash sales ₹9,000; paid rent ₹8,000. Find the closing cash balance.
st: Balance = 44,000 − 14,000 = ₹30,000, written as 'By Balance c/d' on the credit side.
ex.a: ₹30,000 (debit balance)

topics.rl: The canteen at a government office in Lucknow keeps one simple cash book: what came in from meal tokens, what went out for vegetables and gas.

rv.summary: The cash book records all cash receipts (debit side, 'To') and cash payments (credit side, 'By'). It is both a book of original entry and the cash account, and credit transactions never enter it.
focus: Find the closing cash balance
Write receipts and payments on the correct side with To/By
Which transactions do not enter the cash book
remember: Closing balance = Opening + Receipts − Payments
Debit side: receipts, 'To …'; credit side: payments, 'By …'
Opening balance: 'To Balance b/d'; closing balance: 'By Balance c/d'
traps: Don't enter credit sales or credit purchases in the cash book
Don't keep a separate cash account in the ledger as well

topics.t: Double column cash book, cheques and contra entries
topics.h: Most Indian businesses today hold money in two places: the cash drawer and the bank. A double column cash book tracks both side by side.
p: The double column cash book has two amount columns on each side: Cash and Bank. It replaces both the cash account and the bank account in the ledger.
Cheques received (and deposited the same day) go in the bank column of the debit side; cheques issued go in the bank column of the credit side.

Contra entry: a transaction between cash and bank, recorded on both sides of the cash book and marked 'C' in the L.F. column. Cash deposited into bank: debit bank column 'To Cash', credit cash column 'By Bank'.
Cash withdrawn from bank for office use: debit cash column 'To Bank', credit bank column 'By Cash'.
Contra entries are not posted to the ledger, because both aspects are already in the cash book.

ex.q: Cash of ₹25,000 is deposited into the bank. How is it recorded in a double column cash book?
st: Bank balance rises: debit side, bank column, 'To Cash ₹25,000', L.F. 'C'.
Cash balance falls: credit side, cash column, 'By Bank ₹25,000', L.F. 'C'.
No posting to the ledger is needed.
ex.a: Dr side bank column 'To Cash ₹25,000' (C) and Cr side cash column 'By Bank ₹25,000' (C).

topics.rl: A chemist in Indore deposits the day's takings at the bank every evening. In her double column cash book, that is a contra entry every single day.

rv.summary: A double column cash book has cash and bank columns on each side, replacing both accounts in the ledger. Transfers between cash and bank are contra entries, marked 'C' and not posted.
focus: Record cheques received, cheques issued and bank charges
Record cash deposited and cash withdrawn as contra entries
Find new cash and bank balances after transfers
remember: Cash deposited: Dr bank col 'To Cash' / Cr cash col 'By Bank' (C)
Cash withdrawn: Dr cash col 'To Bank' / Cr bank col 'By Cash' (C)
Contra entries are not posted to the ledger
traps: Don't record cheques deposited the same day in the cash column
Bank charges are not a contra entry; only cash–bank transfers are

topics.t: Balancing and posting the cash book; bank overdraft
topics.h: You can never have negative cash in your wallet, but you can owe money to your bank. That single fact explains the trickiest rule of the cash book.
p: Balancing: each column (cash and bank) is totalled separately; the difference is written as 'By Balance c/d' on the smaller side and brought down as 'To Balance b/d'.
The cash column can never show a credit balance, because payments cannot exceed cash available.
The bank column may show a credit balance: that means a bank overdraft, an amount owed to the bank (written as 'To Balance c/d' on the debit side and brought down on the credit side).
Posting: accounts on the debit side of the cash book are credited in the ledger ('By Cash' or 'By Bank'); accounts on the credit side are debited in the ledger ('To Cash' or 'To Bank').
Discount columns (where kept) are memorandum columns: their totals are posted to Discount Allowed (debit) and Discount Received (credit) accounts.

ex.q: Bank column totals: debit side ₹60,000, credit side ₹75,000. What is the balance and what does it mean?
st: The bank has paid ₹15,000 more than the deposits: an overdraft.
Write 'To Balance c/d ₹15,000' on the debit side, bring down 'By Balance b/d ₹15,000' on the credit side.
ex.a: Overdraft (credit balance) of ₹15,000.

topics.rl: Many small traders in Surat's textile markets run a bank overdraft facility during the wedding season, and their cash book's bank column shows a credit balance.

rv.summary: Each cash book column is balanced separately. The cash column can never have a credit balance; a credit balance in the bank column is an overdraft. Debit-side items are credited in the ledger and credit-side items debited.
focus: Balance cash and bank columns and spot an overdraft
Post cash book items to ledger accounts correctly
Spot an impossible cash balance
remember: Cash column: always debit balance or nil
Bank column credit balance = bank overdraft
Cash book Dr side → ledger 'By Cash/Bank'; Cr side → ledger 'To Cash/Bank'
traps: There is no such thing as a cash overdraft; a credit cash balance means an error
Don't post a debit-side item to the debit of the ledger account

topics.t: Petty cash book and the imprest system
topics.h: The head cashier of a big company shouldn't spend her day paying ₹40 for courier and ₹60 for tea. That job goes to the petty cashier.
p: Petty cash book records small, recurring payments such as postage, stationery, conveyance, cartage and refreshments, kept by a petty cashier.
Advantages: saves the main cashier's time, keeps small payments under control, and allows totals to be posted instead of each item.

Imprest system: the petty cashier is given a fixed amount (imprest) at the start of a period. At the end, the main cashier reimburses exactly the amount spent, so the petty cashier again starts with the full imprest.
Imprest advantages: easy checking, fixed responsibility, limits misuse, and regular reimbursement keeps records up to date.
Analytical petty cash book: separate columns for each expense head. At the end, column totals are posted to the debit of the related expense accounts.

ex.q: Imprest ₹5,000. During the week: postage ₹600, stationery ₹1,100, conveyance ₹900, tea ₹450. How much is reimbursed, and what is the balance after reimbursement?
ex.a: Reimbursement ₹3,050; balance after reimbursement ₹5,000.

topics.rl: At a busy AIIMS department office, a petty cash float covers courier fees and photocopies, topped up every month under the imprest system.

rv.summary: The petty cash book records small recurring payments. Under the imprest system the petty cashier gets a fixed amount and is reimbursed exactly what she spent, so she starts each period with the full imprest.
focus: Find the reimbursement and balances under the imprest system
Which payments belong in petty cash
Posting of analytical column totals
remember: Reimbursement = Amount spent = Imprest − Balance left
Balance after reimbursement = Imprest
Each expense column total is debited to its expense account
traps: Don't reimburse the full imprest; reimburse only what was spent
Large payments like salaries do not go through petty cash

topics.t: Purchases book and purchases return book (with GST)
topics.h: A Ludhiana bicycle maker buys parts from 50 suppliers on credit every month. One page in the purchases book replaces 50 journal entries.
p: Purchases book (purchases journal) records only credit purchases of goods. Cash purchases go to the cash book; credit purchase of assets goes to the journal proper.

Columns: Date, Invoice No., Name of supplier (Particulars), L.F., Details, Amount. Trade discount is deducted in the details column; only the net amount is recorded. With GST, input CGST and SGST (or IGST) columns or lines are added.
Posting: each supplier's account is credited with the invoice total; the periodic total is debited to Purchases A/c, and GST totals to Input CGST/SGST (or IGST) accounts.
Purchases return book (return outwards book) records goods returned to suppliers out of credit purchases; the source document is the debit note.
Posting the return book: each supplier is debited; the total is credited to Purchases Return A/c, and the GST on returns is credited to the input tax accounts (reversing the credit).

ex.q: Bought on credit from Kapoor Traders 50 chairs at ₹1,000 each, trade discount 10%, CGST 9% and SGST 9%. What is entered in the purchases book?
ex.a: Net purchases ₹45,000 + CGST ₹4,050 + SGST ₹4,050 = ₹53,100

topics.rl: Large retailers such as DMart record thousands of supplier invoices in their purchase registers each week, with GST columns that later feed their GST returns.

rv.summary: The purchases book records only credit purchases of goods at net amount after trade discount, with input GST. The purchases return book records goods returned to suppliers, supported by debit notes.
focus: Calculate net amount and GST to enter in the purchases book
Post supplier accounts and book totals
Entries for purchase returns with GST
remember: Supplier credited = Net amount (after trade discount) + GST
Total of purchases book → debit Purchases A/c; GST → debit Input CGST/SGST/IGST
Returns: Dr Supplier / Cr Purchases Return, Cr Input GST
traps: Don't record cash purchases or credit purchase of assets in the purchases book
Calculate GST on the amount after trade discount

topics.t: Sales book and sales return book (with GST)
topics.h: A Jaipur block-print exporter sells on credit to boutiques all over India. Each invoice is one line in the sales book, and each return is one line in the sales return book.
p: Sales book (sales journal) records only credit sales of goods. The source document is the sales invoice (outward invoice).
Trade discount is deducted in the book; output CGST and SGST (intra-state) or IGST (inter-state) are added.
Posting: each customer's account is debited with the invoice total; the sales total is credited to Sales A/c and the GST totals are credited to Output CGST/SGST/IGST accounts.
Sales return book (return inwards book) records goods returned by customers out of credit sales. The source document is the credit note issued to the customer.
Posting: each customer is credited; the total is debited to Sales Return A/c, and the related output GST accounts are debited.

ex.q: Sold on credit to Meera Boutique (Delhi) from Jaipur: 40 kurtis at ₹800 each, trade discount 5%, IGST 5%. What amount is debited to Meera Boutique?
st: Rajasthan to Delhi is inter-state: IGST 5% = ₹1,520.

topics.rl: E-commerce sellers on platforms like Meesho process thousands of returns weekly; each return triggers a credit note and a line in the sales return register.

rv.summary: The sales book records only credit sales of goods, at net amount after trade discount plus output GST. The sales return book records goods returned by customers, supported by credit notes.
focus: Calculate the amount debited to a customer including GST
Post sales book and sales return book totals
Intra-state vs inter-state output tax
remember: Customer debited = Net sales + Output GST
Sales total → credit Sales A/c; GST → credit Output CGST/SGST/IGST
Returns: Dr Sales Return, Dr Output GST / Cr Customer
traps: Don't record sale of old assets in the sales book
The sales return book uses credit notes, not debit notes

topics.t: Journal proper and advantages of special purpose books
topics.h: Special books handle the daily rush, but some transactions are rare or unusual. They go to the 'leftover' book, the journal proper.
p: Journal proper records transactions that do not fit any special book: opening entries, closing entries, adjustment entries, rectification entries and transfer entries.
It also records credit purchase or sale of assets, bad debts written off, goods withdrawn by the owner, goods lost by fire or theft, and other rare transactions.
Special purpose books: cash book, purchases book, purchases return book, sales book and sales return book.
Advantages of sub-dividing the journal: division of work, specialisation and efficiency, saving of time (totals are posted), easy reference, easier checking and better internal control.

ex.q: Which book records each? (a) Bad debts written off ₹2,000, (b) Credit purchase of machinery, (c) Cash sales.
st: (a) Bad debts are an adjustment, no special book fits: journal proper.
(b) Credit purchase of an asset, not goods: journal proper.
ex.a: (a) Journal proper, (b) journal proper, (c) cash book.

topics.rl: A cement company's accounts team might have one clerk for the sales register, another for purchases and a third for the cash book, with the senior accountant handling the journal proper.

rv.summary: The journal proper records what fits no special book: opening, closing, adjustment, rectification and transfer entries, credit dealings in assets, bad debts and similar items. Special books divide work and save time.
focus: Choose the right book for a given transaction
Advantages of special purpose books
remember: Special books: cash book, purchases, purchases return, sales, sales return
Journal proper: opening, closing, adjustment, rectification, transfer entries
Credit purchase or sale of assets → journal proper
traps: Don't put credit purchase of furniture in the purchases book
Special books do not remove the need for a ledger

topics.t: Balancing accounts and reading their balances
topics.h: A ledger account is like a cricket scoreboard with runs and wickets on two sides. Balancing tells you the score at the end of the innings.
p: Balancing: total both sides, find the difference, write it on the shorter side as 'Balance c/d' so both totals agree, then bring it down on the opposite side as 'Balance b/d' at the start of the next period.
Debit balance: debit side is larger. Assets, expenses, losses and drawings normally show debit balances.
Credit balance: credit side is larger. Liabilities, capital, incomes and gains normally show credit balances.
A debtor's account normally has a debit balance (he owes us); a creditor's account normally has a credit balance (we owe him).
Nominal (revenue and expense) accounts are not carried forward; they are closed by transfer to the trading or profit and loss account.

ex.q: Kamal's account (a customer): Dr: Sales ₹40,000, Sales ₹25,000. Cr: Cash ₹30,000, Sales Return ₹5,000. Balance it.
st: Balance = ₹30,000 debit: write 'By Balance c/d ₹30,000' on the credit side; bring down 'To Balance b/d ₹30,000'.
ex.a: Debit balance of ₹30,000 (Kamal owes the firm).

topics.rl: Your mobile wallet shows a running balance after every top-up and payment; an accountant does the same for each ledger account at the period end.

rv.summary: To balance an account, total both sides and put the difference on the smaller side as Balance c/d, then bring it down as Balance b/d. Assets and expenses usually have debit balances; liabilities, capital and incomes credit balances.
focus: Balance personal accounts and state who owes whom
Normal balance of each type of account
Which accounts are carried forward and which are closed
remember: Balance = Larger side total − Smaller side total
Debtor: debit balance (owes us); creditor: credit balance (we owe)
Nominal accounts are closed to trading or P&L, not carried forward
traps: Don't write Balance c/d on the larger side
Don't carry forward expense or income accounts

topics.t: Cash book vs pass book and the need for a BRS
topics.h: Your cash book says you have ₹50,000 in the bank. The bank statement says ₹62,000. Nobody is lying. A bank reconciliation statement finds out why.
p: The business keeps the bank column of its cash book; the bank keeps the business's account in its books and sends a copy, the pass book or bank statement.

The two are mirror images: a deposit is debited in the cash book (bank is our asset) but credited in the pass book (the bank owes us). A withdrawal is credited in the cash book and debited in the pass book.

Favourable balance: debit balance in the cash book = credit balance in the pass book (money in the bank). Unfavourable balance (overdraft): credit balance in the cash book = debit balance in the pass book.
A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) is a statement that explains the differences between the two balances on a date and reconciles them.
Importance: it reveals errors in either record, detects frauds and unauthorised payments, highlights delays in clearing cheques, and confirms the correct bank balance.

ex.q: Cash book (bank column) shows a debit balance of ₹40,000. What should the pass book show if both records are complete and correct on the same date?
st: A debit in the cash book means money held in the bank.
For the bank, that money is a liability to the customer, so it shows a credit.
ex.a: A credit balance of ₹40,000 in the pass book.

topics.rl: A small exporter in Tiruppur reconciles her bank account with the bank's monthly e-statement to catch delays in export receipts and any wrong charges.

rv.summary: The cash book (bank column) and the pass book are mirror images of one bank account. A bank reconciliation statement, prepared by the business, explains why their balances differ on a date.
focus: Mirror-image entries in cash book and pass book
