Favourable balance vs overdraft in each record
Purpose and importance of a BRS
remember: Favourable: Dr in cash book = Cr in pass book
Overdraft: Cr in cash book = Dr in pass book
BRS is a statement, not an account; prepared by the business
traps: Don't think a deposit is debited in the pass book; it is credited
A BRS is not part of double entry; no account is posted from it

topics.t: Timing differences: cheques not presented and not credited
topics.h: You hand a cheque to your supplier on 30 March. He deposits it on 3 April. For four days your cash book and bank statement disagree, and that's perfectly normal.
p: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment: the cash book has already reduced the balance; the bank has not. So pass book balance is higher than the cash book balance.
Cheques deposited but not yet collected (credited) by the bank: the cash book has already increased the balance; the bank has not. So pass book balance is lower.
These are timing differences; they disappear when the bank processes the cheques.
Steps in a BRS: start with one balance, add items that make the other balance higher, subtract items that make it lower, and arrive at the other balance.
Starting with the cash book (debit) balance: add cheques issued but not presented; subtract cheques deposited but not credited.

ex.q: Cash book balance ₹50,000 (Dr). Cheques issued not presented ₹12,000. Cheques deposited not credited ₹8,000. Find the pass book balance.
st: Add cheques issued not presented: + ₹12,000 (bank has not paid them yet).
Less cheques deposited not credited: − ₹8,000 (bank has not added them yet).
ex.a: ₹54,000 credit balance as per pass book.

topics.rl: Cheque Truncation System (CTS) has cut clearing times in India to about a day, but cheques issued on 31 March can still cross into the new financial year.

rv.summary: Cheques issued but not presented and cheques deposited but not credited are timing differences. Starting from the cash book, add unpresented cheques and subtract uncredited cheques to reach the pass book balance.
focus: Effect of each timing difference on the two balances
Find the pass book balance from the cash book, and the reverse
remember: From cash book (Dr): + cheques issued not presented, − cheques deposited not credited
From pass book (Cr): reverse the signs
Ask: which record has it already, and does it make that balance bigger or smaller?
traps: Count only the cheques not yet presented, not every cheque issued
Don't use the same signs when starting from the pass book

topics.t: Bank-side items: direct deposits, interest, charges and dishonour
topics.h: Your bank quietly credits interest, debits SMS charges and pays your insurance premium by standing instruction. You find out only when the statement arrives.
p: Direct deposits by customers into the firm's bank account (e.g. NEFT/UPI receipts): recorded by the bank first, so pass book balance is higher.
Interest allowed and dividends collected by the bank on the firm's behalf: pass book higher.
Bank charges, interest on overdraft, and direct payments made by the bank under standing instructions (insurance premium, EMI): pass book lower.
Cheque deposited and dishonoured: the cash book shows it as deposited, but the bank reverses (debits) it, so pass book is lower.
Starting from the cash book (Dr): add direct deposits, interest and dividends credited; subtract bank charges, direct payments, interest on overdraft and dishonoured cheques.

ex.q: Cash book ₹60,000 (Dr). Bank charged ₹500; interest credited ₹1,200; a customer paid ₹7,000 directly; insurance premium ₹3,000 paid by bank. Pass book balance?

topics.rl: Many Indian households set standing instructions for SIPs and loan EMIs; the debit hits the bank account before anyone writes it in a cash book.

rv.summary: Items recorded first by the bank cause differences: direct deposits, interest and dividends raise the pass book balance; bank charges, direct payments, interest on overdraft and dishonoured cheques lower it.
focus: Decide whether each bank-side item raises or lowers the pass book balance
Compute the pass book or cash book balance with several such items
remember: From cash book (Dr): + direct deposits, interest, dividends credited
From cash book (Dr): − bank charges, direct payments (EMI, premium), dishonoured cheques
From pass book (Cr): reverse every sign
traps: A dishonoured cheque lowers the pass book balance; don't add it from the cash book
Bank charges are subtracted from the cash book balance, not added

topics.t: Preparing a BRS from the cash book or the pass book balance
topics.h: Two roads lead to the same destination. You can start a BRS from the cash book or from the pass book; with the right signs, you land on the other balance exactly.
p: Format: Bank Reconciliation Statement as on [date]. Particulars | Plus items (₹) | Minus items (₹). Start with the given balance, list additions and subtractions, and end with the balance as per the other record.

From cash book Dr balance: add cheques issued not presented, direct deposits, interest and dividends credited by bank. Subtract cheques deposited not credited, bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques.

From pass book Cr balance: reverse every sign. Add cheques deposited not credited, bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques; subtract cheques issued not presented, direct deposits, interest credited.
Quick test: for each item ask, 'Which record has it already? Does it make that record's balance bigger or smaller?'

ex.q: Pass book ₹90,000 (Cr). Cheques deposited not credited ₹15,000; cheques issued not presented ₹22,000; bank charges ₹600; interest credited ₹1,600. Find the cash book balance.
st: Add: deposits not credited 15,000 + bank charges 600 = 15,600.

topics.rl: Treasury teams at companies like Tata Steel reconcile dozens of bank accounts every month with software that applies these same plus-and-minus rules.

rv.summary: A BRS starts with one balance, adds items that make the other balance higher, subtracts items that make it lower, and ends with the other record's balance. Starting from the pass book reverses every sign.
focus: Prepare a BRS from the cash book Dr balance
Prepare a BRS from the pass book Cr balance
Handle a mix of timing and bank-side items
remember: From cash book (Dr): + unpresented cheques, direct deposits, interest/dividends; − uncredited cheques, charges, direct payments, dishonour
From pass book (Cr): all signs reversed
Format: Particulars | Plus items ₹ | Minus items ₹
traps: Don't reuse cash-book signs when starting from the pass book
Check every item: which record already has it?

topics.t: Overdraft BRS and errors in the cash book or pass book
topics.h: An overdraft is a minus balance. Treat it like a negative number on a number line, apply the usual adjustments, and the BRS works just the same.
p: Overdraft as per cash book = credit balance in the cash book; overdraft as per pass book = debit balance in the pass book.

Starting with overdraft as per cash book: add cheques deposited not credited, bank charges, interest on overdraft, direct payments and dishonoured cheques (they increase the overdraft); subtract cheques issued not presented, direct deposits and interest credited (they reduce it). The result is the overdraft as per pass book.
Shortcut: treat an overdraft as a negative balance and use the normal favourable-balance signs; a negative result is an overdraft.

Errors by the business: e.g. a deposit of ₹5,400 entered as ₹4,500 makes the cash book ₹900 lower, so starting from the cash book add ₹900. Overcasting the receipts side overstates the cash book, so subtract.
Errors by the bank: e.g. the bank wrongly debits another customer's cheque to our account, making the pass book lower; starting from the cash book, subtract it.

ex.q: Overdraft as per cash book ₹30,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹8,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹5,000; interest on overdraft ₹1,000 charged by bank. Overdraft as per pass book?
st: Cheques issued not presented reduce the overdraft in the bank's books: −30,000 + 8,000 = −22,000.
Cheques not credited and interest increase the overdraft: −22,000 − 5,000 − 1,000 = −28,000.
ex.a: Overdraft of ₹28,000 as per pass book.

topics.rl: Small businesses with a cash-credit limit from a cooperative bank often run on overdraft; their BRS starts from a credit balance in the cash book.

rv.summary: For an overdraft, treat the balance as negative and use the normal signs; a negative answer is an overdraft. Errors in the cash book or pass book are adjusted by how they change that record's balance.
focus: Find overdraft as per pass book from overdraft as per cash book, and the reverse
Adjust for errors such as wrong amounts or undercasting
Adjust for errors made by the bank
remember: Overdraft as per cash book = Cr balance; as per pass book = Dr balance
Shortcut: overdraft = negative balance, then use the normal signs
Wrong entry adjustment = difference between correct and recorded amounts
traps: Unpresented cheques reduce the overdraft as per pass book, they don't increase it
Undercasting payments makes the cash book balance too high, so subtract

topics.t: Amended cash book and BRS from the amended balance
topics.h: Some differences are the cash book's own fault: unrecorded bank charges, direct deposits, dishonoured cheques. Fix those in the cash book first, then reconcile only what's left.
p: Amended (adjusted) cash book: before preparing the BRS, the cash book is corrected for items the bank has recorded but the firm has not, and for the firm's own errors.

Debit side additions: direct deposits, interest and dividends collected by bank, errors that understated the balance. Credit side additions: bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques, interest on overdraft, errors that overstated the balance.
Items NOT corrected in the cash book: cheques issued not presented, cheques deposited not credited, and errors made by the bank. These remain in the BRS.
BRS from the amended balance contains only these remaining items and ends with the pass book balance.
Advantage: the corrected cash book balance is the true bank balance shown in the balance sheet.

ex.q: Cash book ₹40,000 (Dr). Bank charges ₹500; interest credited ₹1,500; cheque dishonoured ₹3,000; unpresented cheques ₹6,000. Find the amended balance and the pass book balance.
st: BRS from amended balance: add unpresented cheques 6,000.
ex.a: Amended balance ₹38,000; pass book ₹44,000.

topics.rl: Auditors of Indian companies ask for the adjusted bank balance, not the raw cash book figure, before signing off the balance sheet.

rv.summary: The amended cash book corrects items the bank recorded but the firm missed, and the firm's own errors. The BRS is then prepared from the amended balance with only timing items and bank errors.
focus: Find the amended cash book balance
Find the pass book balance from the amended balance
Which items are corrected and which stay in the BRS
remember: Dr side additions: direct deposits, interest, dividends, understating errors
Cr side additions: bank charges, direct payments, dishonoured cheques, interest on overdraft
Stay in BRS: unpresented cheques, uncredited cheques, bank's errors
traps: Don't correct unpresented or uncredited cheques in the amended cash book
Don't adjust items twice: once corrected, leave them out of the BRS

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Trial balance: meaning, format and objectives
topics.h: After a month of entries, how do you know your books are at least arithmetically right? You line up every ledger balance and check that debits equal credits.
p: A trial balance is a statement of the debit and credit balances of all ledger accounts on a particular date. Under double entry, total debits must equal total credits.
Format: S. No. | Account title | L.F. | Debit balance (₹) | Credit balance (₹). Heading: 'Trial Balance of [firm] as on [date]'.

Objectives: (1) ascertain the arithmetical accuracy of ledger accounts; (2) help in locating errors; (3) give a summary of all ledger accounts in one place; (4) help in preparing financial statements.
It is a statement, not an account, and it can be prepared on any date, not only at the year-end.

ex.q: Ledger balances on 31 March: Cash ₹20,000 (Dr), Capital ₹1,00,000 (Cr), Purchases ₹90,000 (Dr), Sales ₹1,30,000 (Cr), Furniture ₹40,000 (Dr), Creditors ₹30,000 (Cr), Rent ₹10,000 (Dr), Debtors ₹1,00,000 (Dr). Does the trial balance agree?
st: Both totals are ₹2,60,000: the trial balance agrees.
ex.a: Yes, both sides total ₹2,60,000.

topics.rl: Before closing its quarterly results, a listed company like Hindustan Unilever runs a trial balance from its ERP system; a mismatch means someone checks the postings before results go out.

rv.summary: A trial balance is a statement of all ledger balances on a date. Equal debit and credit totals check the ledger's arithmetical accuracy, help locate errors and help prepare financial statements.
focus: Total a trial balance and find any difference
Objectives and format of a trial balance
What agreement does and does not prove
remember: Format: S. No. | Account title | L.F. | Debit ₹ | Credit ₹
Objectives: arithmetical accuracy, locating errors, summary, preparing statements
It is a statement, not an account; can be prepared on any date
traps: Agreement does not prove the books are free of all errors
A trial balance is not prepared only on 31 March

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Preparing a trial balance by the balances method
topics.h: There's a simple memory hook for trial balances: DEAL CRIL. Drawings, Expenses, Assets, Losses on the debit side; Capital, Revenues, Incomes, Liabilities on the credit side.
p: Balances method (the method used in the CBSE syllabus): list each ledger account's closing balance in the debit or credit column.
Debit balances: assets, expenses, losses, drawings, purchases, sales returns, opening stock, debtors, discount allowed.
Credit balances: capital, liabilities, incomes, gains, sales, purchases returns, creditors, bank overdraft, discount received, provisions.

Opening stock appears in the trial balance (it is a ledger balance). Closing stock normally appears outside the trial balance as an adjustment; it appears inside only if purchases are already adjusted for it.
Correcting a wrong trial balance: move each balance to its proper side, then re-total.

ex.q: Prepare totals: Opening stock ₹25,000; Purchases ₹1,20,000; Sales ₹1,80,000; Returns inwards ₹5,000; Returns outwards ₹3,000; Capital ₹1,00,000; Furniture ₹43,000; Debtors ₹60,000; Creditors ₹30,000; Salary ₹40,000; Discount received ₹2,000; Cash ₹22,000.
ex.a: Both sides ₹3,15,000.

topics.rl: An accounts trainee at a Kolkata CA firm learns DEAL CRIL on day one; it saves hours when clients hand over a box of ledger balances.

rv.summary: Under the balances method each account's closing balance goes in the debit or credit column. Assets, expenses, losses and drawings are debits; capital, liabilities, incomes, gains and provisions are credits.
focus: Place each balance on the correct side
Correct a wrongly prepared trial balance
Treatment of opening and closing stock
remember: Debit: assets, expenses, losses, drawings, purchases, returns inwards, opening stock, discount allowed
Credit: capital, liabilities, incomes, sales, returns outwards, bank overdraft, discount received, provisions
Closing stock usually appears outside the trial balance as an adjustment
traps: Bank overdraft is a credit, not a debit
Moving a balance to the wrong side changes the difference by twice its amount

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Agreement of the trial balance and searching for errors
topics.h: A trial balance that agrees is like a cricket scoreboard that adds up: it doesn't prove the umpire got every decision right.
p: Agreement of totals proves only arithmetical accuracy, not that the books are correct.

Errors NOT disclosed: complete omission of a transaction, errors of principle, compensating errors, recording a wrong amount in the book of original entry, posting to the wrong account but on the correct side.

Errors disclosed (one-sided): wrong totalling of a subsidiary book or account, posting a wrong amount to one account, posting to the wrong side, omitting to post one side, wrong balancing, omitting a balance from the trial balance.
Searching: re-total the trial balance; check that every balance is included and on the correct side; re-check totals of subsidiary books and balances of accounts; check postings.
Tips: halve the difference and look for an item of that amount posted to the wrong side; if the difference is divisible by 9, look for transposed digits (e.g. 54 written as 45) or a slide error.

ex.q: A trial balance shows a difference of ₹1,800. A cheque for ₹900 received from a customer may have been posted to the debit of his account. Is that consistent?
st: Posting ₹900 to the wrong side shifts the total by twice the amount.
So it is a likely cause: check the customer's account.
ex.a: Yes: a wrong-side posting creates a difference of double the amount, 2 × ₹900 = ₹1,800.

topics.rl: Auditors at the Comptroller and Auditor General's office still use the 'divide by 9' trick when checking manually kept government ledgers.

rv.summary: An agreed trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy. Some errors are not disclosed (complete omission, principle, compensating, wrong amount in the original book); one-sided errors are disclosed.
focus: Which errors are and are not disclosed by a trial balance
Steps to search for a difference
Tips: wrong-side postings and differences divisible by 9
remember: Wrong-side posting creates a difference of twice the amount
Transposed digits give a difference divisible by 9
Not disclosed: complete omission, principle, compensating, wrong amount in book of original entry, wrong account on the correct side
traps: A wrong amount in the sales book does not disturb the trial balance
Don't assume an agreed trial balance means no errors

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Types of errors: commission, omission, principle, compensating
topics.h: Errors come in families. Knowing which family an error belongs to tells you at once whether the trial balance will catch it and how to fix it.
p: Errors of commission: wrong recording, posting, totalling, balancing or carrying forward, e.g. wrong amount, wrong account (of the same class) or wrong side.
Errors of omission: complete omission (transaction not recorded at all; trial balance not affected) or partial omission (one side not posted; trial balance affected).
Errors of principle: violating accounting principles, mainly confusing capital and revenue items, e.g. purchase of furniture debited to Purchases, or repairs debited to Machinery.
Compensating errors: two or more errors that cancel each other's effect, e.g. Rahul's account debited ₹100 short and Sunil's account debited ₹100 in excess.
Classification for rectification: one-sided errors affect one account only (and usually the trial balance); two-sided errors affect two or more accounts (and usually not the trial balance).

ex.q: Classify: (a) ₹10,000 paid for a computer debited to Office Expenses; (b) credit sale of ₹2,000 to Leena not recorded at all; (c) sales book totalled ₹100 short.
st: (a) Capital expenditure treated as revenue: error of principle.
(b) Transaction never recorded: complete error of omission.
ex.a: (a) Principle, (b) omission (complete), (c) commission.

topics.rl: Large firms run monthly checks on whether new laptops were wrongly booked as 'office expenses', a classic error of principle that understates assets and profit.

rv.summary: Errors are of commission (wrong recording, posting, totalling), omission (complete or partial), principle (capital vs revenue confusion) and compensating (errors that cancel out). They are one-sided or two-sided for rectification.
focus: Classify an error by type
Decide if the error affects the trial balance
One-sided vs two-sided errors
remember: Complete omission: trial balance agrees; partial omission: it does not
Principle: capital and revenue confused, e.g. furniture debited to Purchases
Wrong account of the same class = commission
traps: Don't call a wrong personal account posting an error of principle
Installation wages are part of the machine's cost, not wages expense

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Rectification before the trial balance: one-sided and two-sided errors
topics.h: Fixing errors is like fixing a recipe: if one ingredient was wrong, you adjust only that; if two were swapped, you fix both together.
p: One-sided errors found before the trial balance is prepared: rectified by an explanatory entry (a note) on the appropriate side of the affected account, without a journal entry. E.g. sales book undercast ₹500: write 'By Undercasting of sales book ₹500' on the credit side of Sales account.

Two-sided errors: rectified by a journal entry. Method: (1) write the wrong entry made; (2) write the correct entry that should have been made; (3) rectifying entry = debit the account short-debited or over-credited, credit the account over-debited or short-credited.
Example: credit sale to Ram ₹2,000 posted to Shyam's account: Dr Ram / Cr Shyam ₹2,000.
Error of principle: repairs ₹5,000 debited to Building: Dr Repairs / Cr Building ₹5,000.
Complete omission: simply record the correct entry now.

ex.q: Furniture bought for ₹12,000 was debited to Purchases. Give the rectifying entry.
st: Wrong entry: Dr Purchases / Cr Cash ₹12,000.
Correct entry: Dr Furniture / Cr Cash ₹12,000.
Cash is correct; Purchases is wrongly debited, and Furniture is not debited.
ex.a: Dr Furniture ₹12,000 / Cr Purchases ₹12,000

topics.rl: Software at banks like Canara Bank never deletes a wrong entry; it posts a correcting entry, keeping a full audit trail, exactly the approach of rectification.

rv.summary: Before the trial balance, one-sided errors are corrected by a note in the affected account and two-sided errors by a journal entry worked out from the wrong entry and the correct entry.
focus: Write the rectifying entry for two-sided errors
Correct one-sided errors with an explanatory note
Rectify errors of principle and complete omission
remember: Method: wrong entry → correct entry → rectifying entry
Debit the account short-debited or over-credited; credit the account over-debited or short-credited
Complete omission: just record the correct entry
traps: Don't use a suspense account before the trial balance is prepared
Sale of an asset credited to Sales: debit Sales, credit the asset, not Cash

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Suspense account: opening it and rectifying through it
topics.h: When the trial balance won't agree and the deadline is tomorrow, accountants park the difference in a temporary waiting room called the suspense account.
p: If the trial balance does not agree and errors cannot be found at once, the difference is placed in a suspense account to make the totals agree temporarily.
If the debit side is short, the suspense account shows a debit balance; if the credit side is short, it shows a credit balance.

After the trial balance, one-sided errors are rectified through the suspense account. E.g. purchases book overcast ₹700: Dr Suspense / Cr Purchases ₹700. Discount allowed ₹200 not posted to Discount account: Dr Discount Allowed / Cr Suspense ₹200.
Two-sided errors are rectified without the suspense account.
Once all errors are corrected, the suspense account closes. The original difference can be found from the balancing figure of the suspense account.

ex.q: Trial balance: debit ₹1,48,500, credit ₹1,50,000. Later found: (i) purchases book undercast ₹1,000; (ii) payment of ₹250 to Ravi not posted to his account; (iii) discount allowed ₹250 not posted to Discount Allowed account. Show that the suspense account closes.
st: Difference = ₹1,500, debit side short: Suspense shows a debit balance of ₹1,500.
ex.a: The suspense account closes: debit ₹1,500 = credits ₹1,500.

topics.rl: At the year-end close, many Indian SMEs see a small suspense balance in their trial balance; their CA's job is to trace and clear it before filing returns.

rv.summary: When the trial balance does not agree, the difference is put in a suspense account. One-sided errors found later are rectified through suspense; two-sided errors are not. Once all are corrected, suspense closes.
focus: Open suspense on the correct side
Rectify one-sided errors through suspense
Find the original difference from the suspense account
remember: Debit side short → suspense debit balance; credit side short → credit balance
Wrong-side posting: rectify with twice the amount
Wrong amount posted: rectify with the difference
traps: Don't use suspense for two-sided errors
A wrong-side posting is corrected by double the amount, not the amount itself

topics.ch: Part I: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors
topics.t: Rectification after final accounts and the effect on profit
topics.h: An error found after the books are closed can't be fixed in last year's P&L account. Instead, it goes into a special account that adjusts the profit next year.
p: Errors in nominal (revenue and expense) accounts change profit. Errors only between real or personal accounts do not change profit.
If an expense is overstated or an income understated, profit is understated; rectification increases profit (and vice versa).

Examples: furniture ₹10,000 debited to Purchases understates profit by ₹10,000; rectification raises profit by ₹10,000. Sales book undercast ₹2,000 understates profit; rectification raises it by ₹2,000.

After final accounts are prepared, nominal accounts are already closed, so rectification of such errors is made through a Profit and Loss Adjustment account; its balance is transferred to the capital account.
Corrected profit = Profit as shown + increases from rectifications − decreases from rectifications.

ex.q: Profit shown ₹1,00,000. Errors: (a) purchase of machinery ₹20,000 debited to Purchases; (b) sales returns ₹3,000 not recorded (two-sided omission); (c) rent ₹5,000 debited to the landlord's personal account. Find the corrected profit.

topics.rl: When a listed company finds a past error, accounting standards require it to restate figures or disclose the correction, because investors rely on profit numbers.

rv.summary: Errors in nominal accounts change profit; errors between real or personal accounts do not. After final accounts, such errors are rectified through a Profit and Loss Adjustment account whose balance goes to capital.
focus: Find the effect of an error on profit
Calculate corrected profit after several errors
Use of the P&L Adjustment account
remember: Expense overstated or income understated → profit understated
Corrected profit = Profit shown + increases − decreases
P&L Adjustment account balance is transferred to capital
traps: Errors between two personal accounts do not change profit
Repairs debited to Machinery overstates profit, not understates it

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Meaning and features of depreciation
topics.h: A brand-new delivery van bought for ₹8 lakh will not be worth ₹8 lakh after five years of Mumbai traffic. Accounting must recognise that steady decline. That is depreciation.
p: Depreciation is the decline in the value of a fixed (depreciable) asset due to use, passage of time or obsolescence. It is the allocation of the asset's cost over its useful life.

Features: it reduces the book value of the asset; it is a non-cash expense (no cash goes out when it is charged); it is a continuing process over the asset's life; it applies to fixed assets only, not to current assets like stock.
Depreciation is charged to the profit and loss account as an expense of each year of use.
Land is not depreciated, because it normally has an unlimited useful life and does not get used up. Buildings on the land are depreciated.

ex.q: A firm buys a machine for ₹5,00,000 with a 10-year life and no scrap value. How much depreciation is charged per year, and is cash paid each year?
st: This amount is charged to the P&L account every year.
No cash goes out when depreciation is charged; the cash was paid when the machine was bought.
ex.a: ₹50,000 a year; it is a non-cash expense.

topics.rl: Indian Railways depreciates its coaches and locomotives over decades of service, but not the land under its stations.

rv.summary: Depreciation is the decline in the value of a fixed asset due to use, time or obsolescence, i.e. allocation of its cost over its useful life. It is a non-cash expense charged to P&L; land is not depreciated.
focus: Meaning and features of depreciation
Annual depreciation in equal amounts
Which assets are and are not depreciated
remember: Equal annual depreciation = Cost ÷ Useful life (no scrap)
Non-cash expense; reduces book value; continuing process; fixed assets only
Land is not depreciated; buildings on it are
traps: Don't depreciate land or current assets like stock
Depreciation does not mean cash leaving the business

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Depletion, amortisation and causes of depreciation
topics.h: Coal India mines coal, a pharma company holds a 20-year patent, and a call centre buys computers. All three lose asset value, but accountants use three different words for it.
p: Depletion: reduction in the value of wasting (natural) assets such as mines, quarries and oil wells, as the resources are extracted. It is usually based on the quantity extracted.
Amortisation: writing off the cost of intangible assets such as patents, copyrights, trademarks and goodwill over their useful life.

Causes of depreciation: (1) wear and tear due to use or passage of time; (2) expiration of legal rights (leases, patents, copyrights); (3) obsolescence, when an asset becomes outdated because of new technology or changes in demand; (4) abnormal factors such as accidents, fire, flood or earthquake.
Depletion is calculated by: (Cost ÷ Total estimated quantity) × Quantity extracted in the year.

ex.q: A mine costing ₹50,00,000 is estimated to contain 1,00,000 tonnes of ore. 8,000 tonnes are extracted this year. Find depletion.

topics.rl: When smartphones replaced feature phones, many Indian factories making keypad phones saw their machines become obsolete long before they physically wore out.

rv.summary: Depletion applies to wasting natural assets like mines and oil wells; amortisation to intangible assets like patents and copyrights. Depreciation is caused by wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence and abnormal factors.
focus: Tell depletion, amortisation and depreciation apart
Identify the cause of decline in value
Calculate depletion and amortisation
remember: Depletion = (Cost ÷ Total estimated quantity) × Quantity extracted
Amortisation = Cost of intangible ÷ Useful (legal) life
Causes: wear and tear, expiry of legal rights, obsolescence, abnormal factors
traps: Don't call writing off a patent 'depletion'
Obsolescence happens even when the asset still works

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Need for depreciation and factors in measuring it
topics.h: If a taxi owner ignored the wearing out of his cab, he'd think he was richer every year, until the day the cab died and he had no money for a new one.
p: Need: (1) matching the cost of the asset with the revenue it helps earn, for correct profit; (2) tax: depreciation is an allowable deduction for income tax; (3) true and fair financial position: assets are not overstated; (4) compliance with law (the Companies Act requires it); (5) retaining funds for replacement, since profit available for distribution is reduced.
Cost of asset (depreciable cost base): purchase price plus all costs to bring it to working condition: freight, cartage, installation, commission, registration.
Estimated net residual (scrap) value: expected sale value at the end of its life, less disposal costs.
Estimated useful life: the period (or production units) over which the asset is expected to be used.
Depreciable amount = Cost − Net residual value.

ex.q: A machine is bought for ₹4,50,000; freight ₹15,000; installation ₹35,000. Estimated scrap ₹50,000; life 9 years. Find the depreciable amount and annual depreciation (equal instalments).
ex.a: Depreciable amount ₹4,50,000; ₹50,000 a year.

topics.rl: An app-cab fleet owner in Hyderabad sets aside the depreciation amount every year so that when the cars wear out, the business can afford new ones.

rv.summary: Depreciation is needed for matching, tax, a true and fair position, legal compliance and keeping funds for replacement. It is measured from cost, net residual value and useful life.
focus: Reasons for charging depreciation
Find the depreciable cost including freight and installation
Find annual depreciation from cost, scrap and life
remember: Cost = Price + freight + cartage + installation + registration
Depreciable amount = Cost − Net residual value
Annual depreciation (equal) = Depreciable amount ÷ Useful life
traps: Don't forget to deduct scrap value before dividing by life
Not charging depreciation overstates both profit and assets

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Straight line method (SLM)
topics.h: Under the straight line method, depreciation is the same every year, like a fixed monthly SIP. Plot the book value on a graph and you get a straight line sloping down.
p: Straight line (fixed instalment or original cost) method: equal depreciation every year. Annual depreciation = (Cost − Net residual value) ÷ Estimated useful life.
Rate of depreciation under SLM = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100. Depreciation can also be found as Cost × Rate ÷ 100.
Advantages: simple to calculate; the asset can be written down to zero (or scrap value) at the end of its life; suitable where use is even across years.

Limitations: ignores the fact that repairs rise as assets age, so the total charge (depreciation + repairs) rises in later years; does not consider the effective use of the asset; interest on capital invested is ignored.
Suitable for: patents, copyrights, leases and furniture, i.e. assets whose usefulness falls evenly with time.

ex.q: Cost ₹1,60,000; scrap ₹10,000; life 5 years. Find annual depreciation, the rate, and book value after 2 years.

topics.rl: A coaching institute in Kota writes off its classroom furniture and its 10-year lease equally each year: the straight line method suits both.

rv.summary: Under the straight line method, equal depreciation is charged every year on original cost, so book value falls in a straight line to scrap value. It is simple but total charge rises as repairs grow.
focus: Calculate annual depreciation and rate under SLM
Find book value after some years
Merits, limitations and suitable assets
remember: Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual value) ÷ Useful life
Rate = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100
Book value after n years = Cost − n × Annual depreciation
traps: Don't apply the SLM rate to the reducing book value
Rate is found on cost, not on depreciable amount

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Written down value method (WDV) and comparison with SLM
topics.h: Under WDV, depreciation is big in the early years and shrinks later, much like a new phone that loses the most value in its first year.
p: Written down value (reducing or diminishing balance) method: a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value each year. Depreciation falls every year.
Under WDV the book value never reaches zero.

Advantages: total charge (depreciation + repairs) stays fairly even, since high depreciation in early years meets low repairs, and vice versa; accepted by income tax authorities; suitable where obsolescence is fast.
Limitations: the asset cannot be fully written off; finding a suitable rate is difficult; calculations are more involved.

Comparison: SLM charges on original cost, equal amounts, book value can become zero, suits patents, leases, furniture. WDV charges on reducing book value, decreasing amounts, never zero, suits plant, machinery, vehicles, and is recognised by income tax law.

ex.q: Machine cost ₹2,00,000; WDV rate 20%. Find depreciation for 3 years and the book value at the end of year 3.

topics.rl: Income tax rules in India prescribe WDV rates for blocks of assets; for example, vehicles and computers are grouped into blocks with their own rates.

rv.summary: Under WDV a fixed rate is applied to the opening book value each year, so depreciation falls yearly and book value never reaches zero. It evens out the total charge and is accepted by income tax law.
focus: Calculate WDV depreciation and book value year by year
Compare SLM and WDV
Which assets suit each method
remember: WDV depreciation = Rate × Opening book value
Book value after n years = Cost × (1 − rate)ⁿ
WDV: plant, machinery, vehicles; SLM: patents, leases, furniture
traps: Don't charge WDV on original cost after year 1
Under WDV the rate stays fixed; the base shrinks

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Depreciation for part of a year, additions and repairs
topics.h: Buy a machine on 1 October and close books on 31 March, and it has worked for you for exactly six months. Depreciation must count those months, not the full year.
p: When an asset is bought during the year, depreciation is charged from the date of purchase to the end of the year: Depreciation = Cost × Rate × Months used ÷ 12 (under SLM; under WDV, on the book value).
Count months carefully: bought 1 July, year ending 31 March: July to March = 9 months. Bought 1 January: 3 months.
If a question says the rate is 'per annum', time is always prorated; if it says depreciation is charged for a full year regardless, follow the instruction.
Additions or extensions that increase capacity or life (a new wing, an extra unit) are capitalised and depreciated separately from their date of addition.
Ordinary repairs and maintenance that only keep an asset working are revenue expenses, charged to P&L; they are not added to the asset.

ex.q: On 1 April 2025 a firm has machinery ₹4,00,000. On 1 October 2025 it adds a machine for ₹1,20,000. Depreciation 10% p.a. SLM; year ends 31 March 2026. Find depreciation for 2025-26.

topics.rl: When Delhi Metro adds new coaches to a line mid-year, each coach is depreciated only from the month it joins service.

rv.summary: For an asset bought during the year, depreciation is charged only for the months it was used. Additions are capitalised and depreciated from their date; ordinary repairs are revenue expenses.
focus: Count months correctly and prorate depreciation
Depreciation on existing assets plus additions
Capital additions vs ordinary repairs
remember: Part-year depreciation = Cost (or BV) × Rate × Months used ÷ 12
Bought 1 July with year end 31 March = 9 months; 1 January = 3 months
Ordinary repairs go to P&L, not to the asset
traps: Don't charge a full year on an asset bought mid-year when the rate is per annum
Don't add routine repairs to the asset's cost

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Recording depreciation: asset account vs provision for depreciation
topics.h: Two firms buy the same ₹1,00,000 machine. After 3 years, one balance sheet shows 'Machinery ₹70,000'; the other shows 'Machinery ₹1,00,000 less Provision ₹30,000'. Same truth, two styles.
p: Method 1: charging depreciation to the asset account. Entries: Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset; then Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation. The asset account shows the reduced book value each year.

Method 2: creating a provision for depreciation (accumulated depreciation) account. Entries: Dr Depreciation / Cr Provision for Depreciation; then Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation. The asset stays at original cost.
Balance sheet (method 1): asset at written down value. Balance sheet (method 2): asset at cost, less provision for depreciation (accumulated), showing net book value.
Advantage of method 2: original cost and total depreciation to date are both visible at a glance, which helps for insurance, tax and replacement decisions.

ex.q: Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a. Show the balance sheet position on 31 March 2026 under both methods.
st: Method 2: Machinery ₹1,00,000 less Provision for depreciation ₹30,000 = ₹70,000.
ex.a: ₹70,000 net under both; method 2 also shows cost ₹1,00,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹30,000.

topics.rl: Schedule III statements of companies like Bajaj Auto show gross block, accumulated depreciation and net block for each class of asset, which is method 2 in action.

rv.summary: Depreciation is recorded either by crediting the asset account (asset shown at written down value) or by crediting a provision for depreciation account (asset kept at cost, with accumulated depreciation shown separately).
focus: Journal entries under both methods
Balance sheet presentation under each method
Balance in the provision account after some years
remember: Method 1: Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset
Method 2: Dr Depreciation / Cr Provision for Depreciation
Both: Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation; balance sheet: Cost − Provision = Net book value
traps: Under the provision method, don't credit the asset account each year
Don't add the provision to the asset; deduct it

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Disposal of an asset: book value, profit or loss, disposal account
topics.h: Selling an old machine is like selling a used bike: whether you 'profit' depends on what it's worth in your books today, not what you paid for it years ago.
p: Steps: find the book value on the date of sale (cost less depreciation up to that date, including depreciation for the part of the year before sale).
Profit on sale = Sale price − Book value (credited to P&L). Loss on sale = Book value − Sale price (debited to P&L).
Entries (asset account method): Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset (for the part year); Dr Bank / Cr Asset (sale proceeds); for profit Dr Asset / Cr P&L; for loss Dr P&L / Cr Asset.

Asset disposal account: transfer the asset's cost (Dr Disposal / Cr Asset), its accumulated depreciation (Dr Provision / Cr Disposal) and sale proceeds (Dr Bank / Cr Disposal); the balance is profit or loss, transferred to P&L.
Partial sale: only the part sold is removed with its depreciation; the remaining assets continue to be depreciated in full.

ex.q: Machine bought 1 April 2023 for ₹1,00,000; SLM 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Sold on 1 October 2025 for ₹70,000. Find profit or loss.
ex.a: Loss of ₹5,000

topics.rl: When State Transport Corporations auction old buses, each sale is compared with the bus's book value to decide profit or loss on disposal.

rv.summary: On disposal, find book value on the date of sale (including part-year depreciation). Sale price above book value is a profit, below it is a loss, both taken to P&L, either through the asset account or an asset disposal account.
focus: Book value on the date of sale
Profit or loss on sale, including partial sale
Entries in the asset disposal account
remember: Profit = Sale price − Book value; Loss = Book value − Sale price
Charge depreciation up to the date of sale
Disposal A/c: Dr cost; Cr provision and sale proceeds; balance = profit or loss
traps: Don't forget part-year depreciation before the sale
In a partial sale, keep depreciating the remaining assets in full

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Disposal with provision for depreciation and insurance claims
topics.h: When a fire destroys a machine, the insurer pays only part of its value. Accounting must show three things: the depreciation written back, the claim and the loss that's left.
p: When a provision for depreciation account is kept, the accumulated depreciation on the asset sold is transferred: Dr Provision for Depreciation / Cr Asset (or Cr Asset Disposal).
The asset account is then credited with sale proceeds and the balance is profit or loss, or all items are collected in an asset disposal account.

Asset destroyed by fire or accident: find book value on that date. Insurance claim admitted: Dr Insurance Claim (or Insurance Company) / Cr Asset (or Disposal). Uncovered loss: Dr Loss by Fire (to P&L) / Cr Asset.
Loss by fire = Book value on the date of fire − Insurance claim admitted (− any scrap value realised).

ex.q: Machine cost ₹2,00,000; accumulated depreciation ₹80,000. Destroyed by fire; insurer admits ₹90,000. Find the loss and pass the entries (provision method).
st: Dr Provision for Depreciation ₹80,000 / Cr Machinery ₹80,000.
Loss = 1,20,000 − 90,000 = ₹30,000: Dr Loss by Fire (P&L) / Cr Machinery ₹30,000.
ex.a: Loss of ₹30,000

topics.rl: After a cyclone hits Odisha's coast, factories that insured their plants record insurance claims for the book value lost, and only the uninsured part hits profit.

rv.summary: With a provision account, accumulated depreciation on the asset sold is transferred out against the asset. For an asset lost by fire, the loss is book value less insurance claim and any scrap realised.
focus: Profit or loss on sale with accumulated depreciation
Entries for insurance claims on destroyed assets
Loss by fire calculation
remember: Book value = Cost − Accumulated depreciation
Dr Provision for Depreciation / Cr Asset (or Disposal)
Loss by fire = Book value − Insurance claim − Scrap realised
traps: Don't forget to deduct scrap realised when finding loss by fire
The claim admitted is debited to Insurance Claim, not credited

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Provisions and the provision for doubtful debts
topics.h: Some customers who owe you money will never pay. You don't know who yet, but experience says about 5%. A provision lets you face that loss before it hits.
p: A provision is an amount charged against profit to provide for a known liability or a likely loss whose amount cannot be determined with certainty.
Examples: provision for depreciation, provision for bad and doubtful debts, provision for taxation, provision for repairs and renewals, provision for discount on debtors.
Bad debts written off: Dr Bad Debts / Cr Debtor; then Dr P&L / Cr Bad Debts. Creating a provision: Dr P&L / Cr Provision for Doubtful Debts.

When a provision already exists, bad debts are transferred to it: Dr Provision for Doubtful Debts / Cr Bad Debts. The charge to P&L = Bad debts + New provision − Old provision. If negative, the excess is credited to P&L.
New provision is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts. In the balance sheet: Debtors less Provision.

ex.q: Debtors ₹2,00,000; further bad debts ₹10,000; new provision 5%; old provision ₹6,000; bad debts during the year ₹4,000. Find the P&L charge.
st: Debtors after further bad debts = ₹1,90,000; new provision = 5% = ₹9,500.
ex.a: ₹17,500 debited to P&L.

topics.rl: RBI requires banks to make provisions on loans that turn doubtful; that is why bank results in India report 'provisions' as a separate charge against profit.

rv.summary: A provision is a charge against profit for a known liability or likely loss of uncertain amount. For doubtful debts, the P&L charge is bad debts plus new provision less old provision.

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Reserves and how they differ from provisions
topics.h: A provision is like an umbrella you must buy because rain is forecast. A reserve is like extra savings you choose to keep from your pocket money, just in case.
p: A reserve is an amount set aside out of profit (an appropriation of profit) to strengthen the financial position, meet contingencies or for specific purposes. It is created after profit is ascertained.
Provision is a charge against profit; reserve is an appropriation of profit.
Provision is made for a known liability or expected loss; reserve is made to strengthen the business or meet future needs, with no specific liability in mind (except specific reserves).
Provision is shown as a deduction from the related asset or under liabilities; reserve is shown under 'Reserves and Surplus' on the liabilities side.
Provision must be made even if there is a loss; reserve is created only when there is profit. Provisions cannot be used for dividend; some revenue reserves can be.

ex.q: Net profit ₹5,00,000 after charging provision for doubtful debts ₹20,000. The owner transfers ₹50,000 to general reserve. Which is a charge and which is an appropriation?
st: Provision ₹20,000 was deducted to arrive at profit: a charge against profit.
₹50,000 transferred out of profit after it was ascertained: an appropriation of profit.
ex.a: Provision: charge against profit; reserve: appropriation of profit.

topics.rl: Banks like SBI transfer a part of their profits to statutory reserves each year: an appropriation that strengthens their capital base.

rv.summary: A provision is a charge against profit for a known liability or expected loss, made even in a loss year. A reserve is an appropriation of profit to strengthen the business, made only when there is profit.

Balance sheet presentation of each
Which can be made in a loss year

Provision: deducted from asset or shown under liabilities; reserve: under Reserves and Surplus

A reserve cannot be created in a loss year

topics.ch: Part I: Depreciation, Provisions and Reserves
topics.t: Types of reserves and secret reserves
topics.h: Some reserves come from everyday trading profit, some from rare capital gains, and some are hidden from view altogether. Each has a different job.
p: Revenue reserves are created out of revenue (trading) profits, e.g. general reserve, dividend equalisation reserve. They can be used for any purpose, including dividends.

Capital reserves are created out of capital profits, e.g. premium on issue of shares or debentures, profit on sale of fixed assets, profit on reissue of forfeited shares, profit prior to incorporation, profit on revaluation of assets. They are generally not available for dividends and are used to write off capital losses.

General reserve: not for any specific purpose. Specific reserves: for a stated purpose, e.g. dividend equalisation reserve, debenture redemption reserve, workmen compensation fund, investment fluctuation fund.
Importance of reserves: meet unforeseen losses, strengthen financial position, help expansion, stabilise dividends, redeem long-term liabilities.

Secret reserve: a reserve not shown in the balance sheet, created by undervaluing assets or overstating liabilities, e.g. excessive depreciation, undervaluing stock, excessive provision for doubtful debts, charging capital expenditure to revenue. Merits: hides fluctuations and strengthens position. Demerits: hides true profit and position, can be misused, and goes against full disclosure and the requirement of a true and fair view.

ex.q: A firm charges depreciation at 25% on a machine when 10% is reasonable. Machine cost ₹4,00,000. What secret reserve is created in year 1 (SLM basis)?
st: Excess = 1,00,000 − 40,000 = ₹60,000: profit is understated and the asset undervalued by this amount.
ex.a: Secret reserve of ₹60,000

topics.rl: Banks and insurers in India must disclose their reserves clearly; hidden cushions are discouraged because depositors and policyholders rely on true accounts.

rv.summary: Revenue reserves come from trading profits and can be used for any purpose; capital reserves come from capital profits and absorb capital losses. Reserves are general or specific. A secret reserve is hidden by undervaluing assets or overstating liabilities.

Ways a secret reserve is created and its merits and demerits
Calculate a secret reserve from excess depreciation

Secret reserve = Depreciation charged − Reasonable depreciation (for excess depreciation)
Specific reserves: dividend equalisation, debenture redemption, workmen compensation, investment fluctuation
traps: Don't use capital reserves for dividends
Secret reserves go against full disclosure and a true and fair view

topics.t: Financial statements and their users
topics.h: All the journalising, posting and balancing of a year leads to two pages: the profit and loss story and the balance sheet snapshot. Those two pages are what everyone wants to read.
p: Financial statements are the end product of the accounting process. For a sole proprietor they are the trading and profit and loss account (performance for a period) and the balance sheet (position on a date).
Objectives: to find the profit or loss of the period, to show the financial position, and to provide information to stakeholders for decisions.

Stakeholders and needs: owners (profit, safety of capital); management (control and planning); lenders (repaying capacity, security); creditors (short-term liquidity); government (tax, policy); employees (job security, bonus); investors (returns, growth).
Importance for a sole proprietor: tells him how much he earned, how much he can draw, what he owns and owes, supports loan applications and tax returns, and helps plan growth.

ex.q: A grocer wants a bank loan to open a second shop. What two statements will the bank ask for, and what does each tell it?
st: Trading and profit and loss account: whether the shop earns enough profit to pay interest and instalments.
Balance sheet: what the grocer owns and owes on a date, i.e. the security behind the loan.
ex.a: The trading and P&L account (earning power) and the balance sheet (financial position).

topics.rl: Under PM SVANidhi and MUDRA loans, small vendors who keep simple financial statements find it easier to move to larger bank loans.

rv.summary: Financial statements are the end product of accounting. For a sole trader they are the trading and P&L account (performance for a period) and the balance sheet (position on a date), used by owners, lenders, creditors, government and others.
focus: Period statement vs date statement
Objectives of financial statements
Which user needs which information
remember: Trading and P&L account → profit or loss for a period
Balance sheet → assets, liabilities and capital on a date
Creditors → short-term liquidity; lenders → repaying capacity; government → taxable profit
traps: Don't say the P&L account is prepared on a date
Financial statements come at the end, not the start, of the accounting process

topics.t: Capital, revenue and deferred revenue expenditure
topics.h: Paying ₹50 lakh for a new printing machine and paying ₹5,000 to oil it are both 'spending', yet one sits in the balance sheet for years and the other vanishes into this year's P&L.
p: Capital expenditure: spent to acquire or improve fixed assets, or to increase earning capacity; benefit lasts more than one year. Shown as an asset in the balance sheet. Examples: buying machinery, freight and installation on it, building extension, legal charges on buying land.
Revenue expenditure: spent on day-to-day running; benefit is used up within the year. Charged to the trading or P&L account. Examples: wages, salaries, rent, repairs, insurance, carriage on goods.
Deferred revenue expenditure: revenue in nature but so large that its benefit is spread over several years, e.g. a heavy advertising campaign to launch a product. It is written off over those years.
Tests: does it create or improve an asset? Is it recurring? How long does the benefit last? Does it increase earning capacity?

ex.q: Classify: (a) wages paid to workers who installed a new machine; (b) wages paid to factory workers for production; (c) ₹30 lakh TV campaign whose effect will last 3 years.
st: (a) Brings the machine into working condition: capital expenditure.
(c) Revenue in nature but long benefit: deferred revenue expenditure, written off over 3 years.
ex.a: (a) Capital, (b) revenue, (c) deferred revenue.

topics.rl: When Indian Railways electrifies a route, the cost is capital expenditure; the electricity bill to run the trains afterwards is revenue expenditure.

rv.summary: Capital expenditure acquires or improves fixed assets with benefit beyond a year and is shown as an asset. Revenue expenditure is for day-to-day running and charged to P&L. Deferred revenue expenditure is written off over the years it benefits.
focus: Classify an expenditure as capital, revenue or deferred revenue
Compute total capital expenditure on an asset
Effect of wrong classification on profit
remember: Capital: machinery, freight and installation on it, extensions, legal charges on land
Revenue: wages, salaries, rent, repairs, insurance, carriage on goods
Deferred revenue: yearly write-off = Total ÷ Years of benefit
traps: Don't add annual repairs to an asset's cost
Wages for installing a machine are capital, not revenue

topics.t: Capital receipts and revenue receipts
topics.h: A shop gets ₹5 lakh from selling biscuits and ₹5 lakh from selling an old freezer. Same cash, very different meaning.
p: Revenue receipts arise from the normal business operations: sales of goods, commission, rent, interest and dividends received. They are credited to the trading or P&L account.
Capital receipts arise from sources other than normal operations: capital introduced by the owner, loans received, sale proceeds of fixed assets. They affect the balance sheet.
Capital receipts either increase a liability (loan, capital) or reduce an asset (sale of a fixed asset).
Only the profit or loss on sale of a fixed asset (sale price minus book value) goes to the P&L account; the full proceeds are a capital receipt.
Classification matters: treating a capital receipt as revenue overstates profit.

ex.q: A firm sells an old car with book value ₹2,00,000 for ₹2,30,000. How much is a capital receipt and how much goes to the P&L?
st: The full ₹2,30,000 is a capital receipt (sale of a fixed asset).
Profit on sale = 2,30,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹30,000, credited to P&L as a gain.
The car (₹2,00,000) is removed from the balance sheet.
ex.a: Capital receipt ₹2,30,000; ₹30,000 profit to P&L.

topics.rl: When a startup raises money from venture capital investors, that is a capital receipt; the subscription fees from its customers are revenue receipts.

rv.summary: Revenue receipts come from normal operations and go to the trading or P&L account. Capital receipts (capital introduced, loans, sale of fixed assets) affect the balance sheet; only the profit on sale of an asset goes to P&L.
focus: Classify receipts as capital or revenue
Profit on sale of a fixed asset vs full proceeds
Effect of wrong classification
remember: Revenue receipts: sales, commission, rent, interest, dividends
Capital receipts: capital, loans, sale proceeds of fixed assets
Profit on sale = Sale price − Book value (to P&L)
traps: Don't credit full sale proceeds of an asset to P&L
A loan received is not income

topics.t: Trading account: gross profit and cost of goods sold
topics.h: The trading account answers one question: how much did we earn just by buying and selling goods, before office rent and salaries?
p: Trading account shows gross profit or gross loss from trading. Gross profit = Net sales − Cost of goods sold.

Debit side: opening stock; purchases less purchases returns; direct expenses: carriage inwards, freight inwards, wages, fuel and power, import duty, octroi, royalty on production, gas and water for the factory.
Credit side: sales less sales returns; closing stock.
Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock.
If the credit side exceeds the debit side, the difference is gross profit (transferred to P&L credit); if not, gross loss (to P&L debit).

ex.q: Opening stock ₹40,000; purchases ₹2,00,000; purchases returns ₹10,000; wages ₹30,000; carriage inwards ₹5,000; sales ₹3,50,000; sales returns ₹15,000; closing stock ₹50,000. Find COGS and gross profit.
ex.a: COGS ₹2,15,000; gross profit ₹1,20,000.

topics.rl: A Firozabad bangle maker's trading account carries fuel for the furnaces and wages of the artisans as direct expenses, because they are part of making the goods.

rv.summary: The trading account finds gross profit or gross loss. Gross profit = Net sales − Cost of goods sold, where COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock.

Which expenses are direct and go to the trading account
Gross profit from a percentage of sales
remember: COGS = Opening stock + Net purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock
Gross profit = Net sales − COGS
Direct expenses: carriage inwards, wages, fuel and power, import duty, factory gas and water

Deduct returns from purchases and sales before using them

topics.t: Profit and loss account: net profit or net loss
topics.h: Gross profit is the cake. The profit and loss account cuts out slices for rent, salaries, advertising and interest. What's left is net profit.
p: The profit and loss account starts with gross profit (credit side) or gross loss (debit side).

Debit side: indirect expenses and losses. Office and administration (salaries, office rent, printing and stationery, telephone, audit fees); selling and distribution (carriage outwards, advertisement, salesmen's commission, bad debts); financial (interest on loan, discount allowed, bank charges); depreciation; losses (loss by fire, loss on sale of assets).
Credit side: other incomes and gains: discount received, commission received, rent received, interest received, dividends, profit on sale of assets.
Net profit = Gross profit + Other incomes − Indirect expenses and losses.
Net profit is transferred to the credit of the capital account (net loss to the debit).

ex.q: Gross profit ₹1,20,000; salaries ₹40,000; rent ₹18,000; advertisement ₹7,000; discount received ₹3,000; interest on loan ₹6,000; commission received ₹8,000. Find net profit.

topics.rl: Listed Indian companies publish a statement of profit and loss every quarter; the net profit line is what makes headlines on business channels.

rv.summary: The P&L account starts with gross profit, adds other incomes and deducts indirect expenses and losses to find net profit, which is credited to capital (net loss debited).
focus: Calculate net profit or net loss
Classify indirect expenses: office, selling, financial, depreciation, losses
Transfer of net profit or loss to capital
remember: Net profit = Gross profit + Other incomes − Indirect expenses and losses
Credit side: discount, commission, rent, interest received, profit on sale of assets
Net profit → Cr Capital; net loss → Dr Capital
traps: Don't put carriage outwards in the trading account
If expenses exceed gross profit plus incomes, it is a net loss

topics.t: Closing entries
topics.h: At the end of the year, every income and expense account must be emptied into the trading and P&L accounts, like pouring many small jars into two big ones.
p: Closing entries transfer the balances of nominal (revenue and expense) accounts to the trading account and P&L account, so those accounts are closed.

Trading account debits: Dr Trading / Cr Opening Stock, Purchases, Wages, Carriage Inwards, other direct expenses. Sales: Dr Sales / Cr Trading. Returns: Dr Purchases Return / Cr Purchases (or Cr Trading); Dr Sales / Cr Sales Return (or Dr Trading / Cr Sales Return).
Closing stock: Dr Closing Stock / Cr Trading. (Closing stock becomes an asset carried to the balance sheet.)
Gross profit: Dr Trading / Cr P&L. Indirect expenses: Dr P&L / Cr each expense account. Incomes: Dr each income account / Cr P&L.
Net profit: Dr P&L / Cr Capital. Net loss: Dr Capital / Cr P&L. Drawings: Dr Capital / Cr Drawings.

ex.q: Give closing entries for: Sales ₹5,00,000; Salaries ₹60,000; Commission received ₹10,000; Net profit ₹80,000.
ex.a: As listed: sales and incomes debited, expenses credited, and net profit credited to capital.

topics.rl: Accounting software used by Indian SMEs runs these closing entries automatically at the year-end, wiping income and expense accounts to zero for the new year.

rv.summary: Closing entries transfer nominal account balances to the trading and P&L accounts. Gross profit goes to P&L, net profit or loss and drawings go to capital; real and personal accounts are not closed.
focus: Closing entries for direct expenses, sales, indirect expenses and incomes
Entries for closing stock, gross profit, net profit or loss and drawings
remember: Expenses: Dr Trading or P&L / Cr Expense; incomes: Dr Income / Cr P&L
Closing stock: Dr Closing Stock / Cr Trading
Net profit: Dr P&L / Cr Capital; drawings: Dr Capital / Cr Drawings
traps: Don't close real accounts like Machinery
Net loss is debited to capital, not credited

topics.t: Operating profit (EBIT)
topics.h: Two tea companies earn the same net profit. One earns it from selling tea; the other mostly from selling a plot of land. Operating profit tells you which one is really good at business.
p: Operating profit is the profit earned from the normal operating activities of the business, ignoring non-operating items.
Operating profit = Net profit + Non-operating expenses − Non-operating incomes.

Non-operating expenses: interest on loans, loss on sale of fixed assets, loss by fire. Non-operating incomes: interest and dividends on investments, profit on sale of fixed assets, rent received from non-business property.
It is also called earnings before interest and tax (EBIT) when computed before interest and tax: EBIT = Net profit before tax + Interest.
Operating profit helps compare the true operating efficiency of firms.

ex.q: Net profit ₹1,50,000; interest on loan ₹20,000; loss on sale of machine ₹10,000; dividend received ₹15,000; profit on sale of land ₹25,000. Find operating profit.

topics.rl: Analysts tracking Indian IT firms on Dalal Street focus on operating (EBIT) margins, because one-off gains from selling property can make net profit look better than the core business.

rv.summary: Operating profit is profit from normal operations: net profit plus non-operating expenses minus non-operating incomes. EBIT = Net profit before tax + Interest.
focus: Calculate operating profit from net profit
Classify items as operating or non-operating
Compare firms' operating efficiency
remember: Operating profit = Net profit + Non-operating expenses − Non-operating incomes
EBIT = Net profit before tax + Interest
Non-operating: interest on loans, loss/profit on sale of fixed assets, loss by fire or theft, dividends on investments
traps: Don't subtract non-operating expenses again; add them back
An item is non-operating only relative to the firm's own business

topics.t: Balance sheet: format and classification
topics.h: The P&L account is a movie of the year. The balance sheet is a photograph taken on the last day: everything owned, everything owed, frozen at that moment.
p: The balance sheet is a statement of financial position on a particular date. In the horizontal form used for sole proprietors, liabilities and capital are on the left and assets on the right.

Assets: non-current assets: fixed assets, tangible (land, building, machinery, furniture, vehicles) and intangible (goodwill, patents, trademarks); long-term investments. Current assets: stock, debtors, bills receivable, cash, bank, prepaid expenses, short-term investments.
Liabilities: non-current (long-term loans) and current (creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses).
Capital is shown as: Opening capital + Additional capital + Net profit − Drawings (− Net loss).
Flow: ledger balances → trial balance → trading and P&L account (nominal items) → balance sheet (real and personal items, plus closing stock and the adjusted capital).

ex.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000; net profit ₹80,000; drawings ₹30,000. Assets total ₹4,50,000. Find closing capital and total liabilities.
ex.a: Closing capital ₹3,50,000; liabilities ₹1,00,000.

topics.rl: When a Kerala houseboat operator applies for a loan, the bank checks his balance sheet: boats (non-current assets), cash (current) and existing loans (liabilities).

rv.summary: The balance sheet shows financial position on a date, with capital and liabilities on the left and assets on the right. Assets and liabilities are classified as non-current or current, and closing capital is adjusted for profit and drawings.

Find closing capital
Use the accounting equation to find a missing figure
remember: Closing capital = Opening capital + Additional capital + Net profit − Drawings (− Net loss)
Current assets: stock, debtors, B/R, cash, bank, prepaid expenses
Current liabilities: creditors, B/P, bank overdraft, outstanding expenses
traps: Sales and expenses never appear in the balance sheet
Goodwill is non-current, not current

topics.t: Grouping, marshalling, opening entry and preparing statements
topics.h: A balance sheet with 60 random lines is hard to read. Grouping and marshalling arrange it like a well-organised kitchen: similar things together, and in a sensible order.
p: Grouping: putting similar items under a common head, e.g. cash in hand and cash at bank as 'Cash and cash equivalents'; sundry debtors under 'Trade receivables'.

Marshalling: arranging assets and liabilities in a particular order. Order of liquidity: assets from most liquid (cash, bank, debtors, stock) to least liquid (goodwill); liabilities from most urgent (bank overdraft, creditors) to capital.
Order of permanence: the reverse. Assets from most permanent (goodwill, land, building) to cash; liabilities from capital to current liabilities. Companies follow this broadly under Schedule III.
Opening entry at the start of a new year: Dr all assets / Cr all liabilities and capital, bringing forward last year's balance sheet.
Preparing statements from a trial balance (no adjustments): nominal items go to the trading and P&L account; real and personal items go to the balance sheet; net profit is added to capital.

ex.q: On 1 April: cash ₹20,000, stock ₹50,000, furniture ₹30,000, creditors ₹25,000. Pass the opening entry.
st: Dr Cash ₹20,000, Dr Stock ₹50,000, Dr Furniture ₹30,000 / Cr Creditors ₹25,000, Cr Capital ₹75,000.
ex.a: Dr Cash, Stock, Furniture (₹1,00,000) / Cr Creditors ₹25,000, Capital ₹75,000

topics.rl: Balance sheets of Indian banks list cash and RBI balances first, close to the order of liquidity, while manufacturing companies like Tata Steel start with property, plant and equipment.

rv.summary: Grouping puts similar items under one head; marshalling arranges them in order of liquidity or permanence. The opening entry brings forward last year's balances. Nominal items go to trading and P&L, real and personal items to the balance sheet.
focus: Order of liquidity vs order of permanence
Pass the opening entry and find opening capital
Decide where each trial balance item goes
remember: Liquidity: cash first ... goodwill last; permanence: the reverse
Opening entry: Dr all assets / Cr all liabilities and capital
Capital = Assets − Liabilities
traps: Don't confuse grouping with marshalling
Under order of permanence, capital comes first on the liabilities side

topics.t: Need for adjustments and the treatment of closing stock
topics.h: The trial balance is a rough draft. Unpaid March salaries, next year's insurance paid today and unsold stock are all missing or misplaced. Adjustments turn the draft into a true picture.
p: Adjustments make the final accounts follow the accrual and matching concepts: every income and expense of the year, and only of the year, is included.

Golden rule: an item given INSIDE the trial balance appears at ONE place in the final accounts; an adjustment given OUTSIDE the trial balance appears at TWO places (double effect), e.g. P&L and balance sheet.
Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower (conservatism).
Closing stock given outside the trial balance: credit side of the trading account and current asset in the balance sheet.
Closing stock given inside the trial balance (with adjusted purchases, i.e. purchases already reduced by closing stock): shown only in the balance sheet, not in the trading account.

ex.q: Closing stock: cost ₹90,000, net realisable value ₹84,000; given outside the trial balance. Show its treatment.
st: Trading account credit side: Closing stock ₹84,000.
Balance sheet assets side: Closing stock ₹84,000.
ex.a: ₹84,000 on the credit of the trading account and as a current asset in the balance sheet.

topics.rl: Pharmacies in India must value near-expiry medicines below cost if they will fetch less; lower of cost or net realisable value keeps profits honest.

rv.summary: Adjustments bring the final accounts onto the accrual and matching basis. A trial balance item appears once; an adjustment outside it appears twice. Closing stock is valued at lower of cost and NRV.
focus: The one-place / two-place rule
Treatment of closing stock outside and inside the trial balance
Valuing closing stock
remember: Inside trial balance → one place; outside → two places
Closing stock outside TB: Cr trading + current asset in balance sheet
Closing stock inside TB (adjusted purchases): balance sheet only
traps: Don't show closing stock in trading when purchases are already adjusted
Don't value closing stock above cost

topics.t: Outstanding and prepaid expenses
topics.h: March salary is paid on 7 April. Next year's insurance is paid in January. Both payments land in the wrong year unless we adjust them.
p: Outstanding expense: incurred during the year but not yet paid. Adjusting entry: Dr Expense / Cr Outstanding Expense.
Treatment: add to the expense in the P&L (or trading) account; show as a current liability in the balance sheet.
Prepaid expense: paid in advance for a period beyond the year. Adjusting entry: Dr Prepaid Expense / Cr Expense.
Treatment: deduct from the expense in the P&L account; show as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Outstanding wages go to the trading account (wages are direct); outstanding salaries, rent and so on go to the P&L account.

ex.q: Rent paid during 2025-26 is ₹55,000 (11 months). Monthly rent ₹5,000. Insurance paid ₹12,000 on 1 October 2025 for one year. Show the adjustments.
st: Rent outstanding = 1 month = ₹5,000; P&L rent = 55,000 + 5,000 = ₹60,000; liability ₹5,000.
Insurance: October to March = 6 months used; prepaid = 6/12 × 12,000 = ₹6,000.
ex.a: Rent ₹60,000 (outstanding ₹5,000 liability); insurance ₹6,000 (prepaid ₹6,000 asset).

topics.rl: Indian companies show 'outstanding expenses' under other current liabilities and 'prepaid expenses' under other current assets in their Schedule III balance sheets.

rv.summary: Outstanding expenses are added to the expense and shown as a current liability; prepaid expenses are deducted from the expense and shown as a current asset.
focus: Find the expense charged to P&L with outstanding or prepaid items
Calculate prepaid amounts by months
Adjusting entries and balance sheet treatment
remember: Outstanding: Dr Expense / Cr Outstanding Expense → current liability
Prepaid: Dr Prepaid Expense / Cr Expense → current asset
Outstanding wages go to the trading account; others to P&L
traps: Don't show prepaid expenses as a liability
Count months correctly when finding the prepaid part

topics.t: Accrued income and income received in advance
topics.h: Your fixed deposit earned interest in March, but the bank credits it in April. You've earned it already. And a tenant who pays April's rent in March? You haven't earned that yet.
p: Accrued income: earned during the year but not yet received, e.g. interest accrued on investments, commission earned not received.
Adjusting entry: Dr Accrued Income / Cr Income. Treatment: add to the income in the P&L account; show as a current asset in the balance sheet.
Income received in advance (unearned income): received during the year for a service to be given next year, e.g. rent received in advance.
Adjusting entry: Dr Income / Cr Income Received in Advance. Treatment: deduct from the income in the P&L account; show as a current liability in the balance sheet.

ex.q: Investments ₹2,00,000 at 9% p.a.; interest received during the year ₹12,000. Rent received ₹60,000 includes ₹10,000 for the next year. Show the treatment.
st: P&L: interest ₹18,000; balance sheet: accrued interest ₹6,000 (current asset).
Rent: P&L 60,000 − 10,000 = ₹50,000; balance sheet: rent received in advance ₹10,000 (current liability).
ex.a: Interest ₹18,000 (accrued ₹6,000 asset); rent ₹50,000 (₹10,000 advance as liability).

topics.rl: Coaching institutes in India often collect a full year's fees upfront; at the financial year-end, fees for months not yet taught are income received in advance.

rv.summary: Accrued income is earned but not received: add it to the income and show it as a current asset. Income received in advance is not yet earned: deduct it from the income and show it as a current liability.
focus: Find the income credited to P&L
Calculate accrued interest on investments
Adjusting entries and balance sheet treatment
remember: Accrued: Dr Accrued Income / Cr Income → current asset
Advance: Dr Income / Cr Income Received in Advance → current liability
Accrued interest = Interest due for the year − Interest received
traps: Don't show income received in advance as an asset
Compare amount received with the amount due before deciding accrued or advance

topics.t: Depreciation and bad debts as adjustments
topics.h: A furniture showroom's balance sheet should not show three-year-old furniture at its original price, nor debtors who have vanished. Two adjustments fix that.
p: Depreciation adjustment: debit P&L account with depreciation; deduct it from the asset in the balance sheet.
If an asset is added during the year, depreciation on the addition is charged only for the months used (unless told otherwise).
Bad debts given inside the trial balance: debited to P&L only (debtors are already reduced).
Further bad debts given as an adjustment: add to bad debts in P&L, and deduct from debtors in the balance sheet.
Bad debts recovered (an amount written off earlier, now received) is credited to P&L as an income.

ex.q: Machinery ₹3,00,000 (including ₹60,000 bought on 1 October 2025). Depreciation 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March 2026. Debtors ₹1,20,000; bad debts in trial balance ₹3,000; further bad debts ₹2,000. Show the treatment.
st: Depreciation on ₹2,40,000 for 12 months = ₹24,000; on ₹60,000 for 6 months = ₹3,000; total ₹27,000.
P&L debit: depreciation ₹27,000; balance sheet: machinery 3,00,000 − 27,000 = ₹2,73,000.
Bad debts in P&L = 3,000 + 2,000 = ₹5,000; debtors in balance sheet = 1,20,000 − 2,000 = ₹1,18,000.
ex.a: Depreciation ₹27,000 (machinery ₹2,73,000); bad debts ₹5,000 (debtors ₹1,18,000).

topics.rl: Small distributors of FMCG products in towns like Nagpur write off unpaid dues of retailers who shut shop, and adjust their debtors list at the year-end.

rv.summary: Depreciation is debited to P&L and deducted from the asset. Bad debts inside the trial balance go only to P&L; further bad debts go to P&L and are deducted from debtors. Bad debts recovered are an income.
focus: Depreciation as an adjustment, including part-year additions
Bad debts inside vs outside the trial balance
Bad debts recovered
remember: Depreciation: Dr P&L; asset shown at cost less depreciation
Further bad debts: add in P&L and deduct from debtors
Bad debts recovered: credit P&L
traps: Don't deduct trial balance bad debts from debtors again
Charge depreciation on additions only for months used

topics.t: Provision for doubtful debts and provision for discount on debtors
topics.h: First remove the debtors who won't pay at all, then the ones who might not, and finally the discount the good ones will take for paying early. The order matters.
