p: Provision for doubtful debts (PDD) is calculated as a percentage of debtors after deducting further bad debts.
P&L charge = Bad debts (trial balance) + Further bad debts + New PDD − Old PDD. If the result is negative, the surplus is credited to P&L.
Balance sheet: Debtors − Further bad debts − New PDD.
Provision for discount on debtors is calculated on debtors after deducting further bad debts and the new PDD (only good debtors receive discount).
It is debited to P&L (less any old provision for discount) and deducted from debtors in the balance sheet.

ex.q: Debtors ₹1,00,000; further bad debts ₹4,000; PDD 5%; provision for discount 2%. Old PDD ₹3,000; bad debts in TB ₹1,000. Find the P&L charges and net debtors.
st: Debtors after bad debts = ₹96,000; new PDD = 5% = ₹4,800.
ex.a: P&L: ₹6,800 for bad and doubtful debts and ₹1,824 for discount; net debtors ₹89,376.

topics.rl: Wholesale traders in Mumbai's Crawford Market often allow a small discount for prompt payment, so they provide for it at year-end on their good debtors.

rv.summary: Provision for doubtful debts is a percentage of debtors after further bad debts. Provision for discount is calculated on debtors after both further bad debts and the new PDD. Both are charged to P&L and deducted from debtors.
focus: Calculate new PDD and the P&L charge or credit
Calculate provision for discount on good debtors
Net debtors in the balance sheet
remember: P&L charge = TB bad debts + Further bad debts + New PDD − Old PDD
Provision for discount = Rate × (Debtors − Further bad debts − New PDD)
Net debtors = Debtors − Further bad debts − New PDD − Provision for discount
traps: Don't calculate discount on gross debtors
A negative P&L charge means the surplus is credited to P&L

topics.t: Manager's commission
topics.h: A store manager is promised 10% of profit. But 10% of which profit: before her commission is deducted, or after? The answer changes her pay.
p: Commission on net profit before charging such commission: Commission = Net profit (before commission) × Rate ÷ 100.
Commission on net profit after charging such commission: Commission = Net profit (before commission) × Rate ÷ (100 + Rate).
The second is smaller, because the base itself is reduced by the commission.
Commission is debited to the P&L account. If unpaid at the year-end, it is shown as outstanding commission, a current liability.

ex.q: Net profit before commission ₹2,20,000. Manager's commission 10% (a) before charging commission, (b) after charging commission.

topics.rl: Retail chains in India often reward store managers with a commission on store profit; contracts specify whether it is calculated before or after the commission itself.

rv.summary: Manager's commission on profit before charging it is Profit × Rate ÷ 100; on profit after charging it is Profit × Rate ÷ (100 + Rate). It is debited to P&L and any unpaid part is a current liability.
focus: Commission before vs after charging such commission
Net profit after commission
Outstanding commission
remember: Before charging: Profit × Rate ÷ 100
After charging: Profit × Rate ÷ (100 + Rate)
Outstanding commission = Commission due − Amount paid (current liability)
traps: Don't use ÷ 100 when the commission is 'after charging such commission'
Always use profit BEFORE commission in both formulas

topics.t: Interest on capital and interest on drawings
topics.h: A proprietor who invests ₹10 lakh could have earned interest in a bank. Charging interest on capital shows whether the business earns more than that bank deposit would have.
p: Interest on capital: an expense of the business, debited to P&L; added to the owner's capital in the balance sheet. Entry: Dr Interest on Capital / Cr Capital.
Interest on drawings: an income of the business, credited to P&L; deducted from capital in the balance sheet (directly or through drawings). Entry: Dr Drawings (or Capital) / Cr Interest on Drawings.
Interest on capital = Capital × Rate × Time. If capital is added during the year, interest on the addition runs from the date of addition.
Interest on drawings = Drawings × Rate × Period for which the money was withdrawn.
These adjustments do not change the owner's final capital in total; they show the true earnings of the business.

ex.q: Capital ₹5,00,000 on 1 April 2025; interest on capital 8% p.a. Drawings ₹40,000 withdrawn on 1 October 2025; interest on drawings 6% p.a. Year ends 31 March 2026.
st: Interest on capital = 5,00,000 × 8% = ₹40,000 (debit P&L; add to capital).
Interest on drawings = 40,000 × 6% × 6/12 = ₹1,200 (credit P&L; deduct from capital).
ex.a: Interest on capital ₹40,000; interest on drawings ₹1,200.

topics.rl: A family-run sweet shop in Agra might find that after charging 8% interest on the owner's capital, the business earns barely more than a bank FD, a useful reality check.

rv.summary: Interest on capital is an expense debited to P&L and added to capital. Interest on drawings is an income credited to P&L and deducted from capital. Interest is calculated only for the period the money was used.
focus: Calculate interest on capital, including additions
Calculate interest on drawings by period
Closing capital after these adjustments
remember: Interest on capital = Capital × Rate × Time
Interest on drawings = Drawings × Rate × Period withdrawn
Entries: Dr Interest on Capital / Cr Capital; Dr Drawings / Cr Interest on Drawings
traps: Don't charge a full year's interest on capital added mid-year
Interest on drawings is an income for the business, not an expense

topics.t: Other adjustments: abnormal loss, goods withdrawn, samples, unrecorded items
topics.h: A godown fire, a proprietor taking goods home and boxes given away as samples all reduce the goods available for sale. Each needs a careful two-place treatment.
p: Abnormal loss of goods (fire, theft, flood) given as an adjustment: credit the trading account with the full cost of goods lost; debit P&L with the loss not covered by insurance; show the insurance claim admitted as a current asset.
Goods withdrawn by the proprietor (adjustment): deduct from purchases in the trading account (at cost) and add to drawings (deducted from capital).
Goods distributed as free samples (adjustment): deduct from purchases and debit advertisement in P&L.
Unrecorded credit sales: add to sales and to debtors. Unrecorded credit purchases (goods included in stock): add to purchases and to creditors.
Goods sent on approval and wrongly recorded as sales, not yet approved: reduce sales and debtors by the sale price, and include them in closing stock at cost.

ex.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 destroyed by fire; insurance claim admitted ₹30,000 (adjustment). Show the treatment.
st: Trading account credit: Loss by fire (goods destroyed) ₹50,000.
Balance sheet assets: insurance claim receivable ₹30,000.
ex.a: Trading Cr ₹50,000; P&L Dr ₹20,000; balance sheet asset ₹30,000.

topics.rl: After warehouse fires in industrial areas like Bhiwandi, traders record the stock lost in the trading account and the insurer's dues as a receivable until paid.

rv.summary: Abnormal loss is credited to trading at full cost, the uncovered part debited to P&L and the claim shown as an asset. Goods withdrawn and samples are deducted from purchases. Unrecorded sales or purchases and goods on approval are corrected in both places.
focus: Treatment of goods lost by fire or theft, with or without insurance
Goods withdrawn by owner and free samples
Unrecorded transactions and goods sent on approval
remember: Fire loss: Cr trading (full cost); Dr P&L (cost − claim); claim = current asset
Drawings of goods: less from purchases, add to drawings
Goods on approval: reduce sales and debtors at sale price; add to stock at cost
traps: Don't credit trading with only the uninsured part of the loss
Goods on approval go into stock at cost, not at sale price

topics.t: Final accounts with multiple adjustments
topics.h: This is the big question of the Class 11 exam: a trial balance with six or seven adjustments. Work methodically, one adjustment at a time, and the balance sheet will tally.
p: Work in order: closing stock; outstanding and prepaid expenses; accrued and advance incomes; depreciation; bad debts and provisions; manager's commission; interest on capital and drawings.
For each adjustment outside the trial balance, record both effects before moving on; tick it off.
Trading account first (gross profit), then P&L (net profit), then the balance sheet.
Capital in the balance sheet: Opening capital + Net profit + Interest on capital − Drawings − Interest on drawings.
If the balance sheet does not tally, check that each adjustment appears twice and each trial balance item once.

ex.q: Gross profit ₹2,00,000. Salaries ₹60,000 (outstanding ₹6,000). Rent ₹24,000 (prepaid ₹2,000). Commission received ₹10,000 (accrued ₹2,000). Depreciation on furniture ₹50,000 at 10%. Find net profit.

topics.rl: Class 11 accountancy papers set on the CBSE pattern regularly carry a long question on final accounts with adjustments; practising a fixed order saves time in the exam hall.

rv.summary: With many adjustments, work in a fixed order, record both effects of each adjustment, prepare trading, then P&L, then the balance sheet, and check that every adjustment appears twice.
focus: Net profit after several adjustments
Closing capital with interest on capital and drawings
Checking why a balance sheet does not tally
remember: Order: stock, outstanding/prepaid, accrued/advance, depreciation, bad debts and provisions, commission, interest
Capital = Opening + Net profit + Interest on capital − Drawings − Interest on drawings
Each adjustment: two places; each TB item: one place
traps: Don't forget the second effect of an adjustment
Don't add income received in advance to income

topics.ch: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records
topics.t: Incomplete records: meaning and features
topics.h: The paan shop near your school probably keeps a notebook of cash and a list of who owes money, and nothing else. That is accounting from incomplete records.
p: Incomplete records (often called the single entry system) are accounting records not kept strictly on the double entry system.
Usually only a cash book and personal accounts of debtors and creditors are kept; real accounts (assets) and nominal accounts (expenses, incomes) are generally not kept.
Features: no uniformity (methods differ from firm to firm); business and personal transactions are often mixed; heavy reliance on vouchers, memory and information from outside sources.
It is suited to small sole traders and partnership firms; companies cannot use it, because the law requires double entry books.

ex.q: A small florist keeps a cash diary and a list of hotel customers who pay monthly. She does not record rent, wages or her shop fittings in any account. What kind of records are these?
st: Only cash and personal (debtors) accounts are kept.
Nominal accounts (rent, wages) and real accounts (fittings) are missing.
So these are incomplete records, not a double entry system.
ex.a: Incomplete records (single entry).

topics.rl: Many street vendors registered under PM SVANidhi keep only cash and dues records; as they grow, digital apps help them shift to complete books.

rv.summary: Incomplete records are records not kept strictly on double entry, usually only a cash book and personal accounts. They lack uniformity, mix personal and business items and rely on vouchers and memory; companies cannot use them.
focus: Which accounts are kept and which are missing
Features of incomplete records
Who can and cannot use them
remember: Kept: cash book + personal accounts (debtors, creditors)
Missing: real and nominal accounts
Companies must keep double entry books by law
traps: Don't think a trial balance can be prepared from incomplete records
Incomplete records are not allowed for companies

topics.ch: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records
topics.t: Reasons for incomplete records and their limitations
topics.h: Incomplete records are cheap and easy, like cooking without a recipe. But when the tax officer or the bank manager asks for proof, the shortcut becomes expensive.
p: Reasons: used by small traders with few transactions; owners lack accounting knowledge; low cost (no trained accountant needed); simple and less time-consuming.

Limitations: no trial balance, so arithmetical accuracy cannot be checked; true profit or loss is hard to find; a proper balance sheet cannot be prepared; not acceptable to tax authorities as complete books; banks hesitate to lend; frauds and errors are hard to detect; no control over assets.
Profit can still be estimated by comparing capital at two dates (the statement of affairs method).
The conversion method (rebuilding full double entry final accounts from incomplete records) is outside the CBSE Class 11 syllabus; only the statement of affairs method is studied.

ex.q: A trader with incomplete records applies for a loan. Give two reasons the bank may hesitate.
st: Without double entry books, his profit figure cannot be verified.
He cannot produce a reliable balance sheet showing assets and liabilities.
So the bank cannot judge his repaying capacity or the security.
ex.a: Profit cannot be verified and no reliable balance sheet exists.

topics.rl: GST registration nudges many small Indian businesses to keep fuller records, because input tax credit needs proper invoices and books.

rv.summary: Small traders keep incomplete records because they are simple, cheap and need little knowledge. But no trial balance, true profit or proper balance sheet is possible, tax authorities and banks distrust them, and frauds are hard to detect.
focus: Reasons for keeping incomplete records
Limitations of incomplete records
Which profit method is in the syllabus
remember: Reasons: few transactions, little accounting knowledge, low cost, simple
Limitations: no trial balance, true profit hard, no proper balance sheet, not accepted by tax, banks hesitate, frauds hidden
Syllabus method: statement of affairs (comparing capitals)
traps: Don't list 'simple and cheap' as a limitation; it is a reason
The conversion method is not in the Class 11 CBSE syllabus

topics.ch: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records
topics.t: Statement of affairs and finding capital
topics.h: If you can't trace every transaction, take two photographs instead: one at the start of the year and one at the end. Each photograph of assets and liabilities is a statement of affairs.
p: A statement of affairs is a statement of all assets and liabilities on a date, prepared from incomplete records. The difference is the capital: Capital = Total assets − Total liabilities.
Format: like a balance sheet, liabilities and capital on the left, assets on the right; capital is the balancing figure.

Statement of affairs vs balance sheet: the statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records and values are often estimates; capital is a balancing figure; omissions are hard to detect. A balance sheet is prepared from a double entry ledger, values come from ledger balances, and capital is taken from the capital account.
Opening statement of affairs gives opening capital; closing statement of affairs gives closing capital.

ex.q: On 1 April: cash ₹15,000, stock ₹60,000, debtors ₹45,000, furniture ₹30,000, creditors ₹40,000. On 31 March: cash ₹20,000, stock ₹75,000, debtors ₹55,000, furniture ₹27,000, creditors ₹47,000. Find opening and closing capital.
ex.a: Opening capital ₹1,10,000; closing capital ₹1,30,000.

topics.rl: Income tax officers in India sometimes estimate a small trader's income by comparing his net worth at two dates, the same idea as a statement of affairs.

rv.summary: A statement of affairs lists assets and liabilities on a date from incomplete records; capital is the balancing figure. Opening and closing statements give opening and closing capital.
focus: Prepare a statement of affairs and find capital
Statement of affairs vs balance sheet
remember: Capital = Total assets − Total liabilities
Statement of affairs: from incomplete records, values often estimated, capital is balancing figure
Balance sheet: from double entry ledger, capital from capital account
traps: Don't take capital from a ledger account in a statement of affairs
A missing asset or liability silently changes the capital figure

topics.ch: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records
topics.t: Finding profit by comparing capitals
topics.h: If your piggy bank grew from ₹1,000 to ₹1,500, did you earn ₹500? Only if you didn't take money out or put extra in. Business profit works the same way.
p: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital.
Drawings are added back because they reduced closing capital but were not a loss of the business.
Additional capital is deducted because it increased closing capital but was not earned.
A negative result means a loss.

The formula can be rearranged to find any missing figure: Opening capital = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Profit; Drawings = Profit + Opening capital + Additional capital − Closing capital.

ex.q: Opening capital ₹2,00,000; closing capital ₹2,60,000; drawings ₹30,000; additional capital ₹40,000. Find profit.

topics.rl: A Kolkata sari trader who doesn't keep full books can still tell her CA how much her business earned by listing what she owned and owed at both year-ends, plus what she took home.

rv.summary: Profit from incomplete records is found by comparing capitals: Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital. A negative answer is a loss, and the formula can be rearranged for any missing figure.
focus: Calculate profit or loss by comparing capitals
Find a missing opening capital, drawings or additional capital
remember: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital
Drawings are added back; additional capital is deducted
Opening capital = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Profit
traps: Don't subtract drawings; add them back
Don't treat additional capital as profit

topics.ch: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records
topics.t: Statement of profit or loss with adjustments
topics.h: The capital-comparison profit is a rough figure. Before reporting it, an accountant charges interest on capital, adds interest on drawings and accounts for items like depreciation that the closing figures may have missed.
p: Statement of profit or loss format: Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital = Adjusted closing capital; less Opening capital = Profit before adjustments.

Then: Less interest on capital; add interest on drawings. Also adjust for depreciation, provision for doubtful debts, further bad debts, outstanding expenses (less) and accrued income or prepaid expenses (add), if they have not already been reflected in the closing statement of affairs.
Interest on capital is usually calculated on opening capital (and on additional capital from its date).
The final figure is the net profit (or loss) for the year.
Best practice: apply asset-related adjustments (depreciation, bad debts, provisions, outstanding items) while preparing the closing statement of affairs, so that closing capital is correct.

ex.q: Profit before adjustments ₹60,000. Opening capital ₹2,00,000; interest on capital 5%. Interest on drawings ₹1,000. Find net profit.

topics.rl: Chartered accountants in small towns often prepare such statements for traders' income tax returns, then advise them to keep complete books from the next year.

rv.summary: A statement of profit or loss starts with adjusted closing capital less opening capital, then deducts interest on capital and adds interest on drawings, and adjusts for items like depreciation not already in the closing statement of affairs.
focus: Prepare a statement of profit or loss
Interest on capital and interest on drawings
Adjustments for depreciation and similar items
remember: Adjusted closing capital = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital
Profit before adjustments = Adjusted closing capital − Opening capital
Net profit = Profit before adjustments − Interest on capital + Interest on drawings (± other adjustments)
traps: Don't add interest on capital; deduct it
Don't adjust depreciation twice if it is already in the closing statement of affairs

qa.q: Which activity of accounting answers the question 'Is this event a financial transaction that should be recorded?'
qa.a: Identifying
qa.e: Identifying means picking out the events that are financial in nature and relevant to the business.

qa.q: A firm records only events that can be expressed in rupees. Which activity of accounting does this describe?
qa.a: Measuring
qa.e: Measuring means quantifying business transactions in money; money is the common unit of accounting.

qa.q: Recording in accounting is done in which order?
qa.a: Chronological order, that is, in order of date
qa.e: Transactions are entered in books of original entry in the order in which they occur (date-wise).

qa.q: Which is the best description of accounting?
qa.a: Identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information to users for decisions
qa.e: Accounting is a complete process that ends with useful information reaching users; recording alone is only one part.

qa.q: Sneha's bakery: she bought flour for ₹6,000, paid wages ₹4,000 and hired a new baker who joins next month. What total amount is recorded today?
qa.e: Flour purchase and wages paid are transactions. Hiring a baker who has not yet worked or been paid involves no money value today.

qa.q: The final stage of the accounting process, in which statements reach owners, lenders and others, is called
qa.a: Communicating
qa.e: Communicating means passing summarised information to users in the form of reports and financial statements.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The resignation of a firm's best salesperson is not recorded in the books.
Reason (R): Accounting records only events that can be measured in money.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Losing a talented person may hurt the business, but it cannot be measured in rupees, so it is not recorded. R explains A exactly.

qa.q: Classifying and summarising are carried out mainly after which activity?
qa.a: Recording
qa.e: Once transactions are recorded in the journal, they are classified into ledger accounts and summarised into statements.

qa.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes book-keeping from accounting?
qa.a: Book-keeping is the recording stage, while accounting also analyses, interprets and communicates
qa.e: Book-keeping is the foundation; accounting is wider and includes analysing and interpreting the recorded data.

qa.q: Why is accounting called the 'language of business'?
qa.a: It communicates the financial results of a business to users in a common, understood form
qa.e: Just as a language passes on ideas, accounting passes on financial information about a business to all interested users.

qa.q: In accounting as an information system, financial statements are the
qa.a: Output
qa.e: Transactions are the input, recording and summarising is the processing, and statements and reports are the output.

qa.q: Which task is part of accounting but NOT of book-keeping?
qa.a: Interpreting the results shown by the financial statements
qa.e: Recording and posting are book-keeping tasks; interpretation of results is done at the accounting stage.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Book-keeping is the base for accounting.
Reason (R): Accounting cannot analyse data until transactions have been recorded and classified.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Analysis and interpretation need recorded data, which book-keeping provides; so book-keeping is the foundation.

qa.q: An accounting information system collects, processes and reports data mainly to help
qa.a: Users make economic decisions
qa.e: The whole purpose of the system is decision-useful financial information for users.

qa.q: Who usually performs book-keeping in a large business?
qa.a: Junior staff or clerks, often using accounting software
qa.e: Book-keeping is routine and clerical, so it is done by junior staff or software; analysis needs senior accountants.

qa.q: A company's software records 5,000 sales a day. What does the processing stage of the accounting information system do with them?
qa.a: Records, classifies and summarises them
qa.e: Processing turns raw transactions into organised, summarised data that can be reported.

qa.q: Which of the following is an internal user of accounting information?
qa.a: Management
qa.e: Management works inside the organisation and uses accounts for planning and control.

qa.q: A bank is deciding whether to grant a long-term loan to a firm. What information does it mainly look for?
qa.a: The firm's ability to repay the loan and pay interest
qa.e: Lenders care about solvency and repaying capacity, which accounts reveal.

qa.q: Suppliers who sell goods on credit to a firm are most interested in its
qa.a: Short-term ability to pay (liquidity)
qa.e: Trade creditors are paid within a short credit period, so they check whether the firm can pay its short-term dues.

qa.q: Which user group uses accounting information mainly to assess taxes such as income tax and GST?
qa.a: Government and tax authorities
qa.e: Tax authorities rely on accounts to work out the tax payable and to check compliance.

qa.q: Workers of a cement company want a higher bonus. Why would they study the company's accounts?
qa.a: Bonus and wage increases depend on the profits the company earns
qa.e: Employees use profit figures to argue for bonus and to judge their job security.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Potential investors are external users of accounting information.
Reason (R): They do not take part in the internal management of the business.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: External users are those outside management; potential investors are not yet part of the firm, so they are external.

qa.q: Case: Kavya plans to buy shares of a listed company. Which information is most useful for her?
qa.a: Profitability, growth and the safety of her investment
qa.e: Investors want to know whether the investment will earn returns and be safe.

qa.q: Customers of a firm that gives long warranties are interested in its accounts because they want to know
qa.a: Whether the firm will continue to exist and honour its commitments
qa.e: Customers want continuity of supply and service, which depends on the firm staying financially sound.

qa.q: Accounting information that is verifiable and free from error and bias is said to be
qa.a: Reliable
qa.e: Reliability means users can depend on the information because it is factual and verifiable.

qa.q: Annual accounts are published 18 months after the year ends. Which characteristic is mainly lost?
qa.a: Relevance
qa.e: Information must be timely to influence decisions; late information loses relevance even if accurate.

qa.q: Comparing Tata Motors' profit this year with its profit last year is an example of
qa.a: Inter-period comparison
qa.e: Comparing the same firm over different periods is inter-period comparison.

qa.q: Why must accounting information be understandable?
qa.a: Users can act only on information they can make sense of
qa.e: If users cannot understand the information, it cannot help them decide, however accurate it is.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Comparability requires that a firm follow consistent accounting methods over time.
Reason (R): If methods change every year, differences in results may arise from the method rather than from performance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Consistent methods make year-to-year figures comparable; R gives the reason.

qa.q: Which feature belongs to relevance rather than reliability?
qa.a: Predictive and feedback value
qa.e: Relevance covers timeliness, predictive value and feedback value; the other three are parts of reliability.

qa.q: Case: Two accountants independently check a firm's records and arrive at the same profit figure. This shows the information is
qa.a: Reliable (verifiable)
qa.e: When independent persons reach the same result, the information is verifiable and hence reliable.

qa.q: How many qualitative characteristics of accounting information are explained in NCERT Class 11?
qa.e: They are reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability.

qa.q: Which of the following is NOT an objective of accounting?
qa.a: Fixing the selling price of goods for the government
qa.e: Price fixing is a business or government decision, not an objective of accounting.

qa.q: Which statement shows the financial position of a business on a particular date?
qa.a: Balance sheet
qa.e: The balance sheet lists assets and liabilities on a date, showing the financial position.

qa.q: Profit or loss for a period is found by
qa.a: Matching revenues of the period with the expenses of the same period
qa.e: Profit = revenues − expenses of the same accounting period.

qa.q: A company has highly loyal, skilled staff, but this is not shown in its accounts. This is because accounting
qa.a: Records only facts that can be measured in money
qa.e: Non-monetary facts like staff quality are ignored by accounting, a known limitation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Accounting information may not show the current value of assets.
Reason (R): Assets are generally recorded at historical cost.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the cost paid at purchase is recorded, later price changes are not reflected.

qa.q: Estimating the useful life of a machine and the amount of bad debts introduces which limitation?
qa.a: Accounting depends on estimates and judgement
qa.e: Several figures depend on estimates, so results may differ from reality.

qa.q: Calling accounting a 'historical record' means that it
qa.a: Records transactions in the order in which they happened
qa.e: Accounting keeps a chronological record of past financial events.

qa.q: Which role of accounting highlights that it helps users know the real wealth of a business today?
qa.a: Current economic reality
qa.e: As current economic reality, accounting aims to show the present financial state of the business.

qa.q: Assets of a firm are ₹8,00,000 and its liabilities are ₹3,00,000. What is the capital?
qa.e: Capital is the owner's claim, which equals assets minus outsiders' claims.

qa.q: Which of the following is a current asset?
qa.a: Debtors
qa.e: Debtors are expected to be collected in cash within the year, so they are current assets.

qa.q: A loan taken from a bank that is repayable after five years is a
qa.a: Non-current liability
qa.e: Liabilities payable after more than one year are non-current (long-term).

qa.q: Capital of a firm is ₹2,40,000 and liabilities are ₹1,60,000. What are the total assets?
qa.e: Assets = Liabilities + Capital.

qa.q: Which of these is a business transaction?
qa.a: Purchase of a computer for the office for ₹45,000
qa.e: Only the purchase involves an actual exchange of money or money's worth now.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Capital is treated as a liability of the business.
Reason (R): The business is separate from its owner and owes the capital to the owner.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the business entity is separate from the owner, the capital is the owner's claim against the business.

qa.q: A firm's assets: land ₹5,00,000, stock ₹1,50,000, cash ₹50,000. Liabilities: creditors ₹1,00,000. What is the owner's capital?
qa.e: Total assets are ₹7,00,000; deducting creditors ₹1,00,000 gives the owner's claim.

qa.q: Bank overdraft is classified as a
qa.a: Current liability
qa.e: An overdraft is money owed to the bank, repayable on demand, so it is a current liability.

qa.q: Goods of list price ₹80,000 are sold at 15% trade discount. What amount is recorded as sales?
qa.e: Trade discount is deducted on the invoice itself and is not recorded, so sales are recorded at the net amount.

qa.q: Goods listed at ₹30,000 are sold at 10% trade discount and 5% cash discount, the buyer paying at once. What is the cash discount?
qa.e: Cash discount is computed on the amount after trade discount.

qa.q: Which of these is a gain rather than revenue?
qa.a: Profit on the sale of an old delivery van
qa.e: A gain arises from incidental events like selling a fixed asset; the others come from regular operations.

qa.q: Why is trade discount not recorded in the books of accounts?
qa.a: It is deducted from the list price on the invoice itself, so only the net amount is the transaction value
qa.e: The transaction takes place at the net price; the list price is never the actual exchange value.

qa.q: Expenditure on buying a machine that will be used for 10 years is
qa.a: Capital expenditure
qa.e: Its benefit lasts beyond one year, so it is capital expenditure; only its depreciation becomes an expense each year.

qa.q: A firm earned revenue of ₹6,50,000 and incurred expenses of ₹7,10,000. What is the result?
qa.e: Expenses exceed revenue, so the firm suffers a loss of ₹60,000.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cash discount allowed is recorded in the books of the seller.
Reason (R): Cash discount is allowed on the list price before the invoice is prepared.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Cash discount is recorded as a loss for the seller, but it is allowed at the time of payment on the invoice amount, not on the list price.

qa.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes expense from expenditure?
qa.a: Expense is the cost used up in earning revenue of a period; expenditure is spending whose benefit may last longer
qa.e: All expenses arise from expenditure, but not all expenditure becomes this year's expense.

qa.q: A furniture dealer buys tables to resell. For him, these tables are
qa.a: Goods
qa.e: Items bought for resale in the regular course of business are goods for that business.

qa.q: The owner withdraws goods costing ₹3,000 for personal use. This is
qa.a: Drawings
qa.e: Any cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use is drawings, which reduces capital.

qa.q: A person to whom the business owes money for goods bought on credit is a
qa.a: Creditor
qa.e: Creditors are those to whom the business owes money.

qa.q: Opening stock ₹25,000, purchases ₹1,75,000, closing stock ₹40,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
qa.e: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock.

qa.q: A firm's capital was ₹2,00,000. The owner withdrew ₹15,000 for personal use and the firm earned a profit of ₹35,000. What is the closing capital?
qa.e: Profit increases capital and drawings reduce it.

qa.q: Which document is an example of a voucher?
qa.a: A cash memo issued for a cash sale
qa.e: A voucher is documentary evidence of a transaction that has taken place; a cash memo proves a cash sale.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Purchases include both cash and credit purchases of goods.
Reason (R): Purchases means buying only fixed assets for the business.
qa.a: A is true but R is false
qa.e: Purchases are goods bought for resale or production, whether for cash or on credit. Buying fixed assets is not 'purchases' in accounting.

qa.q: Total credit sales ₹3,00,000; cash received from these customers ₹2,20,000. What is the amount of debtors at the end?
qa.e: Debtors are customers who still owe the business.

qa.q: GAAP stands for
qa.a: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
qa.e: GAAP are Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the common rules of accounting.

qa.q: The main reason accounting needs a common theory base is to make financial statements
qa.a: Uniform, comparable and reliable
qa.e: Common principles allow users to compare statements across firms and periods and trust them.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a term used for accounting principles?
qa.a: Accounting vouchers
qa.e: Vouchers are documentary evidence; concepts, conventions, postulates and assumptions are names for principles.

qa.q: How do GAAP come into existence?
qa.a: They evolve through experience, usage, professional acceptance and regulation
qa.e: GAAP are man-made and develop gradually; they also change with time.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Accounting principles are subject to change over time.
Reason (R): Accounting principles are man-made and respond to changing business needs.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since principles are man-made, they adapt as business, law and user needs change.

qa.q: Inter-firm comparison of financial statements is meaningful only when the firms
qa.a: Follow common accounting principles
qa.e: Comparisons make sense only when the figures are prepared on the same basis.

qa.q: Case: A trader changes his accounting rules each year so that profit looks steady. Which benefit of GAAP is lost?
qa.a: Reliability and comparability of the statements
qa.e: Changing rules at will makes statements unreliable and impossible to compare across years.

qa.q: Which body in India plays a major role in developing accounting principles and standards?
qa.a: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI)
qa.e: ICAI, through its Accounting Standards Board, formulates accounting standards in India.

qa.q: Which concept requires capital to be shown as a liability in the balance sheet?
qa.a: Business entity concept
qa.e: Because the business is separate from its owner, the capital provided by the owner is owed to the owner.

qa.q: A firm does not record the fact that its managing director has an excellent reputation. Which concept explains this?
qa.a: Money measurement concept
qa.e: Reputation cannot be measured in money, so it is not recorded.

qa.q: Fixed assets are shown at cost less depreciation rather than at their realisable value because of the
qa.a: Going concern concept
qa.e: The firm is expected to keep using the assets, so their forced-sale value is irrelevant.

qa.q: In India, the financial year for accounting purposes generally runs from
qa.a: 1 April to 31 March
qa.e: The Companies Act and income tax law follow the April to March financial year.

qa.q: Which limitation of the money measurement concept is shown when ₹10 lakh spent on land in 2000 is added to ₹10 lakh spent on land in 2025?
qa.a: The value of money changes over time but is treated as stable
qa.e: Rupees of different years have different purchasing power, yet accounts add them as equal.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under the going concern concept, the cost of a machine is spread over its useful life.
Reason (R): The business is assumed to continue long enough to use the machine fully.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since the firm is expected to continue, the cost is charged as depreciation over the years of use.

qa.q: Case: Rakesh's firm withdraws ₹20,000 to pay for his daughter's wedding. Recording this as a business expense violates the
qa.a: Business entity concept
qa.e: Personal spending is drawings; the business entity concept keeps owner's and firm's affairs apart.

qa.q: Why do listed companies prepare quarterly results even though the financial year is twelve months?
qa.a: Users need timely information for decisions; the accounting period concept allows shorter interim periods
qa.e: Interim reporting divides the life of the business into shorter periods to provide timely information.

qa.q: A machine is purchased for ₹4,50,000; carriage ₹20,000 and installation charges ₹30,000 are paid. At what amount is it recorded?
qa.e: All costs to bring the asset into working condition form part of its cost.

qa.q: The accounting equation is based on which concept?
qa.a: Dual aspect concept
qa.e: Every transaction affects two sides equally, so Assets always equal Liabilities + Capital.

qa.q: Under the revenue recognition concept, revenue from a credit sale is recognised
qa.a: On the date the goods are sold
qa.e: Revenue is recognised when the right to receive it arises, i.e. when the sale takes place.

qa.q: Total assets of a business are ₹12,00,000 and outsiders' liabilities are ₹4,50,000. The owner's equity is
qa.e: Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Land bought for ₹50 lakh is still shown at ₹50 lakh though its market value is now ₹80 lakh.
Reason (R): Under the cost concept assets are recorded at acquisition cost.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The cost concept records assets at historical cost; land is not depreciated, so it stays at cost.

qa.q: A firm receives ₹60,000 in March 2026 as advance for goods to be delivered in June 2026. For 2025-26 this amount is
qa.a: A liability (advance from customer), not revenue
qa.e: Revenue arises only when goods are delivered; until then the firm owes the goods.

qa.q: Which item is NOT included in the cost of a newly bought delivery van under the cost concept?
qa.a: Fuel used on the van's daily delivery trips
qa.e: Running costs like fuel are revenue expenses; acquisition costs are capitalised.

qa.q: Under the dual aspect concept, when goods of ₹25,000 are bought on credit,
qa.a: Stock increases by ₹25,000 and creditors increase by ₹25,000
qa.e: An asset (stock) and a liability (creditors) both rise by the same amount.

qa.q: Charging outstanding wages to the current year's profit and loss account follows the
qa.a: Matching concept
qa.e: The wages helped earn this year's revenue, so they are matched with it.

qa.q: A company discloses in notes that a lawsuit against it may cost ₹50 lakh. Which concept requires this?
qa.a: Full disclosure concept
qa.e: Material information that affects users' decisions must be disclosed, even if not yet a liability.

qa.q: A firm uses the straight line method of depreciation one year and the written down value method the next, without any reason or disclosure. Which concept is violated?
qa.a: Consistency concept
qa.e: Consistency requires the same method to be followed from year to year.

qa.q: Insurance premium of ₹24,000 for 12 months is paid on 1 January 2026. Books close on 31 March 2026. How much is the expense for 2025-26?
qa.e: Only 3 months (January to March) relate to 2025-26; the remaining 9 months are prepaid.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A firm may change its method of stock valuation.
Reason (R): The consistency concept allows a change if it gives a better presentation, with disclosure of its effect.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Consistency is not rigid; justified changes are allowed but must be disclosed.

qa.q: Which schedule of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format of the balance sheet and statement of profit and loss, supporting full disclosure?
qa.a: Schedule III
qa.e: Schedule III gives the format and disclosure requirements for company financial statements.

qa.q: Case: In 2025-26 a trader earned ₹5,00,000 revenue. Rent for the year is ₹60,000, of which ₹10,000 is still unpaid. What rent should be charged against this revenue?
qa.e: Matching charges the full rent of the year, paid or unpaid.

qa.q: Which statement about the matching concept is correct?
qa.a: It decides which expenses are charged against a period's revenue
qa.e: Matching links the expenses of a period with the revenue of that same period.

qa.q: Closing stock: cost ₹80,000, net realisable value ₹92,000. At what value is it shown?
qa.e: Stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower; here cost is lower.

qa.q: A firm creates a provision for doubtful debts in anticipation of losses. This follows the
qa.a: Conservatism concept
qa.e: Prudence requires providing for all possible losses.

qa.q: A ₹40 calculator bought for the office is charged as an expense even though it will last 3 years. This follows the
qa.a: Materiality concept
qa.e: The amount is too small to influence any decision, so detailed treatment as an asset is unnecessary.

qa.q: Recording transactions only on the basis of invoices, receipts and other verifiable evidence follows the
qa.a: Objectivity concept
qa.e: Objectivity means accounting figures can be verified and are free from personal bias.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Excessive conservatism is not desirable.
Reason (R): It leads to understatement of profits and creation of secret reserves.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Over-caution hides the true profit and position, which defeats reliability; R explains A.

qa.q: Which treatment follows conservatism?
qa.a: Ignoring an expected profit but recording an expected loss
qa.e: Prudence: anticipate no profit, provide for all possible losses.

qa.q: Case: A firm values its closing stock at its estimated selling price ₹2,50,000 though it cost ₹2,00,000. The concept violated is
qa.a: Conservatism
qa.e: Valuing stock above cost records an unrealised profit, which prudence does not allow.

qa.q: Stock costing ₹60,000 has a net realisable value of ₹45,000. By how much will profit be lower if stock is valued correctly rather than at cost?
qa.e: Valuing stock at the lower NRV reduces closing stock, and so profit, by the difference.

qa.q: Under which system are both aspects of every transaction recorded?
qa.a: Double entry system
qa.e: Double entry records the debit and credit aspects of every transaction.

qa.q: A trial balance can be prepared only under the
qa.a: Double entry system
qa.e: Only double entry gives equal debit and credit totals to check.

qa.q: The single entry system generally maintains
qa.a: Cash book and personal accounts only
qa.e: Small traders keep the cash book and debtors and creditors accounts; other accounts are missing.

qa.q: Which is a merit of the single entry system?
qa.a: It is simple and economical
qa.e: Its only real advantages are simplicity and low cost.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Fraud is easier to hide under the single entry system.
Reason (R): The single entry system does not provide an arithmetical check like the trial balance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without complete records and a trial balance, manipulation is harder to detect.

qa.q: Which business would most likely use the single entry system?
qa.a: A small neighbourhood grocery shop
qa.e: Small traders with limited transactions and little accounting knowledge often keep incomplete records.

qa.q: Case: A trader wants a bank loan but his records show only cash and personal accounts. Why may the bank hesitate?
qa.a: His records are incomplete, so profit and financial position are not reliable
qa.e: Lenders need reliable statements; single entry records cannot give a dependable profit figure or balance sheet.

qa.q: Which statement correctly compares the two systems?
qa.a: Double entry is complete and allows checking of accuracy; single entry is incomplete and does not
qa.e: Completeness and checkability distinguish double entry from single entry.

qa.q: Under the cash basis of accounting, income is recorded when
qa.a: Cash is actually received
qa.e: The cash basis records only actual cash receipts and payments.

qa.q: Which basis of accounting must companies in India follow?
qa.a: Accrual basis
qa.e: The Companies Act, 2013 requires companies to keep books on the accrual basis.

qa.q: During a year, fees earned were ₹8,00,000 (₹7,10,000 received) and expenses incurred were ₹5,00,000 (₹4,40,000 paid). What is the profit under the accrual basis?
qa.e: Accrual basis takes income earned and expenses incurred.

qa.q: During a year, fees received in cash were ₹7,10,000 (fees earned ₹8,00,000) and expenses paid in cash were ₹4,40,000 (expenses incurred ₹5,00,000). What is the profit under the cash basis?
qa.e: Cash basis profit = cash received − cash paid.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The accrual basis gives a truer picture of profit than the cash basis.
Reason (R): The accrual basis matches revenue earned with expenses incurred in the same period.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: By matching earned revenue with incurred expenses, accrual profit reflects the period's real performance.

qa.q: Under the cash basis, which of these items is ignored?
qa.a: Outstanding rent of ₹5,000
qa.e: Outstanding items involve no cash movement, so the cash basis ignores them.

qa.q: Case: A doctor received ₹50,000 in March 2026 for treatment to be given in April 2026. Under the accrual basis, for 2025-26 this is
qa.a: Income received in advance (a liability), not income
qa.e: The service is not yet rendered, so the income is not earned in 2025-26.

qa.q: A firm's accrual profit is ₹2,00,000. Outstanding income is ₹30,000 and outstanding expenses are ₹20,000 (no other differences). What is the cash-basis profit?
qa.e: Remove unreceived income (it was not received in cash) and add back unpaid expenses (not paid in cash).

qa.q: Accounting standards deal with which aspects of transactions?
qa.a: Recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure
qa.e: Standards guide how items are recognised, measured, presented and disclosed.

qa.q: In India, accounting standards are formulated by the
qa.a: Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI
qa.e: The ASB of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India formulates them.

qa.q: IFRS are issued by the
qa.a: International Accounting Standards Board (IASB)
qa.e: The IASB, based in London, issues International Financial Reporting Standards.

qa.q: India's approach to IFRS has been to
qa.a: Converge Indian standards with IFRS (Ind AS)
qa.e: India issued Ind AS converged with IFRS, with some carve-outs suited to Indian conditions.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Accounting standards improve inter-firm comparability.
Reason (R): They reduce the number of alternative accounting treatments available.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Fewer alternatives mean firms treat similar items similarly, so their statements become comparable.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of accounting standards?
qa.a: They cannot override the provisions of law
qa.e: If a statute conflicts with a standard, the statute prevails.

qa.q: The Accounting Standards Board of ICAI was constituted in the year
qa.e: ICAI set up the ASB in 1977 to formulate accounting standards.

qa.q: Case: A listed Indian company prepares its accounts under Ind AS. This helps it mainly because
qa.a: Its statements become comparable with global companies using IFRS
qa.e: Convergence with IFRS improves global comparability and access to foreign capital.

qa.q: GST came into force in India on
qa.a: 1 July 2017
qa.e: GST was rolled out across India from 1 July 2017.

qa.q: A Jaipur dealer sells goods worth ₹80,000 to a Jodhpur dealer. GST is 18%. What is the CGST?
qa.e: Jaipur and Jodhpur are both in Rajasthan, so CGST and SGST each apply at 9%.

qa.q: A Mumbai firm sells goods worth ₹1,20,000 to a buyer in Goa. GST is 18%. Which tax is charged and how much?
qa.e: Maharashtra to Goa is an inter-state supply, so IGST at the full rate applies.

qa.q: A dealer collected output GST of ₹27,000 on sales and paid input GST of ₹19,000 on purchases. How much GST must he deposit with the government?
qa.e: Input tax credit is set off against output tax; only the balance is paid.

qa.q: GST is called a destination-based tax because
qa.a: Tax goes to the state where the goods or services are consumed
qa.e: Under GST, the tax revenue accrues to the consuming (destination) state.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): GST removes the cascading effect of taxes.
Reason (R): Under GST, input tax credit is available for tax paid on purchases.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because input tax is credited, tax is not charged on tax already paid; R explains A.

qa.q: Which tax replaces SGST for intra-state supplies in a union territory without a legislature, such as Chandigarh?
qa.a: UTGST
qa.e: In union territories without a legislature, UTGST is levied along with CGST.

qa.q: Case: Goods worth ₹60,000 are sold within Kerala at 5% GST. What is the total invoice value including GST?
Which source document is issued by a seller for a credit sale?
qa.a: Invoice (bill)
qa.e: An invoice shows quantity, price and terms of a credit sale.

qa.q: When a buyer returns goods to a supplier, the buyer sends a
qa.a: Debit note
qa.e: The buyer debits the supplier's account and informs him through a debit note.

qa.q: Which document is used to deposit cash into a bank account?
qa.a: Pay-in-slip
qa.e: A pay-in-slip is filled when depositing cash or cheques into a bank.

qa.q: A credit note is sent by the
qa.a: Seller to the buyer, when goods are returned
qa.e: The seller credits the buyer's account for returned goods and informs him through a credit note.

qa.q: Which statement best defines a business transaction?
qa.a: An exchange of money or money's worth between the business and another party
qa.e: Only an actual exchange of economic value is a transaction.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Source documents are the basis for recording entries in the books.
Reason (R): They provide written evidence that a transaction took place.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Entries must be supported by evidence; source documents provide that evidence.

qa.q: A salary slip given to an employee is a source document for recording
qa.a: Salary paid
qa.e: It shows the salary payable and paid to an employee.

qa.q: Case: A retailer sells goods for cash and gives the customer a slip showing items and amount. This slip is a
qa.a: Cash memo
qa.e: A cash memo is the proof of a cash sale.

qa.q: A voucher prepared for cash received from a customer is a
qa.a: Credit voucher
qa.e: Cash receipts are recorded on credit (receipt) vouchers.

qa.q: Goods purchased on credit from Rahul for ₹25,000 are recorded on a
qa.a: Transfer (journal) voucher
qa.e: No cash is involved, so a non-cash transfer voucher is used.

qa.q: A voucher records one debit and two credits. It is a
qa.a: Compound voucher
qa.e: One debit with multiple credits (or vice versa) makes a compound voucher.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT normally a content of an accounting voucher?
qa.a: The customer's personal phone contacts
qa.e: Vouchers contain identification, accounts, amounts, narration and signatures, not unrelated personal data.

qa.q: Salary of ₹30,000 and rent of ₹10,000 are paid together by one cheque of ₹40,000. The voucher is a
qa.a: Compound voucher
qa.e: Two debits (salary, rent) and one credit (bank) make it a compound voucher.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Accounting vouchers are prepared on the basis of source documents.
Reason (R): Source documents contain the evidence of transactions that vouchers record.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Vouchers translate the evidence in source documents into debits and credits.

qa.q: Case: A firm buys machinery ₹2,00,000 and furniture ₹50,000, paying ₹1,50,000 by cheque and owing the rest to the supplier. Which voucher is prepared?
qa.a: Complex voucher
qa.e: Two debits (machinery, furniture) and two credits (bank, supplier) make a complex voucher.

qa.q: Under a transaction voucher, how many accounts are debited?
qa.e: A transaction voucher has exactly one debit and one credit.

qa.q: Assets of a firm are ₹10,00,000 and capital is ₹6,50,000. What are the liabilities?
qa.e: Liabilities = Assets − Capital.

qa.q: Furniture is purchased for cash ₹25,000. What is the effect on the accounting equation?
qa.a: One asset increases and another asset decreases; totals unchanged
qa.e: Furniture goes up and cash goes down by the same amount.

qa.q: Which transaction increases both assets and liabilities?
qa.a: Goods purchased on credit
qa.e: Stock (asset) and creditors (liability) both rise.

qa.q: A creditor of ₹18,000 is paid in cash. What happens?
qa.a: Assets and liabilities both decrease by ₹18,000
qa.e: Cash (asset) falls and creditors (liability) fall by the same amount.

qa.q: Opening: assets ₹4,00,000, liabilities ₹1,00,000. The firm takes a bank loan of ₹50,000 in cash. What is the capital after this?
qa.e: A loan raises assets and liabilities equally; capital is unchanged.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Every transaction keeps the accounting equation in balance.
Reason (R): Every transaction has two equal effects.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because each transaction has equal dual effects, both sides change by the same amount or stay unchanged.

qa.q: A creditor of ₹20,000 accepts a bill payable for the amount. What is the effect?
qa.a: One liability decreases and another liability increases
qa.e: Creditors fall and bills payable rise; totals are unchanged.

qa.q: Case: Raghav starts with ₹2,00,000 cash, buys goods for cash ₹80,000 and buys a computer on credit ₹40,000. What are total assets?
qa.e: Cash 1,20,000 + stock 80,000 + computer 40,000.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹50,000 are sold for ₹65,000 in cash. By how much does capital increase?
qa.e: Only the profit (sale price − cost) adds to capital.

qa.q: Salary of ₹12,000 is outstanding at year-end. Its effect on the equation is
qa.a: Liabilities increase and capital decreases by ₹12,000
qa.e: An outstanding expense creates a liability and reduces capital through the expense.

qa.q: The owner takes goods costing ₹6,000 for personal use. The effect is
qa.a: Stock decreases and capital decreases by ₹6,000
qa.e: Drawings reduce both the asset given away and the owner's capital.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000. During the year: profit ₹70,000, drawings ₹25,000, additional capital ₹40,000. What is the closing capital?
qa.e: Closing capital = Opening + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings.

qa.q: Rahul starts business with cash ₹2,50,000. He buys goods on credit ₹60,000 and pays rent ₹8,000 in cash. What is the total of assets?
Meena starts business with cash ₹2,50,000, buys goods on credit ₹60,000 and pays rent ₹8,000 in cash. What is her capital now?
qa.e: Capital falls by the rent expense; the credit purchase does not change capital.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Payment of rent reduces capital.
Reason (R): Expenses reduce the owner's equity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Expenses reduce profit, and so reduce the owner's claim (capital).

qa.q: Interest of ₹4,000 is received in cash. Its effect on the equation is
qa.a: Assets increase and capital increases by ₹4,000
qa.e: Income raises cash and, through profit, capital.

qa.q: Goods purchased on credit from Anil ₹30,000. Which entry is correct?
qa.a: Dr Purchases ₹30,000 / Cr Anil ₹30,000
qa.e: Purchases (expense-type) increase, debit; Anil, a creditor (liability), increases, credit.

qa.q: An increase in a liability is recorded on the
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: Liabilities increase on the credit side and decrease on the debit side.

qa.q: Commission received in cash ₹5,000. The accounts debited and credited are
qa.a: Dr Cash / Cr Commission received
qa.e: Cash (asset) increases, debit; commission (revenue) increases, credit.

qa.q: Which account normally has a credit balance?
qa.a: Capital account
qa.e: Capital, liabilities and incomes normally show credit balances.

qa.q: Loan of ₹1,00,000 repaid by cheque. Which entry is correct?
qa.a: Dr Loan / Cr Bank
qa.e: The liability (loan) decreases, debit; the asset (bank) decreases, credit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Drawings are debited.
Reason (R): Drawings reduce the capital of the owner, and a decrease in capital is debited.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Capital decreases are debited, and drawings reduce capital.

qa.q: Machinery sold for cash at its book value ₹40,000. Which entry is correct?
qa.a: Dr Cash / Cr Machinery
qa.e: Cash rises (debit); machinery, an asset, falls (credit). It is not a sale of goods.

qa.q: Case: Interest on bank loan ₹6,000 is debited by the bank to the firm's account. The firm records
qa.a: Dr Interest on loan / Cr Bank
qa.e: Interest is an expense (debit) and the bank balance falls (credit).

qa.q: Under the traditional approach, Bank account is a
qa.a: Personal account
qa.e: A bank is an artificial person, so its account is personal.

qa.q: The rule 'Debit what comes in, credit what goes out' applies to
qa.a: Real accounts
qa.e: This is the golden rule for real (asset) accounts.

qa.q: Discount allowed is a
qa.a: Nominal account
qa.e: Discount allowed is a loss to the business, so it is nominal.

qa.q: Paid wages ₹8,000 in cash. Under the golden rules, wages are debited because
qa.a: Wages are an expense, and expenses are debited
qa.e: Wages account is nominal; debit all expenses and losses.

qa.q: Goods sold on credit to Meena ₹12,000. Meena's account is debited because
qa.a: She is the receiver of goods
qa.e: Meena is a person receiving goods: debit the receiver.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Capital account is a personal account.
Reason (R): Capital account represents the owner, who is a person.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Capital is the account of the proprietor, so it is personal.

qa.q: Outstanding salary account is classified as a
qa.a: Representative personal account
qa.e: It represents persons (employees) to whom salary is owed.

qa.q: Case: Furniture bought from Jain Furnitures on credit ₹45,000. Using the golden rules, the entry is
qa.a: Dr Furniture / Cr Jain Furnitures
qa.e: Furniture (real) comes in: debit. Jain Furnitures (personal) gives: credit.

qa.q: The journal is called the book of original entry because
qa.a: Transactions are first recorded in it
qa.e: Transactions enter the journal first, before posting to the ledger.

qa.q: Received ₹14,700 from Kiran in full settlement of ₹15,000. What is the discount allowed?
qa.e: Discount = amount due − amount received.

qa.q: ₹14,700 is received from Kiran in full settlement of ₹15,000 due from him. The correct journal entry is
qa.a: Dr Cash ₹14,700, Dr Discount Allowed ₹300 / Cr Kiran ₹15,000
qa.e: Kiran's full debt is cleared (credit ₹15,000); cash and discount allowed (a loss) are debited.

qa.q: Which column of the journal records the page number of the ledger account?
qa.a: L.F. (Ledger Folio)
qa.e: L.F. stands for ledger folio, filled in at the time of posting.

qa.q: Goods returned by Arun, a customer, ₹3,000. The entry is
qa.a: Dr Sales Return / Cr Arun
qa.e: Sales return reduces sales (debit); Arun owes less (credit).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Payment to a creditor with a cash discount is a compound entry.
Reason (R): It has one debit and two credits.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Creditor is debited; cash and discount received are credited, so it is compound.

qa.q: Started business with cash ₹5,00,000 and furniture ₹1,00,000. What amount is credited to Capital?
qa.e: Capital is credited with the total value brought in.

qa.q: Which item is written below each journal entry in brackets?
qa.a: Narration
qa.e: A narration briefly explains the transaction.

qa.q: The proprietor took goods costing ₹7,000 for household use. The entry is
qa.a: Dr Drawings / Cr Purchases
qa.e: Drawings increase (debit) and purchases are reduced (credit) at cost.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹4,000 are distributed as free samples. Which account is debited?
qa.a: Advertisement
qa.e: Free samples promote the business, so they are an advertisement expense.

qa.q: Goods worth ₹80,000 are lost by fire. The insurance company accepts a claim of ₹60,000. What amount is debited to Loss by Fire?
qa.e: Only the part not recovered from the insurer is a loss.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹10,000 given as charity. The correct entry is
qa.a: Dr Charity ₹10,000 / Cr Purchases ₹10,000
qa.e: Charity is an expense; purchases are credited because the goods are no longer for sale.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Purchases account is credited when goods are lost by theft.
Reason (R): Goods lost will never be sold, so the cost of goods available for sale must be reduced.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Crediting purchases removes the cost of the lost goods from goods available for sale.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹30,000 were stolen. Nothing was insured. Which entry is correct?
qa.a: Dr Loss by Theft ₹30,000 / Cr Purchases ₹30,000
qa.e: With no insurance, the full cost is a loss.

qa.q: Case: A trader's goods costing ₹1,20,000 are destroyed by fire; the insurer admits 75% of the loss. What is the insurance claim?
Why are goods withdrawn by the owner recorded at cost and not at selling price?
qa.a: No sale takes place, so no profit should be recorded on them
qa.e: Recording at selling price would show a profit that was never earned.

qa.q: Goods purchased from a dealer in the same state for ₹40,000 plus 18% GST, on credit. The correct entry is
qa.a: Dr Purchases ₹40,000, Dr Input CGST ₹3,600, Dr Input SGST ₹3,600 / Cr Supplier ₹47,200
qa.e: Intra-state purchase: GST split equally as input CGST and SGST, both debited as assets (tax credit).

qa.q: Goods sold to a buyer in another state for ₹60,000 plus 18% GST, on credit. What amount is debited to the buyer?
qa.e: Inter-state: IGST 18% = ₹10,800 is added to the sale value.

qa.q: Output CGST ₹18,000; input CGST ₹11,000. How much CGST is paid in cash after set-off?
qa.e: Input credit is set off against output tax of the same head first.

qa.q: Which set-off is NOT permitted under GST?
qa.a: Input CGST against output SGST
qa.e: CGST credit cannot be used to pay SGST, and SGST credit cannot pay CGST.

qa.q: The journal entry for setting off input SGST ₹6,000 against output SGST is
qa.a: Dr Output SGST ₹6,000 / Cr Input SGST ₹6,000
qa.e: Output tax (a liability) is reduced by debiting it; input tax (an asset) is used up by crediting it.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Input CGST is shown on the debit side as an asset.
Reason (R): It can be used to reduce future GST liability.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Input tax credit is a right to reduce tax payable, so it is an asset.

qa.q: Telephone bill ₹5,000 plus 18% GST paid by cheque (intra-state). The total amount credited to Bank is
qa.e: Bank is credited with the expense plus CGST ₹450 and SGST ₹450.

qa.q: Case: In a month, input IGST ₹9,000, output IGST ₹5,000 and output CGST ₹3,000. After using input IGST first against IGST and then against CGST, what IGST credit is left?
qa.e: ₹5,000 of input IGST pays output IGST, the next ₹3,000 pays output CGST, leaving ₹1,000.

qa.q: The ledger is known as the
qa.a: Principal book of accounts
qa.e: All accounts are kept in the ledger, so it is the principal or main book.

qa.q: Which of these is a temporary account?
qa.a: Wages account
qa.e: Expense and revenue accounts are temporary and closed at year-end.

qa.q: Which statement about the journal and the ledger is correct?
qa.a: The journal records chronologically; the ledger records account-wise
qa.e: Journal entries are date-wise; the ledger groups them by account.

qa.q: What does the debit side of a ledger account contain?
qa.a: Date, particulars, J.F. and amount
qa.e: Both sides of a ledger account have date, particulars, journal folio and amount.

qa.q: Why are permanent accounts carried forward to the next year?
qa.a: They represent assets, liabilities and capital that continue to exist
qa.e: Balance sheet items continue, so their balances are brought down.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The ledger shows the net position of each account.
Reason (R): All transactions relating to one account are collected in one place in the ledger.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: By grouping all entries of an account, the ledger reveals its final balance.

qa.q: J.F. in a ledger account stands for
qa.a: Journal Folio
qa.e: J.F. records the journal page from which the entry was posted.

qa.q: Case: At year-end, the Commission Received account shows a credit balance. What happens to it?
qa.a: It is transferred to the profit and loss account
qa.e: Commission received is a temporary (revenue) account and is closed to P&L.

qa.q: Entry: Dr Rent / Cr Bank ₹12,000. How is it written in the Rent account?
qa.a: Debit side: 'To Bank ₹12,000'
qa.e: In the account debited, the name of the account credited is written with 'To'.

qa.q: Entry: Dr Purchases / Cr Mohan ₹25,000. In Mohan's account, the posting is
qa.a: Credit side: 'By Purchases ₹25,000'
qa.e: Mohan is credited, so the entry goes on his credit side, naming the account debited with 'By'.

qa.q: Cash account: debit total ₹1,45,000, credit total ₹98,000. What is the balance and its nature?
qa.e: Debit side is larger, so it is a debit balance of ₹47,000 (written as 'By Balance c/d' on the credit side).

qa.q: When an account is balanced and the debit side is bigger, 'Balance c/d' is written on the
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: The balancing figure goes on the smaller side so both totals agree.

qa.q: A creditor's account shows credits of ₹80,000 and debits of ₹62,000. The balance is
qa.e: Credit side exceeds debit side, so a credit balance of ₹18,000 is payable.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Posting ensures each journal entry is recorded in two ledger accounts.
Reason (R): Every journal entry has at least one debit and one credit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Each debit and credit in an entry goes to its own account, so at least two accounts are affected.

qa.q: Compound entry: Dr Cash ₹9,800, Dr Discount Allowed ₹200 / Cr Lata ₹10,000. In Lata's account, the credit side shows
qa.a: 'By Cash ₹9,800' and 'By Discount Allowed ₹200'
qa.e: Each debited account is named separately with its amount on the credit side of the account credited.

qa.q: Case: Furniture A/c has opening balance ₹50,000 and additions ₹30,000 on the debit side, nothing on the credit side. What is 'Balance b/d' next year?
qa.e: All entries are on the debit side, so the balance equals their total.

qa.q: The cash book is
qa.a: Both a book of original entry and a ledger account
qa.e: Cash transactions are first recorded in it, and it also acts as the cash account.

qa.q: Opening cash ₹12,000; receipts ₹48,000; payments ₹39,000. What is the closing cash balance?
qa.e: Closing balance = opening + receipts − payments.

qa.q: Which transaction is NOT recorded in a simple cash book?
qa.a: Goods sold on credit to Rina
qa.e: Credit sales involve no cash at the time of sale.

qa.q: Cash received from Gopal ₹7,000 is written in the cash book as
qa.a: Debit side: 'To Gopal ₹7,000'
qa.e: Receipts are on the debit side and use 'To'.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): There is no need to open a separate cash account in the ledger when a cash book is maintained.
Reason (R): The cash book itself serves as the cash account.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because the cash book doubles as the cash account, a separate one would duplicate it.

qa.q: Opening balance ₹5,000. Cash sales ₹22,000. Cash purchases ₹15,000. Paid salary ₹6,000. What is the closing balance?
In the cash book, a payment of rent is written as
qa.a: 'By Rent' on the credit side
qa.e: Payments go on the credit side and name the account for which cash was paid.

qa.q: Case: A trader's cash book total on the debit side is ₹75,000 and on the credit side ₹52,000. What does 'By Balance c/d' show?
qa.e: The balance c/d is the excess of receipts over payments, written on the payments side.

qa.q: Cash withdrawn from the bank for office use ₹10,000 is recorded as
qa.a: Debit cash column 'To Bank' and credit bank column 'By Cash'
qa.e: Cash increases (debit cash column), bank decreases (credit bank column).

qa.q: What is a contra entry?
qa.a: An entry that affects both the cash and bank columns of the cash book
qa.e: Contra entries record transfers between cash and bank, appearing on both sides.

qa.q: Contra entries are identified by writing which letter in the L.F. column?
qa.a: C
qa.e: 'C' marks a contra entry, showing no ledger posting is needed.

qa.q: A cheque of ₹18,000 received from Neeta was deposited the same day. Where is it recorded?
qa.a: Debit side, bank column: 'To Neeta ₹18,000'
qa.e: Bank balance rises, so the bank column on the debit side is used.

qa.q: Rent paid by cheque ₹15,000 is written on the
qa.a: Credit side in the bank column
qa.e: Bank balance falls, so it goes on the payments side in the bank column.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Contra entries are not posted to the ledger.
Reason (R): Both the debit and credit aspects are already recorded in the double column cash book.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The cash book holds both the cash and bank accounts, so posting would double the record.

qa.q: Opening: cash ₹30,000, bank ₹50,000. Cash deposited into bank ₹20,000. What are the new cash and bank balances?
qa.e: Cash falls by ₹20,000; bank rises by ₹20,000; the total stays ₹80,000.

qa.q: Case: Bank charges ₹500 debited by the bank. In the double column cash book, this is
qa.a: Credit side, bank column: 'By Bank Charges ₹500'
qa.e: Bank charges reduce the bank balance, so they are written on the credit side in the bank column.

qa.q: Which statement about the cash column of a cash book is correct?
qa.a: It can never have a credit balance
qa.e: Cash paid cannot exceed cash available, so the cash column always has a debit balance or nil.

qa.q: A credit balance in the bank column of a cash book indicates
qa.a: Bank overdraft
qa.e: A credit balance means the firm owes money to the bank.

qa.q: Bank column: debit total ₹2,00,000, credit total ₹2,35,000. What is the overdraft?
qa.e: Payments exceed deposits by ₹35,000, which the bank has lent.

qa.q: 'To Sales ₹20,000' appears on the debit side of the cash book. In the Sales account, it is posted as
qa.a: Credit side: 'By Cash ₹20,000'
qa.e: Items on the debit side of the cash book are credited in their ledger accounts.

qa.q: 'By Wages ₹9,000' appears on the credit side of the cash book. In the Wages account, it is posted as
qa.a: Debit side: 'To Cash ₹9,000'
qa.e: Items on the credit side of the cash book are debited in the ledger.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The bank column of the cash book may show a credit balance.
Reason (R): A business may withdraw more than its deposits if it has an overdraft facility.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: An overdraft lets payments exceed deposits, giving a credit balance.

qa.q: A cash book shows cash: debit ₹55,000, credit ₹62,000. What can you conclude?
qa.a: There is an error, since the cash column cannot have a credit balance
qa.e: Payments in cash cannot exceed cash available, so the figures must contain an error.

qa.q: Case: Opening cash ₹8,000, bank ₹40,000. Cash sales ₹30,000; cash deposited into bank ₹25,000; cheque issued to a creditor ₹50,000. What is the bank balance?
Under the imprest system, the petty cashier receives at the end of the period
qa.a: The amount actually spent during the period
qa.e: Reimbursing exactly what was spent restores the fixed imprest.

qa.q: Imprest ₹8,000. Spent: postage ₹1,200, stationery ₹2,300, conveyance ₹1,500. What is the reimbursement?
qa.e: The amount reimbursed equals total spending.

qa.q: A petty cashier received an imprest of ₹8,000 and spent ₹5,000 during the month. What is the petty cash balance just before reimbursement?
qa.e: Balance = imprest − amount spent.

qa.q: Which payment is most suitable for the petty cash book?
qa.a: Courier charges of ₹120
qa.e: Petty cash is for small, frequent expenses.

qa.q: In an analytical petty cash book, the total of the 'Stationery' column is
qa.a: Debited to the Stationery account in the ledger
qa.e: Each expense column total is debited to its expense account.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The imprest system gives better control over petty cash.
Reason (R): The petty cashier must account for all spending before being reimbursed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Reimbursement only after vouchers are checked makes misuse easy to detect.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of keeping a petty cash book?
qa.a: It saves the time of the main cashier
qa.e: Small payments are handled separately, freeing the main cashier.

qa.q: Case: A petty cashier had ₹750 left out of an imprest of ₹3,500 at month-end. How much will the main cashier give her?
qa.e: Spent = 3,500 − 750; this amount is reimbursed.

qa.q: The purchases book records
qa.a: Only credit purchases of goods
qa.e: Cash purchases go to the cash book, and assets on credit go to the journal proper.

qa.q: Goods with list price ₹60,000 bought on credit at 10% trade discount. What amount is recorded in the purchases book (before GST)?
qa.e: Trade discount is deducted in the book itself; only the net amount is recorded.

qa.q: Credit purchases from a supplier in another state: ₹40,000 plus 18% IGST. What amount is credited to the supplier?
qa.e: Supplier is credited with goods value plus IGST.

qa.q: The periodic total of the purchases book is posted to the
qa.a: Debit side of the Purchases account
qa.e: Purchases increase, so the total is debited; individual suppliers are credited.

qa.q: The source document for the purchases return book is the
qa.a: Debit note
qa.e: The buyer issues a debit note when returning goods to the supplier.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Trade discount does not appear in the purchases account.
Reason (R): Only the net amount after trade discount is recorded in the purchases book.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The deduction is made in the details column, so only the net figure is posted.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹10,000 plus CGST ₹900 and SGST ₹900 are returned to Batra & Sons. Which entry results from the purchases return book?
qa.a: Dr Batra & Sons ₹11,800 / Cr Purchases Return ₹10,000, Cr Input CGST ₹900, Cr Input SGST ₹900
qa.e: The supplier's account is reduced by the full amount; purchases return and input taxes are credited.

qa.q: Case: Bought from Gill Bros 20 fans at ₹2,500 each, trade discount 20%, CGST 9% and SGST 9%. What total is credited to Gill Bros?
The sales book records
qa.a: Only credit sales of goods
qa.e: Cash sales go to the cash book; sale of assets on credit goes to the journal proper.

qa.q: The periodic total of the sales book is posted to the
qa.a: Credit side of the Sales account
qa.e: Sales increase, so the total is credited; customers are debited.

qa.q: Goods of list price ₹25,000 sold on credit at 20% trade discount plus 18% GST (intra-state). What is the output CGST?
The source document for the sales return book is the
qa.a: Credit note
qa.e: The seller issues a credit note to the customer who returns goods.

qa.q: Goods ₹8,000 plus IGST 18% returned by a customer from another state. What amount is credited to the customer?
qa.e: The customer's account is reduced by the goods value plus the GST charged on them.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Output GST accounts are debited when goods are returned by customers.
Reason (R): The GST liability on the cancelled part of the sale is reduced.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Returns cancel part of the sale, so the related output tax liability is reduced by a debit.

qa.q: A credit sale of old office furniture to Kumar is recorded in the
qa.a: Journal proper
qa.e: Furniture is an asset, not goods, so it goes to the journal proper.

qa.q: Case: From the sales book, credit sales total ₹2,40,000 with output CGST ₹21,600 and SGST ₹21,600. What is the total debited to customers' accounts?
qa.e: Customers are debited with sales plus both GST components.

qa.q: Which of these is recorded in the journal proper?
qa.a: Closing entries at the end of the year
qa.e: Closing entries do not fit any special book.

qa.q: Furniture bought on credit from Aman Furnitures is recorded in the
qa.a: Journal proper
