qa.e: The purchases book is only for goods; credit purchases of assets go to the journal proper.

qa.q: Which is NOT an advantage of special purpose books?
qa.a: They eliminate the need for a ledger
qa.e: Special books still post to the ledger; they only make recording efficient.

qa.q: A debt of ₹5,000 due from Rohan proves irrecoverable and is written off. In which book is it recorded?
qa.a: Journal proper
qa.e: Bad debts are recorded through a journal entry: Dr Bad Debts / Cr Rohan.

qa.q: Interest on capital and depreciation at year-end are examples of
qa.a: Adjustment entries in the journal proper
qa.e: Year-end adjustments are made through the journal proper.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Special purpose books save time in posting.
Reason (R): Only periodic totals of these books are posted to the related nominal accounts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Instead of posting each transaction to Sales or Purchases, only totals are posted.

qa.q: The entry to bring forward last year's assets, liabilities and capital is called the
qa.a: Opening entry
qa.e: The opening entry, made in the journal proper, starts the new year's books.

qa.q: Case: A firm sells an old computer on credit to Sunil for ₹8,000. Where and how is it recorded?
qa.a: Journal proper: Dr Sunil / Cr Computer
qa.e: Sale of an asset on credit goes to the journal proper and credits the asset account.

qa.q: When an account's debit side exceeds its credit side, the account has a
qa.a: Debit balance
qa.e: The excess side gives the nature of the balance.

qa.q: A supplier's account: Cr: Purchases ₹75,000. Dr: Bank ₹50,000, Purchases Return ₹4,000. What is the balance?
qa.e: Credit side exceeds debit side; the firm still owes the supplier.

qa.q: Which account normally shows a credit balance?
qa.a: Interest received account
qa.e: Incomes and gains have credit balances.

qa.q: 'Balance b/d' on the debit side of a creditor's account means
qa.a: The creditor owes the firm (a debit balance)
qa.e: A debit balance in a personal account means the person owes the business, e.g. after an advance payment.

qa.q: Salaries account shows a debit balance of ₹2,40,000 at year-end. What happens to it?
qa.a: It is transferred to the profit and loss account
qa.e: Expense accounts are closed to P&L, not carried forward.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Balance c/d is written on the side with the smaller total.
Reason (R): It makes the totals of both sides equal.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The balancing figure fills the gap on the smaller side so both sides agree.

qa.q: A customer's account: Dr: Balance b/d ₹10,000, Sales ₹55,000. Cr: Bank ₹48,000, Discount Allowed ₹2,000. What is the closing balance?
qa.e: Debit total ₹65,000 less credit total ₹50,000.

qa.q: Case: The Capital account shows Cr: Balance b/d ₹4,00,000, Net Profit ₹80,000 and Dr: Drawings ₹30,000. What is the closing capital?
qa.e: Credit total ₹4,80,000 less debit ₹30,000.

qa.q: An overdraft as per pass book means the pass book shows a
qa.a: Debit balance
qa.e: For the bank, a customer who has overdrawn owes it money, so it shows a debit.

qa.q: A deposit of ₹10,000 into the bank appears in the pass book on the
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: The bank's liability to the customer increases, so it credits the account.

qa.q: Who prepares the bank reconciliation statement?
qa.a: The business (account holder)
qa.e: The firm prepares it to reconcile its cash book with the bank's record.

qa.q: A BRS is prepared to
qa.a: Explain the differences between the cash book and pass book balances
qa.e: It reconciles two records of the same bank account.

qa.q: A credit balance in the bank column of the cash book indicates
qa.a: Overdraft (unfavourable balance)
qa.e: When payments exceed deposits, the firm owes the bank.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Bank reconciliation statement is not a part of the double entry system.
Reason (R): It is only a statement prepared to explain differences, and no ledger account is debited or credited through it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A BRS reconciles balances; entries are made separately (e.g. in the amended cash book).

qa.q: Which is an important use of a BRS?
qa.a: Detecting errors and unauthorised payments
qa.e: Matching the two records brings errors and frauds to light.

qa.q: Case: On 31 March, the cash book shows a debit balance of ₹75,000 and the pass book shows a credit balance of ₹75,000. What does this mean?
qa.a: Both records agree; there are no differences on that date
qa.e: A debit in the cash book matching a credit in the pass book of the same amount means agreement.

qa.q: Cash book shows ₹30,000 (Dr). Cheques issued but not presented ₹7,000. What is the pass book balance?
qa.e: The bank has not yet paid these cheques, so its balance is higher.

qa.q: Cash book shows ₹45,000 (Dr). Cheques deposited but not yet credited ₹9,000. What is the pass book balance?
qa.e: The bank has not yet added these cheques, so its balance is lower.

qa.q: Starting from the pass book (Cr) balance, cheques issued but not presented are
qa.a: Subtracted
qa.e: The pass book balance is higher than the cash book by this amount, so we subtract to reach the cash book.

qa.q: Why do cheques deposited but not credited cause a difference?
qa.a: The cash book records them on deposit, but the bank credits them only after collection
qa.e: This timing gap makes the cash book balance higher than the pass book.

qa.q: Pass book shows ₹62,000 (Cr). Cheques deposited not credited ₹10,000; cheques issued not presented ₹15,000. What is the cash book balance?
qa.e: From the pass book: add deposits not yet credited, subtract cheques not yet presented.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Cheques issued but not presented make the pass book balance higher than the cash book balance.
Reason (R): The cash book has already credited these cheques, but the bank has not yet debited them.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Cash book reduced the balance; the bank has not, so the bank shows more.

qa.q: Cash book ₹80,000 (Dr). Cheques issued not presented ₹20,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹14,000. Pass book balance?
qa.e: Add ₹20,000, subtract ₹14,000.

qa.q: Case: A firm issued three cheques of ₹4,000, ₹6,000 and ₹5,000 on 31 March; only the ₹6,000 cheque was presented by 31 March. Cash book balance ₹25,000 (Dr). Pass book balance?
qa.e: Only ₹4,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹9,000 is unpresented; add it.

qa.q: Cash book ₹25,000 (Dr). Bank charges ₹300 not yet recorded in the cash book. Pass book balance?
qa.e: The bank has deducted charges that the cash book has not, so the pass book is lower.

qa.q: A customer deposited ₹15,000 directly into the firm's bank account. Starting from the cash book balance, this is
qa.a: Added
qa.e: The pass book already shows the deposit, so it is higher.

qa.q: Cash book ₹48,000 (Dr). A cheque of ₹6,000 deposited was dishonoured; the cash book has not recorded it. Pass book balance?
qa.e: The bank has reversed the cheque, so its balance is lower.

qa.q: Pass book ₹70,000 (Cr). Interest credited by the bank ₹2,000, not in the cash book. Cash book balance?
qa.e: Starting from the pass book, interest already included there is subtracted.

qa.q: Which item makes the pass book balance lower than the cash book balance?
qa.a: Payment of telephone bill by the bank under standing instructions
qa.e: The bank has paid out money that the cash book has not yet recorded.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Dividend collected by the bank makes the pass book balance higher.
Reason (R): The bank credits it to the firm's account before the firm records it in the cash book.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The bank records it first, so for now the pass book is higher.

qa.q: Cash book ₹1,00,000 (Dr). Direct deposit ₹12,000; bank charges ₹800; EMI debited by bank ₹9,000. Pass book balance?
qa.e: Add the direct deposit; subtract charges and EMI.

qa.q: Case: Pass book ₹55,000 (Cr). Bank charges ₹400 and a dishonoured cheque ₹5,000 are not in the cash book. Cash book balance?
qa.e: Starting from the pass book, items it has deducted are added back.

qa.q: Cash book ₹35,000 (Dr). Cheques issued not presented ₹8,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹5,000; interest credited ₹700. Pass book balance?
qa.e: Add unpresented cheques and interest; subtract uncredited deposits.

qa.q: Pass book ₹46,000 (Cr). Cheques issued not presented ₹10,000; bank charges ₹500. Cash book balance?
qa.e: From the pass book: subtract unpresented cheques, add back bank charges.

qa.q: When starting from the pass book balance, interest credited by the bank is
qa.a: Subtracted
qa.e: The pass book includes interest that the cash book lacks, so subtract it to get the cash book.

qa.q: Cash book ₹1,20,000 (Dr). Cheques deposited not credited ₹30,000; direct payment of rent by bank ₹12,000; cheques issued not presented ₹25,000. Pass book balance?
qa.e: Add unpresented ₹25,000; subtract uncredited ₹30,000 and direct payment ₹12,000.

qa.q: A BRS starting with the cash book ends with
qa.a: The balance as per the pass book
qa.e: A BRS moves from one record's balance to the other's.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Items added when starting from the cash book are subtracted when starting from the pass book.
Reason (R): The direction of reconciliation is reversed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Moving the other way flips each adjustment.

qa.q: Pass book ₹80,000 (Cr). Cheques deposited not credited ₹18,000; direct deposit by a customer ₹6,000; cheque dishonoured ₹4,000 (not in cash book). Cash book balance?
qa.e: From pass book: add uncredited deposits and dishonour; subtract direct deposit.

qa.q: Case: Cash book ₹22,000 (Dr). Unpresented cheques ₹6,500; uncredited cheques ₹4,000; bank charges ₹250; dividend collected by bank ₹1,750. Pass book balance?
qa.e: Add ₹6,500 and ₹1,750; subtract ₹4,000 and ₹250.

qa.q: Overdraft as per cash book ₹40,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹10,000. Overdraft as per pass book?
qa.e: The bank has not yet paid the cheques, so its overdraft is smaller.

qa.q: Overdraft as per cash book ₹25,000. Cheques deposited not credited ₹7,000; bank charges ₹500. Overdraft as per pass book?
qa.e: Both items mean the bank's overdraft is larger.

qa.q: Overdraft as per pass book ₹60,000. Cheques issued not presented ₹14,000; interest on overdraft ₹2,000 not in cash book. Overdraft as per cash book?
qa.e: From pass book overdraft: unpresented cheques would increase the cash book overdraft; interest already in the pass book is removed.

qa.q: A cheque received for ₹6,300 was entered in the cash book as ₹3,600. Starting from the cash book (Dr) balance, the adjustment is
qa.e: The cash book is understated by 6,300 − 3,600 = ₹2,700; the bank recorded the correct amount.

qa.q: The payments side of the cash book was undercast by ₹1,000. Starting from the cash book (Dr) balance, the adjustment is
qa.a: Subtract ₹1,000
qa.e: Undercasting payments makes the cash book balance ₹1,000 too high.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Treating an overdraft as a negative balance allows the normal BRS signs to be used.
Reason (R): An overdraft is simply a balance below zero.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With negative numbers, the same plus-and-minus rules give the correct overdraft.

qa.q: Cash book shows ₹50,000 (Dr). The bank wrongly debited our account with ₹3,000 belonging to another customer. Pass book balance?
qa.e: The bank's error has reduced the pass book balance.

qa.q: Case: Overdraft as per cash book ₹18,000. Direct deposit by customer ₹5,000; bank charges ₹200. Overdraft as per pass book?
qa.e: The deposit reduces the overdraft; charges increase it.

qa.q: Which item is corrected in the amended cash book?
qa.a: Bank charges not yet recorded by the firm
qa.e: Bank charges are a genuine expense the firm has not recorded; the others are timing items or bank errors.

qa.q: Cash book ₹55,000 (Dr). Direct deposit ₹8,000 and bank charges ₹400 not recorded. Amended cash book balance?
qa.e: Add the deposit on the debit side; enter the charges on the credit side.

qa.q: Amended cash book ₹62,600 (Dr). Cheques issued not presented ₹9,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹4,000. Pass book balance?
qa.e: Only timing items remain: add unpresented cheques, subtract uncredited deposits.

qa.q: A dishonoured cheque of ₹5,000 is recorded in the amended cash book on the
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: The deposit is reversed: the bank balance falls, so it is credited.

qa.q: Which item stays in the BRS even after an amended cash book is prepared?
qa.a: Cheques issued but not yet presented
qa.e: Timing differences are not errors of the cash book; they clear themselves.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The amended cash book balance is shown in the balance sheet.
Reason (R): It includes all items the bank has recorded that the firm had missed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: After correction, the cash book shows the true bank position for the firm.

qa.q: Cash book ₹30,000 (Dr). Interest credited ₹600; EMI paid by bank ₹4,000; dividend collected ₹1,400. Amended balance?
qa.e: Add interest and dividend; subtract the EMI.

qa.q: Case: Cash book ₹70,000 (Dr). Bank charges ₹1,000 and a dishonoured cheque ₹6,000 not recorded. Unpresented cheques ₹12,000. What is the pass book balance?
qa.e: Amended balance = ₹63,000; add unpresented cheques ₹12,000.

qa.q: A trial balance is a
qa.a: Statement of ledger balances on a particular date
qa.e: It lists the balances of all ledger accounts on a date to test equality of debits and credits.

qa.q: The main objective of preparing a trial balance is to
qa.a: Check the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger
qa.e: Equal totals indicate the ledger is arithmetically accurate.

qa.q: Debit balances total ₹4,80,000 and credit balances total ₹4,75,000. What is the difference?
A trial balance can be prepared
qa.a: On any date, whenever needed
qa.e: It can be drawn up at the end of a month, quarter or year, or any date.

qa.q: Which statement about the trial balance is correct?
qa.a: It helps in preparing financial statements
qa.e: Its balances are the raw material for the trading, P&L account and balance sheet.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under double entry, the trial balance totals should agree.
Reason (R): Every debit has an equal and corresponding credit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since each transaction is recorded with equal debits and credits, their totals match.

qa.q: Balances: Capital ₹2,00,000 (Cr), Machinery ₹1,50,000 (Dr), Cash ₹30,000 (Dr), Creditors ₹50,000 (Cr), Wages ₹70,000 (Dr). What is the debit total?
qa.e: Debit balances: machinery, cash and wages.

qa.q: Case: A trial balance shows a debit total of ₹2,50,000 and a credit total of ₹2,50,000. What does this tell us?
qa.a: The trial balance agrees, so the ledger is arithmetically accurate
qa.e: Agreement shows arithmetical accuracy only; some errors may still exist.

qa.q: Which balance appears on the credit side of a trial balance?
qa.a: Returns outwards
qa.e: Returns outwards (purchases returns) reduce purchases and carry a credit balance.

qa.q: Opening stock is shown in the trial balance on the
qa.a: Debit side
qa.e: Opening stock is an asset brought forward and a ledger balance, so it is a debit.

qa.q: A trial balance's debit total is ₹2,96,000 and credit total ₹3,00,000. On checking, sales returns ₹2,000 were wrongly placed on the credit side. What is the corrected debit total?
qa.e: Removing ₹2,000 from credits and adding it to debits makes both sides ₹2,98,000.

qa.q: Which item normally appears OUTSIDE the trial balance as an adjustment?
qa.a: Closing stock
qa.e: Closing stock is valued at the year-end and usually given as an adjustment.

qa.q: Provision for doubtful debts is shown on which side of the trial balance?
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: Provisions have credit balances, as they reduce an asset.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Drawings appear on the debit side of the trial balance.
Reason (R): Drawings reduce capital, and capital has a credit balance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A reduction of a credit-balance account is a debit, so drawings show a debit balance.

qa.q: Debit balances total ₹5,40,000. Credit balances: Capital ₹3,00,000, Creditors ₹90,000, Sales ₹1,40,000. What is the difference in the trial balance?
qa.e: Credit total = ₹5,30,000; debit exceeds credit by ₹10,000.

qa.q: Case: A trainee placed Bank overdraft ₹15,000 on the debit side of the trial balance. By how much does the debit total exceed the correct debit total?
qa.e: The ₹15,000 should be removed from debits (and added to credits).

qa.q: Which error is NOT disclosed by a trial balance?
qa.a: Complete omission of a transaction from the journal
qa.e: If a transaction is never recorded, neither debit nor credit appears, so totals still agree.

qa.q: An amount of ₹600 was posted to the debit instead of the credit side of an account. The trial balance difference is
qa.e: The credit is missing ₹600 and the debit has an extra ₹600, a gap of double the amount.

qa.q: A trial balance difference of ₹270 is divisible by 9. A likely cause is
qa.a: Transposition of digits, e.g. ₹520 recorded as ₹250
qa.e: Differences caused by transposed digits are always divisible by 9.

qa.q: Agreement of the trial balance proves
qa.a: Only arithmetical accuracy of the ledger
qa.e: Several errors leave the totals equal, so agreement is not a guarantee of accuracy.

qa.q: Which is a one-sided error that the trial balance reveals?
qa.a: Purchases book undercast by ₹2,000
qa.e: Undercasting affects only the Purchases account, so the totals differ.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An error of principle is not revealed by the trial balance.
Reason (R): The debit and credit amounts are both recorded correctly, though in the wrong class of account.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Equal debits and credits keep totals equal even though the classification is wrong.

qa.q: Credit sale of ₹4,500 to Mohit was recorded in the sales book as ₹5,400. Will the trial balance agree?
qa.a: Yes, because both Sales and Mohit's account have the same wrong amount
qa.e: An error in the book of original entry is carried to both accounts equally.

qa.q: Case: The difference in a trial balance is ₹3,000. Which first step makes sense?
qa.a: Re-total the trial balance and check that no balance is omitted
qa.e: Start with the simplest checks before tracing postings.

qa.q: Purchase of furniture ₹15,000 was debited to Purchases account. This is an error of
qa.a: Principle
qa.e: A capital item (furniture) was treated as a revenue item (purchases of goods).

qa.q: A credit sale to Kavya was not recorded in the sales book. This is
qa.a: An error of complete omission
qa.e: Nothing about the transaction was recorded.

qa.q: Rahul's account was debited ₹500 short and Ravi's account was debited ₹500 in excess. This is
qa.a: A compensating error
qa.e: The two mistakes cancel each other's effect on the totals.

qa.q: Cash received from Suresh ₹2,000 was correctly entered in the cash book but not posted to Suresh's account. Which type and will the trial balance agree?
qa.a: Partial omission; the trial balance will not agree
qa.e: One side (credit to Suresh) is missing, so the totals differ.

qa.q: Wages paid for installation of a new machine were debited to Wages account. The correct account to be debited is
qa.a: Machinery account
qa.e: Installation wages are part of the cost of the asset (capital expenditure).

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two-sided errors generally do not affect the agreement of the trial balance.
Reason (R): They affect two accounts in a way that keeps debits equal to credits.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because both accounts are affected equally, the totals still match.

qa.q: A sale of ₹3,000 to Neha was posted to the debit of Neeta's account. This is an error of
qa.a: Commission
qa.e: It is posted to a wrong account of the same class (both personal accounts).

qa.q: Case: The purchases book was overcast by ₹1,000 and the sales book was also overcast by ₹1,000. What is the net effect on the trial balance?
qa.a: No difference; the errors compensate
qa.e: Purchases (debit) and Sales (credit) are both ₹1,000 too high, so the totals stay equal.

qa.q: Repairs to machinery ₹3,000 were debited to Machinery account. The rectifying entry is
qa.a: Dr Repairs ₹3,000 / Cr Machinery ₹3,000
qa.e: Repairs is short-debited and Machinery over-debited, so debit Repairs and credit Machinery.

qa.q: Goods sold on credit to Kunal ₹6,000 were posted to the debit of Kamal's account. Rectifying entry?
qa.a: Dr Kunal ₹6,000 / Cr Kamal ₹6,000
qa.e: Kunal should be debited; Kamal's wrong debit must be removed by a credit.

qa.q: The sales book was undercast by ₹800, found before preparing the trial balance. How is it rectified?
qa.a: By an explanatory note 'By Undercasting of sales book ₹800' on the credit side of Sales account
qa.e: A one-sided error before the trial balance is corrected by a note in the affected account.

qa.q: A credit purchase of ₹9,000 from Gopal was not recorded at all. The rectifying entry is
qa.a: Dr Purchases ₹9,000 / Cr Gopal ₹9,000
qa.e: For complete omission, the correct entry is simply recorded.

qa.q: Salary of ₹20,000 paid to an employee was debited to his personal account. Rectifying entry?
qa.a: Dr Salary ₹20,000 / Cr Employee's account ₹20,000
qa.e: Salary is short-debited; the personal account is wrongly debited and must be credited.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): One-sided errors found before preparing the trial balance are corrected without a journal entry.
Reason (R): Only one account is affected, so a note on the appropriate side of that account corrects it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: There is no second account to debit or credit, so an explanatory note is used.

qa.q: Cash received from Pooja ₹4,000 was credited to Puja's account. The rectifying entry is
qa.a: Dr Puja ₹4,000 / Cr Pooja ₹4,000
qa.e: Puja's wrong credit is reversed by a debit; Pooja is credited correctly.

qa.q: Case: An old car sold for ₹50,000 was credited to Sales account. Rectifying entry?
qa.a: Dr Sales ₹50,000 / Cr Car ₹50,000
qa.e: Sales is over-credited; the Car (asset) account should have been credited.

qa.q: Trial balance: debit total ₹2,40,000, credit total ₹2,42,500. The suspense account will show
qa.a: A debit balance of ₹2,500
qa.e: The debit side is short, so suspense is placed on the debit side.

qa.q: The purchases book was overcast by ₹1,500 (found after the trial balance). Rectifying entry?
qa.a: Dr Suspense ₹1,500 / Cr Purchases ₹1,500
qa.e: Purchases has too much debit; credit it. The other side goes to suspense.

qa.q: Discount received ₹300 was not posted to the Discount Received account. Rectifying entry?
qa.a: Dr Suspense ₹300 / Cr Discount Received ₹300
qa.e: Discount received must be credited; the creditor side was already correct, so suspense takes the debit.

qa.q: A payment of ₹1,800 to Akash was posted to his account as ₹180. What amount is taken to the suspense account in the rectifying entry?
qa.e: Akash's account is short-debited by the difference.

qa.q: Cash paid to Bina ₹600 was posted to the credit of her account. Rectifying entry?
qa.a: Dr Bina ₹1,200 / Cr Suspense ₹1,200
qa.e: First cancel the wrong credit (₹600), then make the correct debit (₹600): ₹1,200 in total.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Two-sided errors are not rectified through the suspense account.
Reason (R): Two-sided errors do not affect the agreement of the trial balance.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Suspense is used only for errors that created the trial balance difference.

qa.q: After rectifying all errors, the suspense account was found to have needed an opening credit balance of ₹2,000. This means the original trial balance had
qa.a: Its credit side short by ₹2,000
qa.e: A credit suspense balance fills a shortfall on the credit side.

qa.q: Case: After rectification, the suspense account shows on its debit side 'Sales (undercast) ₹900', and on its credit side 'Discount Allowed (not posted) ₹400' and 'Wages (undercast) ₹1,500'. The account closes. What was its opening (original) balance?
qa.e: Credits (₹400 + ₹1,500 = ₹1,900) exceed debits (₹900) by ₹1,000, so suspense had an opening debit balance of ₹1,000.

qa.q: Net profit before rectification was ₹1,50,000. Furniture purchased for ₹25,000 was debited to Purchases. What is the corrected net profit (ignore depreciation)?
qa.e: Purchases were overstated, so profit was understated by ₹25,000.

qa.q: Repairs of ₹7,000 were debited to Machinery account. What is the effect of this error on profit?
qa.a: Profit overstated by ₹7,000
qa.e: An expense was treated as an asset, so expenses were too low and profit too high.

qa.q: Which error has NO effect on profit?
qa.a: Cash received from Sunita posted to Sumita's account
qa.e: Both accounts are personal accounts, so profit is unaffected.

qa.q: Profit shown ₹2,00,000. Errors: sales book undercast ₹6,000; purchases book undercast ₹4,000. Corrected profit?
qa.e: Sales correction +₹6,000; purchases correction −₹4,000.

qa.q: After final accounts are prepared, an error in a nominal account is rectified through
qa.a: Profit and Loss Adjustment account
qa.e: Last year's nominal accounts are closed, so a P&L Adjustment account is used and its balance goes to capital.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rectification of an error between two personal accounts does not affect profit.
Reason (R): Profit is affected only by errors in nominal accounts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Personal and real accounts do not enter the P&L, so swapping them does not change profit.

qa.q: Profit ₹95,000. Commission received ₹5,000 was credited to the agent's personal account by mistake. Corrected profit?
qa.e: Income was not recorded in P&L, so profit was understated.

qa.q: Case: Profit ₹1,20,000. (i) Wages of ₹10,000 for installing a machine debited to Wages; (ii) sale of old machinery ₹15,000 credited to Sales. Corrected profit (ignore depreciation)?
qa.e: (i) Wages overstated: +₹10,000. (ii) Sales overstated: −₹15,000.

qa.q: Depreciation means
qa.a: A decline in the value of a fixed asset due to use, time or obsolescence
qa.e: Depreciation allocates the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life.

qa.q: Why is depreciation called a non-cash expense?
qa.a: No cash is paid out when depreciation is charged
qa.e: Cash was spent when the asset was bought; depreciation only spreads that cost.

qa.q: On which of these is depreciation NOT charged?
qa.a: Land
qa.e: Land has an unlimited life and is not used up.

qa.q: A machine costs ₹2,40,000, has no scrap value and a life of 8 years. Annual depreciation (equal amounts)?
qa.e: Spread cost equally over 8 years.

qa.q: Depreciation is charged on
qa.a: Fixed (depreciable) assets
qa.e: Only fixed assets used over several years are depreciated.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Depreciation reduces the profit of a business.
Reason (R): Depreciation is a charge against profit shown in the profit and loss account.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Being an expense, depreciation lowers net profit.

qa.q: Which feature of depreciation is shown when a machine's book value falls each year it is used?
qa.a: Decline in book value
qa.e: Each year's depreciation reduces the asset's book value.

qa.q: Case: A school buys a bus for ₹30,00,000 (life 10 years, no scrap) and a plot of land for ₹50,00,000. What is the total annual depreciation on equal instalments?
qa.e: Only the bus is depreciated; land is not.

qa.q: Reduction in the value of a quarry as stone is extracted is called
qa.a: Depletion
qa.e: Depletion applies to wasting natural assets.

qa.q: Writing off the cost of a copyright over its life is called
qa.a: Amortisation
qa.e: Amortisation applies to intangible assets.

qa.q: A machine is still in working condition but is replaced because a faster model has come into the market. The cause of decline in its value is
qa.a: Obsolescence
qa.e: Obsolescence is loss of usefulness due to new technology.

qa.q: An oil well costing ₹1,20,00,000 is estimated to yield 6,00,000 barrels. 45,000 barrels are extracted this year. What is the depletion?
qa.e: Depletion is based on the quantity extracted.

qa.q: A 10-year lease of a shop loses value every year until it ends. This is caused by
qa.a: Expiration of legal rights
qa.e: The right to use the shop runs out as time passes.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Patents are amortised, not depleted.
Reason (R): Patents are intangible assets, while depletion applies to natural resources.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Intangibles are amortised; wasting natural assets are depleted.

qa.q: Which of these is an abnormal cause of decline in value of an asset?
qa.a: Damage by fire
qa.e: Accidents, fire and floods are abnormal factors.

qa.q: Case: A copyright bought for ₹6,00,000 has a legal life of 12 years. What is the annual amortisation?
qa.e: Cost is spread equally over the legal life.

qa.q: A machine is purchased for ₹3,80,000; cartage ₹5,000; installation ₹15,000. What is its cost for depreciation?
qa.e: All costs to bring the asset into use are included.

qa.q: Cost ₹4,00,000; scrap value ₹40,000; useful life 12 years. Annual depreciation (equal instalments)?
qa.e: Depreciable amount is cost less scrap, spread over the life.

qa.q: Which is NOT a factor in measuring depreciation?
qa.a: Market price of the firm's shares
qa.e: Depreciation depends on cost, residual value and useful life only.

qa.q: Providing depreciation helps in replacing assets because
qa.a: It reduces distributable profit, so funds stay in the business
qa.e: Charging depreciation keeps profits, and hence cash, within the business.

qa.q: If depreciation is not charged, what happens to profit and assets?
qa.a: Profit is overstated and assets are overstated
qa.e: Leaving out an expense inflates profit, and the asset stays at a value it no longer has.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Depreciation is charged in order to match costs with revenues.
Reason (R): A fixed asset helps earn revenue over several years, so its cost should be spread over those years.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Spreading cost over the years of benefit matches it with revenue.

qa.q: Net residual value means
qa.a: The estimated amount realisable at the end of an asset's life, less disposal costs
qa.e: It is the expected net scrap or sale value at the end.

qa.q: Case: A truck costs ₹12,00,000 plus registration ₹50,000. Estimated scrap after 5 years is ₹2,50,000. What is the annual depreciation (equal instalments)?
qa.e: Cost = ₹12,50,000; depreciable amount = ₹10,00,000; ÷ 5.

qa.q: Cost ₹3,00,000; residual value ₹20,000; useful life 7 years. Annual depreciation under SLM?
qa.e: Depreciable amount ₹2,80,000 spread over 7 years.

qa.q: A machine costing ₹2,50,000 is depreciated by ₹25,000 every year. What is the rate of depreciation under SLM?
qa.e: Rate = annual depreciation ÷ cost × 100.

qa.q: Furniture costing ₹90,000 is depreciated at 10% p.a. on SLM. What is its book value at the end of the 4th year?
qa.e: Depreciation ₹9,000 a year for 4 years = ₹36,000.

qa.q: SLM is also known as
qa.a: Fixed instalment method
qa.e: Equal instalments give it the name fixed instalment or original cost method.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of SLM?
qa.a: Total charge of depreciation plus repairs rises in later years
qa.e: Repairs grow as the asset ages while depreciation stays fixed, so the total burden rises.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under SLM, the book value graph is a straight line.
Reason (R): The same amount of depreciation is deducted every year.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Equal yearly reductions give a straight line falling to residual value.

qa.q: Under SLM, depreciation is calculated on
qa.a: The original cost of the asset
qa.e: SLM uses original cost (less scrap) each year; WDV uses the reducing book value.

qa.q: Case: A van bought for ₹6,00,000 has a scrap value of ₹60,000 after 6 years. What is the rate of depreciation under SLM on cost?
qa.e: Annual depreciation = ₹90,000; rate = 90,000 ÷ 6,00,000 × 100.

qa.q: Machine cost ₹5,00,000; WDV rate 10%. Depreciation for the second year?
qa.e: Year 1 leaves BV ₹4,50,000; 10% of that is year 2's charge.

qa.q: Cost ₹1,00,000; WDV 20%. What is the book value at the end of 2 years?
qa.e: BV after year 1 = ₹80,000; after year 2 = ₹64,000.

qa.q: Under the WDV method, the book value of an asset
qa.a: Never becomes zero
qa.e: A percentage of a positive number always leaves something, so it never reaches zero.

qa.q: Which method is recognised by income tax law in India for most assets?
qa.a: Written down value method
qa.e: Income tax rules allow depreciation on the WDV of blocks of assets.

qa.q: Which asset is most suited to the WDV method?
qa.a: Plant and machinery
qa.e: Machinery has high obsolescence and rising repairs, so WDV evens out the total charge.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under WDV, the total charge of depreciation plus repairs stays more even over the years.
Reason (R): Depreciation is higher in early years when repairs are low, and lower in later years when repairs are high.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The falling depreciation balances the rising repairs.

qa.q: Depreciation under WDV falls every year because
qa.a: The rate is applied to a smaller book value each year
qa.e: The rate stays fixed; the base (book value) shrinks.

qa.q: Case: A car costs ₹10,00,000. Under 15% WDV, what is the depreciation in year 2?
A machine costing ₹80,000 is bought on 1 July 2025. Depreciation 10% p.a. SLM; year ends 31 March 2026. Depreciation for 2025-26?
qa.e: July to March is 9 months.

qa.q: Furniture of ₹36,000 is bought on 1 December 2025; depreciation 10% p.a.; books close on 31 March 2026. Depreciation?
qa.e: December to March is 4 months.

qa.q: A machine is bought on 1 October 2024 for ₹2,00,000; WDV 20% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Depreciation for 2025-26?
A firm builds an extension to its factory for ₹5,00,000. How is it treated?
qa.a: Capitalised and depreciated separately from the date of addition
qa.e: An extension adds capacity, so it is a capital item.

qa.q: Routine repairs of ₹8,000 on a delivery van are
qa.a: A revenue expense charged to P&L
qa.e: Routine repairs only maintain the asset; they do not increase its life or capacity.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Depreciation on an asset bought during the year is charged only for the months it was used.
Reason (R): Depreciation is a charge for the use of the asset over time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since depreciation reflects use over time, it is prorated for part of a year.

qa.q: On 1 April 2025, machinery ₹3,00,000. On 1 January 2026, more machinery ₹80,000. SLM 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March 2026. Total depreciation?
qa.e: ₹30,000 on old machinery plus ₹2,000 for 3 months on the new.

qa.q: Case: A computer bought on 1 September 2025 for ₹90,000 is depreciated at 20% p.a. SLM. Year ends 31 March 2026. Depreciation?
qa.e: September to March is 7 months.

qa.q: Under the method of charging depreciation to the asset account, the entry for depreciation is
qa.a: Dr Depreciation / Cr Asset
qa.e: Depreciation is debited and the asset itself is credited, reducing its balance.

qa.q: Under the provision for depreciation method, the asset appears in the ledger at
qa.a: Its original cost
qa.e: Depreciation accumulates in the provision account; the asset account is untouched.

qa.q: A machine costing ₹2,50,000 is depreciated at 10% p.a. on SLM using a provision account. What is the balance in the provision account after 3 years?
qa.e: ₹25,000 accumulates every year.

qa.q: Machinery costs ₹2,50,000 and the provision for depreciation on it is ₹75,000. How is machinery shown in the balance sheet?
qa.e: The provision is deducted from cost to show net book value.

qa.q: The depreciation account is finally closed by transfer to the
qa.a: Profit and loss account
qa.e: Depreciation is an expense of the year: Dr P&L / Cr Depreciation.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under the provision method, the balance sheet shows both the cost of the asset and depreciation to date.
Reason (R): The asset account remains at cost while depreciation accumulates in a separate account.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Keeping the two in separate accounts lets both figures be shown.

qa.q: A van costs ₹4,00,000; WDV 25% p.a.; depreciation charged to the asset account. What is the balance in the Van account at the end of year 2?
Case: A firm wants its balance sheet to show how old and how depreciated its machines are. Which recording method helps more?
qa.a: Provision for depreciation method
qa.e: Accumulated depreciation against cost shows how much of the asset's life is used up.

qa.q: A machine with a book value of ₹45,000 is sold for ₹52,000. The result is
qa.e: Sale price exceeds book value, so there is a profit of ₹7,000.

qa.q: Machinery bought 1 April 2024 for ₹1,00,000; WDV 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Sold on 30 September 2025 for ₹80,000. Loss on sale?
qa.e: BV at 31 March 2025 = ₹90,000; 6 months' depreciation ₹4,500; BV at sale ₹85,500.

qa.q: Loss on sale of a fixed asset is
qa.a: Debited to the profit and loss account
qa.e: It is a loss, so it reduces profit.

qa.q: When an asset disposal account is used, the cost of the asset sold is
qa.a: Debited to the disposal account
qa.e: Dr Asset Disposal / Cr Asset transfers the cost.

qa.q: In an asset disposal account, the sale proceeds appear on the
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: Dr Bank / Cr Asset Disposal records the proceeds.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Depreciation for the part of the year before sale must be charged.
Reason (R): The asset was used by the business during that period.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The asset earned revenue till its sale, so it bears depreciation for that time.

qa.q: A firm bought three machines of ₹1,00,000 each on 1 April 2024 and depreciates them at 10% p.a. on SLM (year ends 31 March). One machine is sold on 1 April 2025 for ₹85,000. Loss on sale?
Case: A firm bought three machines of ₹1,00,000 each on 1 April 2024 (SLM 10% p.a.) and sold one of them on 1 April 2025. What is the depreciation for 2025-26 on the two remaining machines?
qa.e: SLM on original cost: 2 × ₹1,00,000 × 10%.

qa.q: Two machines of ₹1,00,000 each were bought on 1 April 2024 and are depreciated at 20% p.a. on WDV (year ends 31 March). One machine is sold on 1 April 2025 for ₹75,000. What is the loss on sale?
qa.e: The machine sold has a book value of ₹80,000 after one year at 20% WDV; it fetched ₹75,000, so the loss is ₹5,000. The other machine is not affected.

qa.q: Machine cost ₹1,50,000; accumulated depreciation ₹60,000; sold for ₹80,000. Loss on sale?
qa.e: Book value is ₹90,000; sale price ₹80,000.

qa.q: On sale of an asset, the accumulated depreciation on it is
qa.a: Debited to Provision for Depreciation and credited to the asset (or disposal) account
qa.e: The provision relating to the asset sold is written back against it.

qa.q: Machine BV on date of fire ₹75,000; insurer admits ₹50,000. Loss by fire?
qa.e: Loss = book value − claim.

qa.q: The entry for an insurance claim admitted on an asset destroyed is
qa.a: Dr Insurance Claim / Cr Asset (or Disposal) account
qa.e: The claim is a receivable; the asset account is credited.

qa.q: Machine cost ₹3,00,000; accumulated depreciation ₹1,20,000; destroyed by fire; scrap sold ₹10,000; insurer pays ₹1,40,000. Net loss?
qa.e: BV ₹1,80,000 less scrap ₹10,000 and claim ₹1,40,000.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under the provision method, the asset account continues to show the asset at original cost until disposal.
Reason (R): Depreciation is credited to the provision account, not to the asset account.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since depreciation never touches the asset account, cost stays there until the asset leaves.

qa.q: Machine cost ₹1,00,000; accumulated depreciation ₹40,000; sold for ₹68,000. Profit on sale?
Case: In an asset disposal account, the debit side shows cost ₹2,00,000; the credit side shows provision transferred ₹1,10,000 and bank ₹70,000. What is the balancing figure (the loss on sale)?
qa.e: Credits ₹1,80,000 fall short of the debit ₹2,00,000 by ₹20,000, a loss transferred to P&L.

qa.q: A provision is
qa.a: A charge against profit for a known liability or likely loss of uncertain amount
qa.e: Provisions are charged before arriving at profit.

qa.q: Debtors ₹1,50,000; further bad debts ₹6,000; provision for doubtful debts 5%. New provision?
qa.e: Provision is calculated after deducting further bad debts.

qa.q: Bad debts ₹5,000; old provision ₹8,000; new provision ₹6,000. What is the P&L effect?
Bad debts ₹2,000; old provision ₹9,000; new provision ₹4,000. What happens?
qa.a: ₹3,000 is credited to P&L
qa.e: 2,000 + 4,000 − 9,000 = −3,000, so the excess old provision is written back.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of a provision?
qa.a: Provision for taxation
qa.e: Tax is a known liability whose exact amount is not yet settled.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): A provision for doubtful debts is created on the basis of conservatism.
Reason (R): Conservatism requires providing for all likely losses.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Prudence demands that expected losses from debtors be provided for.

qa.q: The entry to write off a bad debt of ₹4,000 due from Vinod is
qa.a: Dr Bad Debts ₹4,000 / Cr Vinod ₹4,000
qa.e: The loss is debited to Bad Debts; Vinod's account is closed by credit.

qa.q: Case: Debtors ₹3,00,000; further bad debts ₹20,000; provision 10%; bad debts in trial balance ₹8,000; old provision ₹15,000. What amount is charged to P&L?
qa.e: New provision = 10% of ₹2,80,000 = ₹28,000; bad debts total ₹28,000; less old provision ₹15,000.

qa.q: A reserve is
qa.a: An appropriation of profit
qa.e: Reserves are set aside out of profit after it is calculated.

qa.q: Which statement is true?
qa.a: A provision is made even if the business suffers a loss
qa.e: Provisions are charges that must be made regardless of profit.

qa.q: Profit before provisions ₹4,00,000; provision for taxation ₹1,20,000; transfer to general reserve 10% of profit after tax. Amount transferred to reserve?
qa.e: Profit after tax = ₹2,80,000; reserve = 10% of that.

qa.q: Provision for doubtful debts is shown in the balance sheet
qa.a: As a deduction from debtors
qa.e: It reduces the debtors to their expected realisable amount.

qa.q: The main purpose of creating a reserve is to
qa.a: Strengthen the financial position of the business
qa.e: Reserves retain profits for growth and contingencies.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Provisions reduce net profit.
Reason (R): Provisions are charged to the profit and loss account before net profit is found.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: As charges against profit, provisions lower the profit figure.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.a: Provision: charge against profit; Reserve: appropriation of profit
qa.e: This is the core difference between the two.

qa.q: Case: A firm makes a loss of ₹50,000. Can it create (a) a provision for doubtful debts and (b) a general reserve?
qa.a: (a) Yes, (b) No
qa.e: Provisions are compulsory charges even in a loss year; reserves need profits to appropriate.

qa.q: Which is a capital reserve?
qa.a: Premium received on issue of shares
qa.e: Securities premium is a capital profit, not earned from trading.

qa.q: Capital reserves are generally used to
qa.a: Write off capital losses
qa.e: Capital profits are not normally distributed; they absorb capital losses.

qa.q: A reserve created to maintain a stable rate of dividend is the
qa.a: Dividend equalisation reserve
qa.e: It is a specific revenue reserve to even out dividends over years.

qa.q: Which of these creates a secret reserve?
qa.a: Valuing stock far below its cost deliberately
qa.e: Deliberate undervaluation of assets hides profit in the books.

qa.q: Machine cost ₹5,00,000; reasonable depreciation 10% SLM, but 30% is charged in year 1. Secret reserve created?
qa.e: Excess depreciation = 30% − 10% = 20% of ₹5,00,000.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Secret reserves violate the full disclosure concept.
Reason (R): They hide the true profit and financial position from users.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Users cannot see the real position, so disclosure is not full.

qa.q: Which is an important reason for creating reserves?
qa.a: Meeting unforeseen losses and strengthening the business
qa.e: Reserves act as a cushion and support growth.

qa.q: Case: A company sets aside part of profits each year to repay debentures due after 5 years. This reserve is a
qa.a: Debenture redemption reserve (specific reserve)
qa.e: It is created for a specific stated purpose.

qa.q: A sole trader wants one statement that lists what his business owns and owes on 31 March. Which statement is it?
qa.a: Balance sheet
qa.e: The balance sheet is a statement of assets and liabilities on a date.

qa.q: The profit and loss account is prepared
qa.a: For a period, such as a year
qa.e: It summarises revenues and expenses over a period.

qa.q: Financial statements are described as the
qa.a: End product of the accounting process
qa.e: They are prepared after recording, classifying and summarising.

qa.q: A supplier selling on 60 days' credit mainly studies a firm's statements to judge its
qa.a: Short-term ability to pay
qa.e: Trade creditors care about liquidity over the credit period.

qa.q: For a sole proprietor, financial statements help him decide
qa.a: How much he can safely withdraw and whether the business is growing
qa.e: Knowing profit and position guides drawings and plans.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Financial statements are useful to both internal and external users.
Reason (R): They summarise the performance and position of the business in a standard form.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A common format makes them useful to everyone from managers to banks.

qa.q: Which pair correctly describes the two main statements of a sole trader?
qa.a: Trading and P&L account: performance for a period; Balance sheet: position on a date
qa.e: One is a period statement, the other a date statement.

qa.q: Case: The income tax department asks Mr Rao for his business accounts. Which information is it mainly checking?
qa.a: The correct taxable profit
qa.e: Tax is based on profit, which the P&L account shows.

qa.q: Which of these is capital expenditure?
qa.a: Freight paid on a new machine
qa.e: Freight to bring a fixed asset into use is part of its cost.

qa.q: Which of these is revenue expenditure?
qa.a: Repairs and maintenance of machinery
qa.e: Repairs only keep the asset working.

qa.q: A company spends ₹24 lakh on an advertisement campaign expected to benefit 4 years. How much is written off each year?
qa.e: Deferred revenue expenditure is spread over the period of benefit.

qa.q: Capital expenditure appears in
qa.a: The balance sheet as an asset
qa.e: It creates an asset of lasting benefit.

qa.q: A firm buys a machine for ₹3,00,000, pays freight ₹10,000, installation ₹20,000 and annual repairs ₹5,000. Total capital expenditure?
qa.e: Repairs are revenue; the rest is capital.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Treating capital expenditure as revenue expenditure understates profit.
Reason (R): The full amount is charged to the P&L account instead of being shown as an asset.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Charging it as an expense lowers profit and leaves the asset out of the balance sheet.

qa.q: Which feature distinguishes revenue expenditure?
qa.a: Its benefit is used up within the accounting year
qa.e: Revenue expenditure is recurring and short-lived in benefit.

qa.q: Case: A school spends ₹2,00,000 on replacing its old roof sheets with stronger ones that extend the building's life by 15 years. This is
qa.a: Capital expenditure
qa.e: It improves the asset and extends its life.

qa.q: Which of these is a revenue receipt?
qa.a: Commission received
qa.e: Commission arises from regular operations.

qa.q: Sale proceeds of an old building are a
qa.a: Capital receipt
qa.e: They arise from the sale of a fixed asset.

qa.q: Machinery with book value ₹1,20,000 is sold for ₹1,50,000. What amount is credited to the P&L account?
qa.e: Only the profit on sale goes to P&L.

qa.q: A loan of ₹5,00,000 received from SIDBI is
qa.a: A capital receipt that increases a liability
qa.e: Loans are capital receipts and are repayable.

qa.q: Treating a capital receipt as a revenue receipt will
qa.a: Overstate the profit
qa.e: Revenue receipts go to P&L; adding a capital receipt there inflates profit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Rent received from sub-letting part of the shop is a revenue receipt.
Reason (R): It is a recurring receipt in the normal course of business, not from sale of a fixed asset or borrowing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Recurring income like rent is revenue in nature.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly classified?
qa.a: Sale of goods: revenue; additional capital: capital
qa.e: Normal sales are revenue; capital introduced is a capital receipt.

qa.q: Case: During the year, a firm received: sales ₹8,00,000, interest ₹10,000, loan ₹2,00,000, sale proceeds of furniture ₹15,000 (book value ₹15,000). What are the total revenue receipts?
qa.e: Only sales and interest are revenue receipts; furniture sold at book value gives no profit.

qa.q: Which expense is debited to the trading account?
qa.a: Carriage inwards
qa.e: Carriage inwards is a direct expense of bringing goods in.

qa.q: Opening stock ₹30,000; net purchases ₹2,40,000; direct expenses ₹20,000; closing stock ₹50,000. COGS?
qa.e: COGS = OS + net purchases + direct expenses − CS.

qa.q: Net sales ₹4,00,000; COGS ₹3,20,000. Gross profit?
qa.e: GP = Net sales − COGS.

qa.q: Closing stock is shown in the trading account on the
qa.a: Credit side
qa.e: Closing stock reduces the cost of goods sold, so it is credited.

qa.q: Sales ₹6,00,000; sales returns ₹25,000; opening stock ₹50,000; purchases ₹4,00,000; purchases returns ₹15,000; wages ₹45,000; closing stock ₹70,000. Gross profit?

Assertion (A): Wages are shown on the debit side of the trading account.
Reason (R): Wages are a direct expense incurred in producing or bringing goods to a saleable state.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Direct expenses form part of the cost of goods and go to the trading account.

qa.q: If the debit side of the trading account exceeds the credit side, the difference is
qa.a: Gross loss
qa.e: Costs exceed sales value, so there is a gross loss.

qa.q: Case: Sales ₹5,00,000; gross profit is 20% of sales. What is the cost of goods sold?
qa.e: GP = ₹1,00,000; COGS = sales − GP.

qa.q: Which item appears on the credit side of the P&L account?
qa.a: Interest received
qa.e: Incomes and gains are credited.

qa.q: Gross profit ₹2,00,000; indirect expenses ₹1,30,000; other incomes ₹15,000. Net profit?
qa.e: NP = GP + other incomes − indirect expenses.

qa.q: Carriage outwards is debited to the
qa.a: Profit and loss account
qa.e: It is a selling and distribution expense, not a cost of buying goods.

qa.q: Gross profit ₹60,000; total indirect expenses ₹75,000; no other income. The result is
qa.e: Expenses exceed gross profit, so there is a net loss of ₹15,000.

qa.q: A net loss is transferred to the
qa.a: Debit side of the capital account
qa.e: Loss reduces the owner's capital.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Loss on sale of furniture is debited to the P&L account.
Reason (R): It is a loss not related to the trading of goods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Such losses are indirect and reduce net profit.

qa.q: Which is a financial expense in the P&L account?
qa.a: Interest on bank loan
qa.e: Interest relates to financing the business.

qa.q: Case: GP ₹1,50,000. Salaries ₹50,000; rent ₹24,000; depreciation ₹16,000; bad debts ₹5,000; rent received ₹12,000; discount received ₹3,000. Net profit?
qa.e: Credits ₹1,65,000; debits ₹95,000.

qa.q: The closing entry for wages is
qa.a: Dr Trading / Cr Wages
qa.e: Wages are a direct expense closed to the trading account.

qa.q: The closing entry for discount received is
qa.a: Dr Discount Received / Cr P&L
qa.e: Income accounts with credit balances are debited to close them.

qa.q: The entry for closing stock is
qa.a: Dr Closing Stock / Cr Trading
qa.e: Closing stock is brought into the books as an asset and credited to trading.

qa.q: Net loss of ₹25,000 is closed by
qa.a: Dr Capital ₹25,000 / Cr P&L ₹25,000
qa.e: A loss reduces capital.

qa.q: Which account is NOT closed by a closing entry at the year-end?
qa.a: Machinery account
qa.e: Machinery is a real (balance sheet) account carried forward.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): After closing entries, nominal accounts show no balance.
Reason (R): Their balances are transferred to the trading and P&L accounts.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Transfer empties each nominal account.

qa.q: Drawings at the year-end are closed by
qa.a: Dr Capital / Cr Drawings
qa.e: Drawings reduce capital, so they are transferred to the debit of capital.

qa.q: Case: Trading account totals: debit ₹4,20,000 and credit ₹5,10,000. What is the gross profit?
qa.e: The credit side exceeds the debit side by ₹90,000: Dr Trading / Cr P&L.

qa.q: Operating profit is calculated as
qa.a: Net profit + Non-operating expenses − Non-operating incomes
qa.e: Remove the effect of non-operating items from net profit.

qa.q: Net profit ₹2,40,000; interest on debentures ₹30,000; profit on sale of investments ₹20,000. Operating profit?
qa.e: Add back interest; deduct the profit on sale.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-operating expense?
qa.a: Loss on sale of a fixed asset
qa.e: It does not arise from normal operations.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-operating income?
qa.a: Dividend received on investments
qa.e: For a trading firm, dividends do not come from operations.

qa.q: Net profit before tax ₹5,00,000; interest on long-term loan ₹60,000. EBIT?
qa.e: EBIT adds interest back to profit before tax.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Operating profit gives a better idea of operating efficiency than net profit.
Reason (R): It excludes incomes and expenses not related to normal business operations.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Removing one-off items shows how well the core business performs.

qa.q: Net profit ₹90,000 included a profit of ₹30,000 on sale of land. Loss by theft ₹5,000 was charged. Operating profit?
qa.e: Deduct the profit on land; add back the theft loss.

qa.q: Case: Firm A and Firm B both report net profit ₹10 lakh. Firm A's profit includes ₹6 lakh gain on sale of a building. Which has the higher operating profit (no other non-operating items)?
qa.a: Firm B
qa.e: A's operating profit is ₹4 lakh; B's is ₹10 lakh.

qa.q: A balance sheet shows
qa.a: The financial position on a particular date
qa.e: It is a statement of assets, liabilities and capital on a date.

qa.q: Goodwill is classified as a
qa.a: Non-current intangible asset
qa.e: It has no physical form and benefits many years.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹2,50,000; additional capital ₹50,000; net profit ₹60,000; drawings ₹40,000. Closing capital?
qa.e: Capital + additional capital + profit − drawings.

qa.q: Which item is a current liability?
qa.a: Bills payable
qa.e: Bills payable are due within a short period.

qa.q: Which of the following does NOT appear in the balance sheet?
qa.a: Sales
qa.e: Sales is a nominal account closed to the trading account.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Closing stock appears in both the trading account and the balance sheet when given outside the trial balance.
Reason (R): An adjustment outside the trial balance is shown at two places.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Closing stock reduces COGS and is also a current asset.

qa.q: Total assets ₹6,80,000; long-term loan ₹1,50,000; creditors ₹80,000. What is the capital?
qa.e: Capital = Assets − all outside liabilities.

qa.q: Case: A trader's balance sheet shows a net loss of ₹20,000 for the year. Opening capital ₹1,50,000; drawings ₹10,000. Closing capital?
qa.e: A loss and drawings both reduce capital.

qa.q: Arranging assets and liabilities in a particular order in the balance sheet is called
qa.a: Marshalling
qa.e: Marshalling sets the order; grouping puts similar items together.

qa.q: Under the order of liquidity, the first asset shown is
qa.a: Cash in hand
qa.e: The most liquid asset comes first.

qa.q: Under the order of permanence, the first item on the liabilities side is
qa.a: Capital
qa.e: Capital is the most permanent claim.

qa.q: Showing 'Sundry debtors' and 'Bills receivable' together under 'Trade receivables' is an example of
qa.a: Grouping
qa.e: Similar items are combined under one head.

qa.q: Assets on 1 April: cash ₹15,000, debtors ₹45,000, machinery ₹1,40,000. Liabilities: creditors ₹30,000, loan ₹50,000. Capital credited in the opening entry?
qa.e: Capital = total assets − total liabilities.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): An opening entry is passed at the beginning of each accounting year.
Reason (R): It brings forward the balances of assets, liabilities and capital from the previous year's balance sheet.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Real and personal account balances continue, so the opening entry restarts them.

qa.q: From a trial balance without adjustments, which item goes only to the balance sheet?
qa.a: Creditors
qa.e: Creditors are a personal (liability) account.

qa.q: Case: From a trial balance, gross profit is ₹1,20,000, indirect expenses ₹70,000, other incomes ₹10,000; capital ₹2,00,000; drawings ₹20,000. Closing capital in the balance sheet?
qa.e: Net profit = ₹60,000; capital + profit − drawings.

qa.q: Closing stock given outside the trial balance is shown
qa.a: On the credit side of the trading account and as an asset in the balance sheet
qa.e: As an adjustment outside the trial balance, it has two effects.

qa.q: Closing stock: cost ₹1,20,000, NRV ₹1,35,000. At what value is it taken?
qa.e: Lower of cost and NRV.

qa.q: The trial balance shows 'Adjusted purchases ₹3,40,000' and 'Closing stock ₹60,000'. Closing stock will appear
qa.a: Only in the balance sheet
qa.e: Purchases are already adjusted for closing stock.

qa.q: Why are adjustments made before preparing final accounts?
qa.a: To include all incomes and expenses of the period, following accrual and matching
qa.e: Adjustments bring the accounts to the accrual basis.

qa.q: An item appearing in the trial balance is shown in the final accounts at
qa.a: One place
qa.e: Its double entry is already done in the ledger.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Closing stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower.
Reason (R): The conservatism concept requires anticipating no profit but providing for all possible losses.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Valuing at the lower figure avoids recording unrealised profit and provides for expected loss.

qa.q: Net sales ₹5,00,000; opening stock ₹60,000; purchases ₹3,50,000; closing stock (outside the trial balance) cost ₹80,000, NRV ₹70,000. Gross profit?
qa.e: Closing stock is taken at ₹70,000.

qa.q: Case: Trial balance shows adjusted purchases ₹2,80,000 and closing stock ₹40,000; sales ₹4,00,000; no opening stock or direct expenses in the trading account. Gross profit?
qa.e: Adjusted purchases already equal cost of goods sold here; closing stock is not credited again.

qa.q: Outstanding salaries are shown in the balance sheet as a
qa.a: Current liability
qa.e: They are owed to employees.

qa.q: Salaries paid ₹2,20,000; outstanding salaries ₹20,000. Amount debited to the P&L account?
qa.e: The full year's salary is charged.

qa.q: The adjusting entry for prepaid insurance is
qa.a: Dr Prepaid Insurance / Cr Insurance
qa.e: Part of the expense is moved to an asset account.

qa.q: Insurance paid ₹36,000 on 1 July 2025 for one year. Books close on 31 March 2026. Prepaid insurance?
qa.e: July to March is 9 months used; 3 months (April to June) are prepaid.

qa.q: Prepaid expenses are shown in the balance sheet as a
qa.a: Current asset
qa.e: The business is entitled to a service in the next year.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Outstanding wages are added to wages in the trading account.
Reason (R): Wages are a direct expense and outstanding amounts belong to the current year.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Wages are direct, and the unpaid part is still this year's cost.

qa.q: Rent paid ₹66,000 includes ₹6,000 for April of the next year. What rent is charged to P&L?
qa.e: Remove the prepaid portion.

qa.q: Case: Trial balance: Rent ₹44,000 (paid for 11 months). Adjustment: one month's rent outstanding. Show the P&L charge and the liability.
qa.e: Monthly rent = ₹4,000; one month outstanding.

qa.q: Accrued interest is shown in the balance sheet as a
qa.a: Current asset
qa.e: It is an amount receivable.

qa.q: Commission received ₹30,000; commission earned but not received ₹5,000. Amount credited to P&L?
qa.e: Add the accrued part.

qa.q: Rent received ₹96,000 includes ₹8,000 for the next year. Rent credited to P&L?
qa.e: The advance is not yet earned.

qa.q: Income received in advance is shown as a
qa.a: Current liability
qa.e: The firm owes the service to the payer.

qa.q: The adjusting entry for accrued commission is
qa.a: Dr Accrued Commission / Cr Commission
qa.e: An asset (receivable) is created and income increased.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Accrued income is added to the related income in the P&L account.
Reason (R): Under accrual, income earned during the year is recognised whether or not it is received.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Earned income belongs to the year, received or not.

qa.q: Investment of ₹1,50,000 at 10% p.a.; interest received ₹7,500. Accrued interest?
qa.e: Full-year interest ₹15,000 less ₹7,500 received.

qa.q: Case: A landlord received rent of ₹1,30,000 during 2025-26 at ₹10,000 per month. What adjustment is needed at year-end?
qa.a: ₹10,000 is rent received in advance (one month)
qa.e: 12 months' rent is ₹1,20,000; the extra ₹10,000 is for next year.

qa.q: Bad debts of ₹4,000 appear in the trial balance. They are shown
qa.a: Only on the debit side of the P&L account
qa.e: Debtors in the trial balance are already net of these bad debts.

qa.q: Debtors ₹2,00,000; further bad debts ₹5,000 (adjustment). Debtors in the balance sheet?
qa.e: An adjustment outside the trial balance reduces debtors.

qa.q: Plant ₹4,00,000; depreciation 15% (adjustment). What amount of depreciation is debited to the P&L account?
qa.e: Depreciation debited to P&L = 15% of ₹4,00,000 = ₹60,000; the plant then appears at ₹3,40,000 in the balance sheet, but that value is not what is asked.

qa.q: Furniture in the trial balance ₹90,000 includes ₹30,000 bought on 1 October 2025. Depreciation 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March 2026. Total depreciation?
qa.e: ₹60,000 for a full year and ₹30,000 for 6 months.

qa.q: Bad debts recovered ₹2,000 are shown
qa.a: On the credit side of the P&L account
qa.e: It is an income, since the amount was earlier written off.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Further bad debts given as an adjustment are deducted from debtors in the balance sheet.
Reason (R): An adjustment outside the trial balance has a double effect.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: One effect in P&L, the other on debtors in the balance sheet.

qa.q: Which is the correct treatment of depreciation given as an adjustment?
qa.a: Debit P&L; deduct from the asset in the balance sheet
qa.e: Depreciation is an expense and also reduces the asset.

qa.q: Case: Trial balance: Debtors ₹1,50,000; Bad debts ₹6,000. Adjustment: further bad debts ₹4,000. Total bad debts in P&L and debtors in balance sheet?
qa.a: Bad debts ₹10,000; debtors ₹1,46,000
qa.e: Add the further bad debts in P&L; reduce debtors by only the further amount.

qa.q: Debtors ₹1,60,000; further bad debts ₹10,000; PDD 4%. New PDD?
qa.e: PDD is on debtors after further bad debts.

qa.q: Bad debts (TB) ₹2,000; further bad debts ₹3,000; new PDD ₹7,000; old PDD ₹6,000. Amount debited to P&L?
qa.e: Bad debts + further + new − old.

qa.q: Bad debts ₹1,000; new PDD ₹2,000; old PDD ₹5,000. What is the P&L effect?
Debtors ₹50,000; PDD 10%; provision for discount 2%. Provision for discount?
qa.e: Discount is on debtors after PDD: 2% of ₹45,000.

qa.q: Provision for discount on debtors is calculated on
qa.a: Debtors after deducting further bad debts and provision for doubtful debts
qa.e: Only good debtors will take the discount.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Provision for discount is created only on good debtors.
Reason (R): Doubtful debtors are not expected to pay promptly and claim a cash discount.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Discount is for prompt payment, which only good debtors make.

qa.q: Debtors ₹2,00,000; further bad debts ₹8,000; PDD 5%. Net debtors in the balance sheet?
Case: Old PDD ₹4,000. Debtors ₹90,000; no further bad debts; new PDD 5%; bad debts in TB ₹500. What is the P&L effect?
Net profit before commission ₹4,40,000. Manager is entitled to 10% commission after charging such commission. Commission?
qa.e: Use Rate ÷ (100 + Rate).

qa.q: Net profit before commission ₹3,00,000. Commission 5% on net profit before charging it. Commission?
qa.e: Use Rate ÷ 100.

qa.q: Net profit before commission ₹2,10,000. Commission 5% after charging. Net profit after commission?
Outstanding manager's commission is shown as a
qa.a: Current liability
qa.e: It is owed to the manager.

qa.q: Under which basis is the manager's commission smaller, at the same rate and profit?
qa.a: After charging such commission
qa.e: The base is reduced by the commission itself.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Commission on profit after charging such commission is calculated as Profit × Rate/(100 + Rate).
Reason (R): The profit after commission plus the commission equals the profit before commission.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: If C = r% of (P − C), then C = P × r/(100 + r).

qa.q: Net profit before commission ₹6,00,000; commission 20% after charging it. Commission?
Case: Net profit before commission ₹1,65,000. The manager gets 10% after charging her commission; ₹5,000 has been paid. What outstanding commission is shown in the balance sheet?
Interest on capital is
qa.a: Debited to P&L and added to capital
qa.e: It is an expense of the business and a gain for the owner.

qa.q: Interest on drawings is
qa.a: Credited to P&L and deducted from capital
qa.e: It is an income for the business and a cost to the owner.

qa.q: Capital ₹6,00,000; interest on capital 5% p.a. Interest for the year?
Capital ₹4,00,000 on 1 April; additional capital ₹1,00,000 on 1 October. Interest 10% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Interest on capital?
qa.e: ₹40,000 on opening capital plus ₹5,000 on the addition for 6 months.

qa.q: Drawings ₹30,000 made on 1 January; interest 8% p.a.; year ends 31 March. Interest on drawings?
qa.e: Money was out for 3 months.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Charging interest on capital reduces the net profit of the business.
Reason (R): Interest on capital is debited to the profit and loss account.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: As an expense, it lowers net profit (though the owner's capital rises by the same amount).

qa.q: Opening capital ₹2,00,000; net profit (after interest) ₹50,000; interest on capital ₹10,000; drawings ₹30,000; interest on drawings ₹1,000. Closing capital?
qa.e: Add profit and interest on capital; deduct drawings and interest on drawings.

qa.q: Case: The entry for interest on drawings of ₹2,500 is
qa.a: Dr Drawings ₹2,500 / Cr Interest on Drawings ₹2,500
qa.e: Drawings (and so capital) increase; the business earns interest income.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹80,000 were destroyed by fire; the insurer admitted ₹60,000. What is debited to the P&L account?
qa.e: Only the uninsured part is a loss.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹80,000 were destroyed by fire and the insurer admitted a claim of ₹60,000. In the final accounts, the trading account is
qa.a: Credited with ₹80,000
qa.e: Goods destroyed reduce the cost of goods available for sale.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹12,000 taken by the proprietor (adjustment). Treatment?
qa.a: Deduct ₹12,000 from purchases and add to drawings
qa.e: They are no longer for sale and are a withdrawal by the owner.

qa.q: Free samples worth ₹6,000 (cost) distributed. Treatment?
qa.a: Deduct from purchases; debit advertisement in P&L
qa.e: Samples are a promotional expense.

qa.q: Credit sales of ₹15,000 were not recorded. Treatment?
qa.a: Add ₹15,000 to sales and to debtors
qa.e: Both the income and the receivable were missed.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): The full cost of goods lost by fire is credited to the trading account even when insured.
Reason (R): Those goods are no longer available for sale, whatever the amount recovered.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The trading account must reflect the cost of goods actually available for sale.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹30,000 were lost by theft and were not insured (given as an adjustment). What amount is debited to the P&L account as loss by theft?
qa.e: With no insurance, the whole cost of the goods stolen is a loss; the trading account is credited with the same ₹30,000.

qa.q: Case: Purchases ₹4,00,000. Goods withdrawn by owner ₹8,000 and free samples ₹2,000. What purchases figure goes to the trading account?
qa.e: Both reduce purchases.

qa.q: Goods costing ₹8,000 were sent to a customer on approval at a price of ₹10,000 and wrongly recorded as sales. The customer has not yet approved them at the year-end. What is the correct treatment?
qa.a: Reduce sales and debtors by ₹10,000 and add ₹8,000 to closing stock
qa.e: No sale has taken place until approval, so the wrong sale is cancelled at the sale price; the goods are still the firm's stock and are valued at cost.

qa.q: GP ₹1,80,000; salaries ₹48,000 with ₹4,000 outstanding; insurance ₹12,000 with ₹3,000 prepaid. Net profit (no other items)?
qa.e: Salaries ₹52,000 and insurance ₹9,000.

qa.q: Machinery ₹2,00,000; depreciation 15%. Debtors ₹80,000; PDD 5%. Total P&L charge for these two adjustments (no old provision)?
qa.e: Depreciation ₹30,000 + PDD ₹4,000.

qa.q: Net profit before manager's commission ₹1,32,000; commission 10% after charging. Net profit transferred to capital?
Opening capital ₹3,00,000; net profit ₹90,000; interest on capital ₹15,000; drawings ₹40,000; interest on drawings ₹2,000. Closing capital?
qa.e: Add profit and interest on capital; deduct drawings and interest on drawings.

qa.q: A balance sheet does not tally after adjustments. Which check is most useful first?
qa.a: Verify that each adjustment has been shown at two places
qa.e: Missing one effect of an adjustment is the commonest cause.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Outstanding salaries increase the P&L charge and appear as a liability.
Reason (R): Each adjustment given outside the trial balance has two effects.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The adjustment affects the expense and creates a liability.

qa.q: Rent received ₹36,000 (₹6,000 relates to next year); interest received ₹9,000 (₹3,000 more accrued). Total of these incomes credited to P&L?
qa.e: Rent ₹30,000 + interest ₹12,000.

qa.q: Case: GP ₹2,50,000. Expenses as per trial balance ₹1,20,000; outstanding expenses ₹10,000; prepaid expenses ₹5,000; depreciation ₹15,000; bad debts written off further ₹5,000; accrued income ₹4,000. Net profit?
Under incomplete records, which accounts are generally maintained?
qa.a: Cash book and personal accounts
qa.e: Small traders keep cash and debtors/creditors records.

qa.q: Which business can NOT keep its accounts on incomplete records?
qa.a: A company
qa.e: Companies must keep double entry books by law.

qa.q: Which is a feature of incomplete records?
qa.a: Lack of uniformity among different firms
qa.e: Each trader keeps records in his own way.

qa.q: Incomplete records are often called the
qa.a: Single entry system
qa.e: The term single entry refers to incomplete records.

qa.q: Why are real accounts like furniture usually missing in incomplete records?
qa.a: The trader does not maintain a complete ledger
qa.e: Only a few accounts are kept, so assets often go unrecorded.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Under incomplete records, private and business transactions may get mixed.
Reason (R): The business entity concept is not strictly followed by small traders.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without proper books, owners often pay personal expenses from business cash without recording them separately.

qa.q: Which source is often used to gather missing information under incomplete records?
qa.a: Vouchers, bank statements and the trader's memory
qa.e: The accountant pieces together data from available documents.

qa.q: Case: A sole trader keeps a cash book, a debtors' list and a creditors' list only. Can he prepare a trial balance?
qa.a: No, because nominal and real accounts are missing
qa.e: A trial balance needs all ledger balances, which are not available.

qa.q: Which is a reason why small traders keep incomplete records?
qa.a: It is simple and economical
qa.e: Simplicity and low cost are its attractions.

qa.q: Which is a limitation of incomplete records?
qa.a: Arithmetical accuracy cannot be checked through a trial balance
qa.e: Missing accounts make a trial balance impossible.

qa.q: Why is it difficult to find true profit from incomplete records?
qa.a: Nominal accounts of incomes and expenses are not maintained
qa.e: Without income and expense accounts, a P&L account cannot be drawn up directly.

qa.q: Which method of finding profit from incomplete records is in the CBSE Class 11 syllabus?
qa.a: Statement of affairs method
qa.e: Only the statement of affairs (net worth) method is prescribed.

qa.q: Tax authorities may not accept incomplete records because
qa.a: They do not give a verifiable, complete picture of income
qa.e: Tax assessment needs reliable and complete records.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Frauds are difficult to detect under incomplete records.
Reason (R): There is no complete double entry check on transactions and assets.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Without full records and cross-checks, misuse can go unnoticed.

qa.q: Which limitation makes it hard for a trader with incomplete records to get a bank loan?
qa.a: Absence of a reliable balance sheet and profit figure
qa.e: Banks need dependable financial statements to judge a borrower.

qa.q: Case: A trader says, 'I don't need complete books; I have few transactions and can't afford an accountant.' He is giving
qa.a: Reasons for keeping incomplete records
qa.e: Few transactions and low cost are typical reasons.

qa.q: A statement of affairs is prepared to find
qa.a: The capital of a business on a date
qa.e: Capital = assets − liabilities on that date.

qa.q: Assets on 1 April 2025: ₹4,20,000; liabilities ₹1,20,000. Opening capital?
qa.e: Capital is the excess of assets over liabilities.

qa.q: In a statement of affairs, capital is
qa.a: The balancing figure
qa.e: With no capital account, it is found as the difference.

qa.q: Which statement is true of a balance sheet but NOT of a statement of affairs?
qa.a: It is prepared from ledger balances under double entry
qa.e: Both show assets, liabilities and capital on a date; only the balance sheet uses complete double entry records.

qa.q: On 31 March: cash ₹25,000; bank ₹50,000; stock ₹1,00,000; debtors ₹75,000; machinery ₹1,50,000; creditors ₹80,000; bills payable ₹20,000. Closing capital?
qa.e: Assets ₹4,00,000 less liabilities ₹1,00,000.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Omissions are hard to detect in a statement of affairs.
Reason (R): Capital is the balancing figure, so any missing asset or liability simply changes the capital.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: There is no independent capital figure to check against.

qa.q: Values of assets in a statement of affairs are often
qa.a: Estimated from available information
qa.e: Without complete records, some values are estimates.

qa.q: Case: Rina's assets: shop fittings ₹40,000, stock ₹90,000, cash ₹10,000, debtors ₹30,000. She owes suppliers ₹50,000 and has a loan of ₹20,000. Her capital?
qa.e: Assets ₹1,70,000 less liabilities ₹70,000.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹1,50,000; closing capital ₹1,90,000; drawings ₹24,000; no additional capital. Profit?
qa.e: Drawings are added back to closing capital.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹3,00,000; closing capital ₹3,80,000; additional capital ₹50,000; drawings ₹20,000. Profit?
qa.e: Add drawings; deduct additional capital.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹2,00,000; closing capital ₹1,70,000; drawings ₹10,000. Result?
Closing capital ₹2,40,000; drawings ₹36,000; additional capital ₹30,000; profit ₹46,000. Opening capital?
qa.e: Opening = Closing + Drawings − Additional capital − Profit.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹1,00,000; closing capital ₹1,30,000; profit ₹45,000; no additional capital. Drawings?
qa.e: Drawings = Profit + Opening capital − Closing capital.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Drawings are added to closing capital when finding profit.
Reason (R): Drawings reduce capital but are not a business loss.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Adding them back removes their effect, so only business profit remains.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹80,000; closing capital ₹1,20,000; profit ₹25,000; drawings ₹15,000. Additional capital introduced?
qa.e: Additional capital = Closing + Drawings − Opening − Profit.

qa.q: Case: A trader's statements of affairs show capital ₹1,60,000 on 1 April and ₹2,10,000 on 31 March. He withdrew ₹2,000 per month and brought in ₹20,000 received as a gift from his father as additional capital. Profit?
qa.e: Drawings = ₹24,000 (12 × 2,000); additional capital ₹20,000.

qa.q: Profit before adjustments ₹1,00,000; interest on capital ₹12,000; interest on drawings ₹2,000. Net profit?
qa.e: Deduct interest on capital; add interest on drawings.

qa.q: In a statement of profit or loss, interest on capital is
qa.a: Deducted
qa.e: It is an expense of the business.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹2,50,000; closing capital ₹3,10,000; drawings ₹30,000; interest on capital 8% on opening capital. Net profit?
qa.e: Profit before adjustments ₹90,000; less interest ₹20,000.

qa.q: Which item is added to the profit before adjustments?
qa.a: Interest on drawings
qa.e: Interest on drawings is an income of the business.

qa.q: Profit before adjustments ₹75,000 (closing statement of affairs ignored depreciation). Depreciation on furniture ₹40,000 at 10% is now to be charged. Net profit?
qa.e: Depreciation ₹4,000 reduces profit.

qa.q:
Assertion (A): Adjustments like depreciation should preferably be made in the closing statement of affairs.
Reason (R): They change the closing values of assets and liabilities and hence the closing capital.
qa.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Applying them to closing figures gives the correct closing capital directly.

qa.q: Opening capital ₹1,80,000; additional capital ₹20,000 introduced at the start of the year; interest on capital 10% p.a. Interest on capital?
qa.e: Both amounts were in the business for the whole year.

qa.q: Case: Capital 1 April ₹1,20,000; 31 March ₹1,50,000. Drawings ₹18,000; additional capital ₹10,000. Interest on capital 5% on opening capital; interest on drawings ₹600. Net profit?
qa.e: Profit before adjustments ₹38,000; less IOC ₹6,000; add IOD ₹600.
